The “Input Description” table in the SOFiMSHA manual (Service Pack 2025-4, Build 146) functions as the master index for all finite‐element input records that SOFiMSHA will recognize when importing or exporting model data.  It appears at the beginning of chapter 3 (page 3-1) and breaks the input side of the application into nine logical blocks.  Each block corresponds to one or more record types in the SOFiSTiK input deck and is cross-referenced by page number for quick navigation.  Below is a detailed, RAG-ready description of each table entry:

1. 3.1 Nodes (page 3-1)  
   • Purpose: Defines the fundamental point entities in the model.  Each node record specifies a unique node number and its spatial coordinates (X, Y, Z).  
   • Typical usage: Creating geometric skeletons, specifying boundary attachments, coupling nodes, or interpolation points for load application.

2. 3.2 Elements (page 3-1)  
   • Purpose: Declares finite-element connectivity.  This covers truss, cable, beam, plane, solid, spring and pile elements.  
   • Fields include element ID, type code, node list, material cross-section or property references, orientation vectors if applicable.

3. 3.3 Results (page 3-2)  
   • Purpose: Sets up output requests.  Defines which results (displacements, forces, stresses, etc.) are to be written to result files.  
   • Parameters cover result set numbers, type flags, format options, and associated elements or groups.

4. 3.4 Restart (page 3-2)  
   • Purpose: Manages restart file generation and use.  Users can save intermediate analysis states or resume from a previous run.  
   • Options include file names, frequency of write-out, and load-case selection for restart.

5. 3.5 Input Records (page 3-2)  
   • Purpose: Collects “generic” or auxiliary record definitions not covered by the main categories—often housekeeping or advanced controls.  
   • Examples: comment records, macro calls, parameter definitions, or conditional directives.

6. 3.6 Hints for Transition from GENF (page 3-5)  
   • Purpose: Provides guidance for users migrating legacy GENF input files to the current SOFiMSHA syntax.  
   • Contains mapping tables, renamed fields, deprecated commands, and compatibility notes.

7. 3.7 SYST – Global System Definition (page 3-6)  
   • Purpose: Controls the global degree-of-freedom numbering, coordinate system defaults, and numerical tolerances.  
   • Key parameters: coordinate‐system identifiers, numbering order flags, precision settings.

8. 3.8 CTRL – Control of Analysis (page 3-9)  
   • Purpose: Orchestrates the overall analysis flow—load‐case sequencing, non-linear settings, convergence criteria, and solver options.  
   • Includes flags for dynamic vs. static, iterative‐ vs. direct‐solver choices, and automatic step subdivision.

9. 3.9 GRP – Group Control (page 3-12)  
   • Purpose: Defines and manipulates sets of nodes or elements for batch operations—applying loads, prescribing supports, or extracting results.  
   • Fields: group number, membership definitions (lists, ranges, Boolean operations), group attributes.

How this fits into the manual’s workflow: once the geometric entities (nodes, elements) are defined in sections 3.1–3.2, users proceed to tell the program what to compute (3.3–3.4), how to handle input and legacy data (3.5–3.6), and finally how to control and group the analysis (3.7–3.9).  By indexing each record type alongside its starting page, the table ensures that engineers can rapidly locate the exact syntax and field definitions needed to build or modify their SOFiMSHA input decks.

  • 3.29.1 SNAP (p. 3-81)

3. Navigation and scope  
 • Pages span roughly 3-12 through 3-93, covering input definitions for nearly 25 distinct element or command types.  
 • Nested subsections provide both conceptual theory (e.g. coordinate systems, support conditions) and practical hints (special properties, examples).  
 • This table drives a RAG-based ingestion by mapping each command/element name to its documentation location, enabling fine-grained retrieval.  

In summary, this table is a densely structured index of all input commands and object definitions offered by SOFiMSHA for finite-element import/export, organized by functional group and page reference to facilitate quick lookup and downstream vector-store embedding.

The “Input Description” table (chapter 3 of the SOFiMSHA Import/Export manual) is a hierarchical listing of all commands you use to build, modify and import finite‐element data. It is organized into 37 primary sections (3.1–3.37), each corresponding to a distinct input task or command group. Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. Sections 3.1–3.9  
   • These first nine subsections cover the core building blocks of a SOFiMSHA model—defining nodes, elements, materials, boundary conditions, loads and other fundamental data. (Specific command names for 3.1–3.9 aren’t shown in the excerpt, but you can expect geometry and property definitions here.)  

2. Section 3.29.3 “Examples” (page 3-82)  
   • A catch-all spot for miscellaneous commands and illustrative snippets just before the specialized tools.  

3. Section 3.30 LOFT – Lofting / Interpolation (page 3-83)  
   • Generates smooth surfaces or solids by interpolating between cross‐section profiles.  

   3.30.1 Examples (page 3-84)  
   • Sample scripts demonstrating typical LOFT workflows.  

4. Section 3.31 MIRR – Mirroring (page 3-85)  
   • Reflects nodes and elements about user-defined planes to produce symmetric geometry.  

5. Section 3.32 UMSH – Unstructured Mesh Generation (page 3-87)  
   • Automates the creation of triangular (2D) or tetrahedral (3D) meshes in arbitrary domains.  

   3.32.1 UBND – Boundary Definition for UMSH (page 3-88)  
   • Specifies edge loops or face contours that bound the meshing region.  

   3.32.2 2D Mesh Generation (page 3-88)  
   • Conditions and parameters for planar unstructured meshes.  

   3.32.3 3D Mesh Generation (page 3-89)  
   • Settings and controls for volumetric mesh creation.  

6. Section 3.33 INTF – Generation of Interfaces (page 3-91)  
   • Constructs interface elements between adjacent mesh regions or subdomains (e.g., contact zones).  

7. Section 3.34 RSET – Result Set (page 3-93)  
   • Defines how and where to collect analysis results, grouping them for post-processing.  

8. Section 3.35 EXPO – ANSI Export of Data (page 3-95)  
   • Exports model definitions and results in ANSI‐compliant formats for external tools.  

9. Section 3.36 IMPO – Import of Data (page 3-96)  
   • Reads external data sets into SOFiMSHA;  

   3.36.1 Generic Import Interface (page 3-97)  
   • A flexible routine for parsing user-defined file structures.  

10. Section 3.37 ECHO – Control of the Output (page 3-98)  
    • Adjusts verbosity levels and selects which messages or data blocks appear in the command window and output files.  

Taken together, these 37 sections provide a complete index of all pre-processing and data‐exchange commands available in SOFiMSHA’s 2025-4 build. Users refer to this table to locate the detailed syntax, parameter lists and examples for each command. Subsequent chapter 4 then describes the resulting output structures (group attributes, nodal values, element definitions, system statistics and timing), completing the full data‐flow documentation from model input through to post-processing.

Any structure, like a plane structure for example, must in general be interpreted as a geomet- rical infinitely indeterminate structure. The Finite Element method is now used to convert this infinite system to a finite one, i.e. to discretizise it.
 A discrete solution, consisting of n unknowns, is computed instead of the continuous solution. For the static analysis these unknowns are for instance the displacements of particular points, the so-called nodes. These nodes are connected to each other by means of mechanically simplified members, the so-called elements. One can obtain the displacements of the entire region through interpolation of the nodal values inside the elements. The continuous plane structure is thus represented by a large - yet finite - number of elements.
 The power of Finite Elements lies in their universal applicability to any geometrical shape and almost any loading. This is achieved by the following building block principle. Individual ele- ments, which describe parts of the structure in a computer oriented manner, are assembled into a complete structure. Regular frame structures must be understood as a special case of this principle, in which a finite number of nodes leads to an exact solution.
 The task of SOFIMSHA is to export or import the total volume of nodes and elements with high effectiveness. Generating features are on a first glance left to the CADINP possibilities, however there are very mighty options available for the generation, copying and extrusion. Complex irregular structures should be defined via SOFIMSHC or SOFiPLUS.
 Exactly one database is available for each system, to which each module has unlimited access. A system is seen as the entirety of the parts forming a structure or a substructure, which co- operate statically during the systems life-span. During the design a partial system can be analysed separately.
 With a restart one may modify boundary conditions or add new nodes and elements. Elements may be changed, however nodes and especially used nodes are not allowed to have their coordinates changed.

The image presents a simple three‐dimensional, right‐handed Cartesian coordinate system, drawn in a schematic, perspective view, and labelled as “Figure 2.1: Coordinate system.”  At the origin, three heavy lines (axes) emerge, each capped with an arrowhead that indicates its positive direction.  The axes are distinguished by labels ‘X’, ‘Y’ and ‘Z’, and by their spatial orientations:

  •  X-Axis: A solid line projects from the origin toward the upper right of the page and slightly out of the plane, terminating in an arrowhead labeled “X.”  This vector represents the first horizontal axis in the global system.  
  •  Y-Axis: Another heavy line extends from the same origin point toward the right but slightly downward and receding into the plane; it ends in an arrowhead labeled “Y.”  This line is oriented roughly 90° counterclockwise from the X-axis when viewed from above (birds-eye view), consistent with a right-handed horizontal axis designation.  
  •  Z-Axis: A vertical line drops straight down from the origin, terminating in an arrowhead at its lower end; it is labeled “Z.”  In this depiction the Z-axis points toward the observer’s feet (i.e., into or out of the page depending on the viewing convention), making it orthogonal to both the X and Y axes.

In addition to the primary axes, a fourth arrow labelled “Vₙᵧ” (rendered here as Vᵧ) appears parallel to the Y-axis but displaced to the right of the origin.  This auxiliary vector likely represents a component of displacement or force in the Y-direction—consistent with the accompanying text, which describes nodal displacements (Vᵧ), loads, and reaction forces in a global Cartesian right-handed system.

Stylistically, the diagram is minimalist: no gridlines, no scale bars, and no shading—just the axes and vector arrows sketched in bold strokes.  The viewer’s perspective is slightly elevated, allowing all three axes to be seen in a single view.  From this vantage point, the X- and Y-axes appear as diverging lines in the horizontal plane, while the Z-axis projects vertically downward.  This orientation is typical of structural analysis and finite‐element schematics where the Z-axis is often aligned with the direction of gravity.

Below the graphic, a centered caption reads:
Figure 2.1: Coordinate system

Contextually, the figure illustrates the conventions conforming to DIN 1080 for describing nodal coordinates, displacements, rotations, forces, and moments in 3D analyses.  The primary axes define the global right‐handed system, and any input in polar, cylindrical, or spherical coordinates must be transformed into these Cartesian axes.  Positive vector components (displacement, rotation, force, moment) follow the right‐hand rule: translations are positive in the direction of each axis arrow; rotations are positive when they produce a clockwise twist about the axis as seen from the arrow tip.  For torsional warping, a seventh scalar degree of freedom augments these six conventional components.  When analyzing plane structures, only the X-Y (or Y-X) plane is used, and for axisymmetric problems, the X-axis becomes the axis of rotation.

The coordinate systems and the notations conform to DIN 1080.
 The nodal coordinates, displacements and rotations as well as loads and reaction forces are described in a global cartesian right-handed system X-Y-Z. The input can also be given in polar, cylindrical or spherical coordinates, which are however transformed automatically by the program to cartesian ones. Local coordinate systems, which are described in the next section, exist for the elements as well.
 The displacements and rotations are vectors with three components along the coordinate di- rections. These components are positive when they act in the positive coordinate axis direction. Rotational components are positive if they rotate clockwise about the given axis when looking into the positive direction of the axis. The same holds for forces and moments. For warping torsion we have a seventh scalar degree of freedom for the warping.
 If the observer is looking from the birds eye view he will believe to see a right or left handed 2D coordinate system depending on the orientation of the vertical axis . We use the designation of the ”first” and the ”second” horizontal axis in the counter clock wise orientation. It is advisable in some countries to define the global coordinate system such that the Z-axis coincides with the direction of gravity. In case of plane structures only the Y-X plane is considered. For axisymmetric analysis the X-axis is the axis of rotation.
 A general 3D rotation of the coordinate system (NODE, TRAN, MATE etc.) is not a simple task and may be performed within SOFiSTiK with different methods:

The figure is a three-stage schematic illustrating how a right-handed Cartesian coordinate frame (X, Y, Z) is successively rotated by the Eulerian angles (ψ, ϑ, φ) to align with an arbitrarily inclined plane (hatched). Each subfigure shows (i) the current orientation of the three orthogonal axes, (ii) the fixed reference plane rendered with diagonal hatching, and (iii) the angle of rotation about the appropriate axis. By convention in rock mechanics these three rotations must be applied in the precise order ψ–ϑ–φ and cannot be interchanged.

1. Initial Frame and Precision Angle ψ  
• In the left-most panel the original coordinate axes are drawn bold in black: X pointing obliquely upward-right, Y pointing horizontally into the plane (not shown explicitly), and Z vertically downward.  
• The reference plane (for example, a geological bedding or fault plane) is depicted as a large quadrilateral shaded with parallel diagonal lines.  
• A curved double-headed arrow between the X-axis and the first rotated axis x′, lying in the plane, is labeled ψ. This “precision” or “meridian” angle represents a rotation of the entire coordinate system about the fixed vertical Z-axis by ψ, bringing X into x′ and Y into y′, both now lying in the plane.

2. Nutation Angle ϑ about x′  
• The middle panel (sharing the same hatched plane) shows the axes after the first rotation: x′ and y′ lie in the plane, while the new z′ axis coincides with the original Z.  
• A second curved arrow, emanating from the origin and sweeping from z′ toward z″, is labeled ϑ. This “nutation” or “tilting” angle represents a rotation about the already-rotated x′ axis. Under this tilt, the vertical axis z′ is swung out of the vertical into the plane, becoming the inclined z″.

3. Spin (Pure Rotation) φ about z″  
• In the rightmost panel the axes x′ (now coincident with x″ by construction), y′, and z″ form the intermediate tilted frame. The coordinate origin and the hatched plane remain fixed for visual continuity.  
• A final curved arrow around z″, measured between y′ and the new y″ axis in the plane, is labeled φ. This “spin” or “pure rotation” rotates the system about the inclined z″-axis by φ, aligning y′ into y″ while x″ remains along the same line as x′.

Below the three panels the caption reads:  
“Figure 2.2: The sequence of the rotations may not be interchanged!”  
This emphasizes that in the context of structural geology or rock mechanics, the order ψ (about Z), then ϑ (about x′), then φ (about z″) must be strictly followed to obtain the correct final orientation of the coordinate axes with respect to the geological plane.

This is for example a sequence of three independent rotations with the so called Eulerian angles as they are used in rock mechanics:
 • The precision or meridian angle ψ rotates the coordinate system about the vertical z-axis
 • The nutation or tilting angle ϑ rotates about the new x’-axis of the coordinate system
 • An angle of the pure rotation φ rotates about the now inclined z”-axis

Nodes are no elements in the general sense, they may be created automatically for any gen- eration of elements. There is geometric filtering avoiding to generate double nodes at a given position. If a special or multiple node numbers should be used at a selected position, it is therefore necessary to define that node before any generation takes place.
 A very important feature is a list of nodes, called a FIT within SOFIMSHA / SOFIMSHC. These lists are saved to the database and my be used as a singkle element, partly or in combination for other generations, loadings or boundary conditions. A FIT will be created for any generation of nodes along a line automatically, but it may be created also from existing nodes by a special selection. If that selection requires a combination of lists, the sequence is calculated on base of a minimum travelling path measured in number of nodes.

The truss or cable element can only carry one constant axial force. In case of a non-linear analysis, the cable element can not sustain any compression. For the local coordinate axis only the x-axis of the beam direction is available.

These elements are defined by two nodes and their straight connection, which is either the centrobaric axis or the origin of the sectional coordinate system. It is also the x-axis of the local coordinate system. The element in-between can either be prismatic or arbitrarily haunched with cross section jumps. Several elements may be combined with the same or a continuous number to a continuous beam element. In case of plane structures the direction of the z-axis is defined such that this is the main laoding direction, i.e. bending occurs only about the y- axis. In case of three-dimensional structures however, the orientation of the coordinate system should be specified explicitly.
 The cross section is defined with the program AQUA, in any parallely shifted y’-z’ coordinate system. Internal forces and moments of the beams are positive, when they act at the positive section in the positive direction.

The illustration presents a three-dimensional sketch of a prismatic beam element together with its local coordinate system and the points of application for axial force, shear force and bending moments. It is labeled “Figure 2.3: Local coordinate system of a beam.” Key features of the drawing can be described as follows:

1. Overall Geometry  
   • The beam is shown in oblique projection as a straight, rectangular‐cross‐section bar connecting two end-nodes.  
   • Each node is represented by a solid black disc: one disc at the left top corner of the beam, the other at the right top corner. These discs mark the element’s two endpoints in a finite‐element model.

2. Local Coordinate Axes  
   • A bold arrow labeled “X” runs along the longitudinal axis of the beam, pointing from left to right. This is the local x-axis (axial direction).  
   • On the right‐hand end section, the local y- and z-axes lie in the cross-sectional plane:  
     – “My” is drawn as an arrow pointing diagonally backward and downward from the section face, indicating bending moment about the local y-axis.  
     – “Mz” is a vertical downward arrow at the same section, denoting bending moment about the local z-axis.  
   • Two additional force resultants are shown at this same section:  
     – “N” is drawn as an arrow projecting outward and slightly upward from the section’s center, marking the normal (axial) force.  
     – “S” is a horizontal arrow pointing diagonally toward the viewer, marking the shear force in the plane of the cross section.

3. Special Points in the Cross Section  
   • Two red dots highlight important cross-sectional points:  
     – On the left portion of the beam a red dot sits near mid-height inside the section; vertical arrows labeled “Y′s” (slanted arrow to the left) and “Z′s” (vertical arrow down) emanate from it. These indicate the local shear-center axes Y′s and Z′s.  
     – On the right end cross section, another red dot marks the location where the shear force “S” is applied (i.e., the shear center).  

4. Relation to Global Coordinates (Context from SOFiSTiK)  
   • Although the diagram itself concerns a beam, the same conventions of local versus global axes apply: in planar systems the beam’s local coordinate system (X, Y′s, Z′s) coincides with the global system unless otherwise specified.  
   • The local z-axis (here vertical Mz and downward Z′s) is perpendicular to the beam’s midplane.  
   • The local x-axis is aligned with the beam’s axis in such a way that its projection onto the global XY-plane does not exceed 90° from the global X-axis.  
   • Moments m-xx, m-yy, shear forces Q-xy etc., in plate or beam elements follow the same sign and location conventions: positive bending moments cause tension on the opposite (bottom) side of the section, and the index notation refers to the plane in which the force or moment acts, not to the actual direction vector.

Altogether, the figure clarifies how axial force (N), shear (S), bending moments about y (My) and z (Mz), and the local axes (X, Y′s, Z′s) are positioned and sign-conventioned for a beam element in a structural finite-element context.

The figure presents two schematic views of a single four-sided (“quad”) plate element, each drawn as a slightly elevated, rectangular block. Both views share the same local coordinate axes (x to the right, y toward the viewer’s left) and illustrate how internal forces and bending moments are resolved in the element’s own plane and across its thickness.

Left sub-figure (“Forces and Moments of plates”):

- The plate is shown in an isometric projection, with its top face slanted away.  
- A local x-axis arrow emerges horizontally from the right face; a local y-axis arrow points horizontally from the left rear edge.  
- On the front right edge of the bottom face, two opposing arrows along that edge denote the bending moment m-xx, labeled “mxx.” These arrows lie in the plane of the plate, parallel to the x-axis, indicating plate bending about the y-axis.  
- On the left back edge, two arrows along that edge are labeled “m-yy” and lie parallel to the y-axis; they denote bending about the x-axis.  
- On both the front left and back right edges, short paired arrows angled at 45 degrees to each edge are labeled “m-xy.” These represent twisting or torsional moments coupling the x– and y–directions.  
- Two vertical arrows below the bottom face—one beneath the front edge labeled “v-x,” the other beneath the side labeled “v-y”—represent the transverse shear resultants in the x and y directions, respectively, acting through the element thickness.

Right sub-figure:

- A similar isometric plate block with local axes in the same orientation.  
- Instead of bending and shear resultants, this view shows in-plane normal force resultants.  
- On the front right edge of the bottom face, a horizontal arrow pointing outward is labeled “n-x,” indicating axial force in the x-direction.  
- On the left rear edge, a horizontal arrow pointing outward is labeled “n-y,” indicating axial force in the y-direction.

Contextual details (from SOFiSTiK plate theory):

- These illustrations tie into the element’s local coordinate system: the z-axis (not drawn) is taken perpendicular to the plate midplane, defined by the vector product of node diagonals (3–1) × (2–4). When nodes are numbered counter-clockwise, the positive z-direction points “up.”  
- Positive bending moments mxx and myy produce tension on the bottom fibers opposite the moment’s orientation (per Reissner–Mindlin plate theory with discrete Kirchhoff conditions).  
- The in-plane axes x and y lie in the element plane, with their sign conventions most significant for shear and axial load results. By default, the local x-axis is chosen within 90° of the global X-axis projection, unless otherwise user-specified.

Together, these two views succinctly demonstrate how a general four-node quadrilateral plate element resolves its internal bending moments, shear forces, and in-plane normal forces within its own local coordinate framework.

The dashed diagonals establish the normal direction, the in-plane X and Y set up membrane/shear and bending directions, and the small global triad underscores the default alignment when modelling planar systems.

The plane element of SOFiSTiK is a general quadrilateral element with four nodes (QUAD), which can degenerate to a triangle. The structural behavior is modeled with separate plane elements for membrane shear and plate bending. As the hyperbolic geometry of a quadrilateral element is accounted for a coupling of both effects, this element may describe curved shells with sufficient precision. A triangular element is not suited for that purpose!
 The sixth degree of freedom, the rotation within the plane of the membrane part is accounted for by different methods:
 - Small artificial stiffness to avoid numerical problems
 Internal constraint from the differences of the displacements (ASE)
 - Variational approach according Hughes with a rotational field (DYNA)
 The plate bending properies are avaluated according to the Reissner-Mindlin theory. Due to the usage of discrete Kirchhoff conditions and an optional penalty term for the shear deformation, it is applicable for thin plates or shells The simplest implementation is equivalent to the Bathe- Dvorkin element. A significantly improved accuracy is achieved through non-conforming or "‘assumed strains"’ formulations. Especially the constant bending properties of a rectangular single element do match those of a beam element. Thus the implementation of higher order isoparametric elements with six to nine nodes is not necessary.
 There is always a local coordinate system for internal forces and loads. Note that the indexes of the designation used for moments and shear forces, rather describe their position and not their direction. Thus a plate moment m-xx corresponds to a moment vector MY.
 For planar systems, the default of the local coordinate system is equal to the global coordinate system. The local coordinates may be defined as follows:
 The local z-axis is perpendicular to the midplane of the element and it is defined by the vec- tor product of the node diagonals (3-1) x (2-4). If one numbers the element nodes counter- clockwise, then one looks into the positive z-direction from ”above”. Positive moments cause tension on the opposite bottom side of the plate.

The local z-axis is perpendicular to the midplane of the element and it is defined by the vec- tor product of the node diagonals (3-1) x (2-4). If one numbers the element nodes counter- clockwise, then one looks into the positive z-direction from ”above”. Positive moments cause tension on the opposite bottom side of the plate..
 The local x- and y-axes both lie within the element’s plane. The sign of the x- and y-axes is only meaningful for loadings or the results of shear forces.
 The local x-axis can be oriented, upon request, inside the surface of an element with a slight deviation with respect to the positive or negative direction of any of the three global coordinate axes.
 If no such request is made, the local x-axis will lie in the element’s plane parallel to the global X-Y plane, such that the angle of the projection on the X-Y plane and the global X-axis will not be larger than 90 degrees.

The solid element of SOFiSTiK is a general six-sided element with eight nodes (BRIC), which can degenerate down to a tetrahedron. As a rule, a significantly improved accuracy is achieved through non-conforming formulations, so that the introduction of the 21-noded elements is not necessary.
 The element does not possess a local coordinate system of its own, and stresses are always output for their global components. The surfaces can be described by special QUAD-elements, which can also be employed for the display of stresses in the BRIC-elements.

Elastic elements with general properties are available in several variants:
 - Anisotropic spring element with non-linear effects between two nodes or as a support condition (SPRI)
 - Generalised stiffness with up to six nodes (FLEX)
 - Elastic foundation along a line with a boundary element (BOUN) Plane foundation for quadrilateral elements (QUAD) in the local z-direction and/or tangential

The partitioning of a mesh is based on two requirements. On the one hand the mesh should be as fine as possible, so as to obtain the most accurate results. The factors opposing that are:
 - The computing times increase by n2, when the number of elements n are increased.
 - In case of very fine partitioning, round-off errors are amplified so that the solution may become unusable. As a rule of thumb, a logical partitioning of a free span consists of 5 up to 20 elements.
 - In construction practice it is not sensible to attempt to model and design all types of singularities. One should strive for a partitioning that is not too fine.

The image (Figure 2.6 “Nodal loads”) is laid out in two major rows—one for a coarse three-node mesh, one for a refined six-node mesh—and in each row shows three loading cases (uniform, two-point, single-point) first as distributed‐or‐point arrows on a bar, then as equivalent nodal loads on discrete nodes.

Coarse‐mesh row (top half of the figure):

1. Uniform load  
   - Left: A single horizontal bar bearing a dense string of downward arrows (the classical continuous distributed load).  
   - Directly below: The same bar now carries only two downward arrows, located at its two end‐nodes—these are the equivalent nodal forces obtained by lumping the continuous load into the two end nodes of the coarse mesh.  
   - Below that: The same bar again, now with one arrow at its central node, illustrating the case where the uniform load has been lumped into the single middle node only.

2. Equivalent nodal representation  
   - To the right of each of the three bars, there is a simplified schematic: a straight line with open circles marking the mesh nodes, and downward arrows at those circles corresponding exactly to the bars’ arrow configuration.  
     • First schematic: open circles at end and middle, each with an arrow (the uniformly lumped case).  
     • Second schematic: arrows only at the two outer circles.  
     • Third schematic: arrow only at the center circle.

Refined‐mesh row (bottom half of the figure):

1. Uniform load on refined mesh  
   - Left: A horizontal bar with a denser string of downward arrows (same continuous distributed load, now applied over more, smaller elements).  
   - Below: Equivalent nodal loads on the refined mesh’s end nodes (still two arrows, but their magnitudes are different because of the finer subdivision).  
   - Below that: A single arrow on the refined mesh’s central node.

2. Equivalent nodal representation for refined mesh  
   - Again, to the right of each bar is the corresponding node‐and‐arrow schematic (open circles for the six nodes, arrows only on those circles that carry nonzero nodal forces).

What this juxtaposition makes clear:

- A true point load applied at a node (cases 2 and 3 in each row) remains exactly the same when the mesh is refined.  
- A uniform (distributed) load, when converted into equivalent nodal forces, changes its per-node values as the mesh is refined: the finer the mesh, the more nodes share the load, and the numerical magnitude at each node evolves accordingly.

Thus the figure illustrates the critical distinction between “point loads” (constant under mesh refinement when applied directly at a node) and “nodal loads” derived from converting distributed loads (which do depend on element size and mesh density).

The Finite-Element system is a discrete system and it can thus only handle discrete loads. Every loading must therefore be converted to so-called nodal loads. A nodal load should not be confused with a point load. The difference is illustrated in the following figure
 A mesh refinement leads to new nodal loads in case of a uniform load (a and d), but not in case of point loads.
 On one hand, this means that a given mesh has a limited resolution for loadings. The coarser mesh (a, b, c) can not make the differentiation between two point loads and a uniform load upon the element grid or a point load at the middle of the element.
 It also means on the other hand, that a loading can be applied as a point load on a node only when its load induction area is smaller than the size of the adjacent elements. When inducing , for example, a point load upon a plate, each new mesh refinement in the area of the load will compute larger shear forces each time, due to the better modelling of the singularity. Therefore, one should either select an element size that will not be smaller than the plate thickness, or define the loads in the form of distributed loading with their actual contact surfaces.

To a large extent an exact description of the geometry is possible in the case of beam elements. A single beam element may be used from one support to the next. However, a typical FE partitioning of the geometry is necessary in the following cases:
 - Kinematic constraint with elastic foundation (Boundary element)
 - Dynamic analyses (nodal masses)
 - Buckled centrobaric axis (e.g. haunches)
 - Large deformations according to 3rd order theory
 The partitioning may only become so fine, that the lengths of the individual beams are approx- imately the same as their cross section dimensions. When their lengths become smaller than these dimensions, it is required that the correct shear deformation areas of the cross sections are defined. Artificially large stiffnesses must also be avoided, as well as the direct combination of elements with very different lengths.
 The results of the element can be obtained at all of its sections. Superpositioning and dimen- sioning can only take place at these sections.

The image is a two-part schematic (labelled “Figure 2.7: Conversion of triangular mesh to quadrilateral mesh”) showing, side by side, a single triangular element and its equivalent quadrilateral partition. Both subfigures share the same outer shape: an upright triangle with a straight, horizontal base and two equal-length sides meeting at a single apex at the top.

Left subfigure (“before”):  
• A simple, unpartitioned triangle.  
• Three straight edges: one horizontal bottom edge and two equal-length sloping edges rising to a single top vertex.  
• No interior nodes or subdivision lines; the triangle is shown as one finite element.

Right subfigure (“after”):  
• The same outer triangle is retained.  
• Three new nodes are introduced—one along the midpoint of each side of the outer triangle—and a single interior node is placed roughly in the geometric center of the triangle.  
• Straight-line segments connect the interior node to each of the three mid-side nodes.  
• These connections divide the original triangle into three four-sided (quadrilateral) subelements. Each quadrilateral is bounded by:  
  – One original side segment of the large triangle,  
  – Two new line segments running from a midpoint node to the central node,  
  – A short portion of an adjacent original side, or the remainder of that side between its midpoint and a vertex.  
• All newly formed elements are convex (no re-entrant corners), and each contains exactly four edges and four vertices.

Beneath the two diagrams runs the caption:  
“Figure 2.7: Conversion of triangular mesh to quadrilateral mesh.”

This illustration demonstrates how any pure triangular finite element can be transformed into an all-quadrilateral mesh by inserting a single interior node and linking it to the midpoints of the triangle’s edges. It ensures that each element in the resulting mesh has the preferred quadrilateral shape—allowing for more internal stress states (six) than triangular elements (one)—while maintaining convexity and avoiding re-entrant corners.

The image shows a two‐dimensional finite‐element mesh covering exactly one quarter of a circular plate (a 90° “slice” bounded by two straight edges meeting at a right angle and by a curved outer edge). All of the elements in the mesh are four‐sided quadrilaterals—no triangles appear—though their shapes are slightly distorted in order to follow the curvature of the outer boundary. The partitioning exhibits the following key features:

1. Overall Geometry  
   • Domain: a quarter of a disk (plate) with two perpendicular, straight edges meeting at the lower‐left corner and an arc forming the convex, curved outer boundary.  
   • Straight edges correspond to supports or symmetry lines; the curved edge follows the plate’s circular perimeter.

2. Element Layout  
   • Concentric “rings” of elements radiate outward from the plate’s center (bottom‐left corner), with each ring subdivided into roughly the same number of elements, producing curved layers of quadrilaterals that approximate circular arcs.  
   • Radial “spokes” (mesh lines) emanate from the plate corner and subdivide each concentric ring into wedge‐shaped strips. These spokes are slightly curved or angled such that the quadrilateral elements along the curved boundary remain reasonably regular (no re‐entrant corners).

3. Element Shape and Quality  
   • Each element has four edges and four nodes. Internal angles vary but remain convex, ensuring that no element has indentations or negative Jacobians.  
   • Moving from the inner corner toward the curved boundary, elements gradually change in size and shape: inner elements are more nearly square, while outer elements stretch slightly to accommodate curvature.  
   • The mesh does not contain any triangular elements; by design it avoids mixed or pure triangular partitions in favor of quadrilaterals, which can capture multiple internal stress states (at least six) versus only one in triangles.

4. Refinement and Approximation  
   • The elements near the outer arc are smaller and more numerous to better approximate the circular shape and to capture higher stress gradients that typically occur near free edges or load application regions.  
   • The straight edges at the bottom and left are meshed more coarsely, reflecting the lower expected stress variation in those directions (assuming symmetry or simple support conditions).

5. Intended Use of Nodal and Gauss‐Point Values  
   • Although not shown graphically, each quadrilateral element supports evaluation of stresses or moments at (a) the element center, (b) standard Gauss integration points inside the element, and (c) extrapolated averages at its four corner nodes.  
   • The element‐center values would be used for design checks (e.g. required reinforcement), the Gauss‐point values for internal stress‐state fidelity, and the nodal averages for smooth graphical output and error‐indicator calculations.

6. Caption and Figure Reference  
   • The figure is labeled “Figure 2.8: Partitioning of a quarter‐plate.” It illustrates one possible method of converting an arbitrary triangular partition (not shown) into a pure quadrilateral mesh, here applied to a circular plate segment.

Overall, the drawing highlights a practical quadrilateral finite‐element partition that respects curvature without introducing triangular elements, maintains convexity of each element, and provides a basis for accurate stress analysis and design in plate‐bending or planestress problems.

For the geometry, squares and equilateral triangles are the optimal shape. Certain devia- tions from this shape are allowed, as long as no re-entrant corners appear. Two triangles are not equivalent to a quadrilateral, since the quadrilateral possesses at least six internal stress states whereas the triangle only one. Quadrilateral meshes are therefore always preferable to mixed or pure triangular meshes. Any triangular element partition can be converted to a pure quadrilateral mesh:
 This method can for example also be used to easily partition a circular plate with quadrilateral elements:
 The results for this element are obtained at the following points:
 - At the centre of the element
 - At the so-called Gauss-points inside the element
 - As extrapolated average values at the nodes
 The values at the element’s centre point must be used for the dimensioning of the element. The so computed value of the required reinforcement must then be applied to the entire area of the element. Through proper selection of the element size and location, one can carry out direct calculations conforming to the various design rules. In case of wide supports or restraints it is for example sensible to place the centre of the element on the edge of the support.
 The Gauss-points are only necessary for the accurate capture of the element’s stress state and are usually not needed by the user.
 The values at the element nodes can be extrapolated from the Gauss-points. Due to the ap- proximate formulation of the FEM-solution these values are not identical at a node, therefore the average value is computed. These values are of prime importance for the graphical rep- resentations. However in case of coarse element partitioning, the nodes at fixed edges or point supports should also be considered during the design, because otherwise the maximum values are not captured.
 Special care should be taken for three-dimensional structures or load application regions in order to avoid the averaging of all the internal forces and moments at the nodes. In case of sudden changes in the element thickness the dimensioning should be made separately on each side.

Whatever was said for the QUAD-elements essentially holds for the solid elements as well.

For the simplest case the boundary conditions at the nodes are specified by suppressing the corresponding degrees of freedom. An elastic support is obtained by means of appropriate elements.
 There is however a frequent need for special support conditions, which the engineer would like to model using infinitely large stiffnesses. Due to numerical reasons the modelling should not be done with elements possessing very large stiffnesses, but with dependent degrees of freedom (kinematic constraints) instead. The need for such constraints arises e.g. for oblique supports or rigidly connected nodes. In general, every dependent degree of freedom can be expressed as a linear combination of other displacements or rotations:
 d = 1d1 + 2d2 + ...
 (2.6)
 These conditions are explicitly considered in the assembly of the global stiffness matrix and they are therefore numerically stable instead of any artificially rigid elements.
 These combinations can be directly formulated with the record KINE and they can be arbi- trarily convoluted. However, the memory requirements for solving a problem increase with the number of constraints and especially with the number of recursive associations.
 Coupling conditions have a distinct direction, they can be defined recursively up to 99 levels. Cyclic references or overlapping reference definitions are not possible however. When defining the boundary conditions multiple definitions will be combined in general based on a vector approach.
 Standard conditions are available for the most frequent cases of constraints in the record NODE and the node coupling conditions.
 In the node output dependent degrees of freedom are designated by a * or a negative equation number. All displacements are always output, and they comply to the specified dependencies. With ECHO REAC (program ASE, SEPP, TALPA ...) the support reactions can either be calcu- lated separately for each node or in pairs for coupled nodes; in the latter case they represent the forces transmitted through the kinematic constraint.
 Attention: Inappropriate use of kinematic constraints of the KINE type or the slave kinematic constraints (KPX through KPZ) may lead to mechanically absurd results (forces moved by kinematic constraints may violate the moment equilibrium).

A skewed support for a node can be always described by a single direction. The node is then either only supported in that direction (PR or MR) or it is supported in all directions transvers to that direction (PT or MT) . The latter case then allows a displacement only in that selected direction.

All couplings between distant nodes will generate rigid body contributions which are needed to fulfill the equilibrium of moments. The kinematic constraints KP, KL, KQ and KF describe rigid bodies to which the dependent nodes are connected through a hinge (KP), or through a connection with fixed rotation about one (KQ=KP+KMR), two (KL=KP+KMT) or all three (KF) directions. One single plane may be activated in special cases (KPEX, KPEY, KPEZ and KFEX, KFEY, KFEZ). This is for instance the case when defining a slab, which allows lateral bending but not in-plane distortion.

Symmetry conditions are a rarely needed special case of kinematic constraints. Whereby the respective symmetry or anti-symmetry conditions are assigned to the mid-perpendicular of the line connecting two nodes. In most cases the definition of a symmetry condition is more sensi- ble by means of an inclined support. The direction of the support must then be perpendicular to the symmetry plane. PRMT defines a symmetry and PTMR an anti-symmetry.

Eccentric connections, e.g. between a beam and a plate, can be specified with KF. Beam elements may have explicit excentricities or implicit by the definition of the sectional coordinate system. For shell elements the mid surface or the upper or lower side may be positioned in the plane of the nodes.

A special class of kinematic constraints imposes the same displacements or rotations to several nodes (KPX to KMT). Their application is useful e.g. in the description of rigid foundation plates, which are not allowed to rotate. These kinematic constraints act upon particular degrees of freedom and are thus more flexible. The danger on the other hand is that their inappropriate use can produce undesired offset moments.

The formulation of the boundary conditions of plate elements is not uncritical. Especially the Mindlin-element has some peculiarities which should be considered.
 According to Kirchhoff’s theory two internal forces exist at an edge, namely the bending mo- ment and the equivalent shear force. The latter consists of the shear force and the torsional moment, and that is why both can have values along a free edge different from zero. By contrast, Mindlin’s theory recognises three support conditions for the three internal forces i.e. bending moment, torsional moment and shear force. A support for the torsional moment would for example suppress the rotations perpendicular to the edge.
 Free edges do not have constraints of any type. The reaction forces along such edges are, within the bounds of computing accuracy, zero. However the internal forces inside the elements are not always exactly zero, due to the numerical method.
 Perfectly fixed edges can be input without any problems. For the interpretation of the results
 however, it is important to know that the torsional reaction moments must be taken up. This takes place automatically in the output of the BOUN-elements, whereby these are converted to corresponding support loadings.
 Here one has a choice between the so-called soft support (only PZ) and the hard support (PZ+MT). In case of the soft support, shear deformations are still allowed along the edge, and thus a shear force too; in some cases this can lead to considerable deviations from Kirchhoff’s plate theory. On the other hand is the soft support more suitable for the manipulation of uplifting corners as well as of re-entrant corners. Particularly in the case of obtuse corners, the hard support leads to an undesired fixation.
 There are generally four ways to describe such supports:
 • Point- or line-support
 This type of support is mainly used for thin supports (width < plate thickness). The size of the adjacent elements should be selected in such a way that their gravity centre lies on the round section which is critical for the punch-through check. The dimensioning of the shear force takes place inside the element; for the moment, on the safe side, in the nodes of the support.

This type of support is mainly used for thin supports (width < plate thickness). The size of the adjacent elements should be selected in such a way that their gravity centre lies on the round section which is critical for the punch-through check. The dimensioning of the shear force takes place inside the element; for the moment, on the safe side, in the nodes of the support..
 • Pivoting column head support
 The column is described by a node having a fixed support and a possible rotational spring stiffness, this node is usually is not an element node. The column area is described by means of a single element as well as coupling conditions between the four element nodes and the column node, which specifies that the cross section will remain plane without a restraint of the moment (KP for columns, KQ for walls). The size of the element can be between 2/3 of the column area (e.g. for circular columns) and the actual column area (e.g. for rectangular column cross section). The size also depends on where one wants to arrange the resultant of the bearing stress.
 The central element has a zero shear force and thus a uniform moment corresponding to the moment of the section along the face of the column. One should arrange additional elements for the shear force check, whereby their gravity centre lies on the round section used for that check , or directly carry out a punch-through check.
 • Elastic foundation
 This option is ideal for elastic supports of large areas, for which a rounded moment above the support is desired. Large Winkler coefficients however, result in undesired restraints. The selection of the Winkler coefficient is thus critical, and this option should only be applied to minor foundations.
 • Special conditions
 In principle any arbitrary conditions can be formulated through kinematic constraints. The effect though must be checked in every case.

The modelling of joists in plate structures presents a special problem. Besides the option of modelling them with folded structure elements or solid elements, which are ruled out for
 practical processing, one has a choice between two other options:
 • The joist is modelled as an eccentric beam connected to a plane shell (plate- and disk action). The area of the joist and its moment of inertia are determined from the protruding part of the joist.
 For the dimensioning the results of the shell and the beam should be combined into the total internal forces and moments for a T-beam.
 This is a general method and always correct. It captures the effective widths and their distribution in the system.
 • The joist is modelled as an additional element to a plate, by defining all its cross sectional values (area, moment of inertia) as follows:
 Additional values = Total values of T-beam effective
 - contributions of the plate to the effective width
 The total stiffness is correctly modelled in this manner. When dimensioning joists with small heights one should always make constructive decisions, e.g. assembling the individual values and applying them to a T-beam cross section.

The table defines recommended upper bounds for key finite-element (FE) preprocessing identifiers and grouping structures. These limits serve two main purposes: (1) ensure that node and element labels remain within the printable field widths typically available in FORTRAN-style or fixed-column output (seven columns), and (2) avoid addressing or indexing overflow in data structures while still providing ample range for realistic models.

Summary of Table Entries and Context  

1. Largest node number  
   • Recommended maximum: 9 999 999  
   • Theoretical maximum: up to 999 999 999 (nine digits), but print-field constraints usually limit labeling to seven digits.  
   • Purpose: Each FE node (corner, mid-side, etc.) is assigned a unique integer. Staying below 10 million guarantees that the node index can be formatted in standard seven-character fields without truncation or overflow.

2. Largest element number  
   • Recommended maximum: 9 999 999  
   • Theoretical maximum: up to 999 999 999  
   • Purpose: As with nodes, each finite element (bar, shell, solid) requires a unique ID. Adhering to the seven-column guideline ensures that output listings and solver input decks remain aligned and human-readable.

3. Numbers of primary groups  
   • Range: 0 – 999  
   • Purpose: FE models often group elements into “primary groups” for material assignment, load sets, or submodeling. Limiting the count to three digits preserves column formatting and simplifies lookups in group tables.

4. Number of elements per group  
   • Recommended maximum: 999 999 (six digits)  
   • Purpose: Within any single group, the maximum number of elements should not exceed one million. This cap ensures that group-to-element mappings (which may be stored or printed in limited-width arrays) do not overflow their storage fields.

Additional Considerations  

• Print-Column Limitations  
  – Standard legacy output routines often allocate exactly seven character positions for an integer index. Exceeding 9 999 999 either forces a wider field (breaking established formats) or leads to truncated/garbled labels.  

• Indexing and Memory  
  – While modern systems support integers up to 2^31–1 or beyond, imposing a 10 million ceiling avoids large sparse index arrays that waste memory or incur performance penalties during fill and access operations.  

• Numerical Precision  
  – Typical single-precision floats (32-bit) offer about seven significant decimal digits; double precision (64-bit) yields around 15 digits.  
  – In most FE analyses, absolute displacements are less important than relative differences (strains, deflections between neighboring nodes). Attempting to resolve beyond the solver’s inherent precision (e.g. the 7th decimal in single precision) is futile—round-off and cancellation errors will dominate.  

• Sensitivity to Model Variations  
  – FE results can be highly sensitive to abrupt stiffness changes, minute element-size disparities, or long chains of elements between supports.  
  – Keeping element counts and numbering schemes within the recommended bounds helps maintain numerical stability, prevents inadvertent index wrap-around, and ensures that solver printouts and postprocessing remain consistent.

The following limits can not or should not be exceeded in principle to prevent limitations for the print out (number of columns) or the adressing of input data:
 9 999 999 (recommended)
 9 999 999 (recommended)
 The node and element numbers are possible up to 999 999 999, but for the printout there are in most cases only seven columns available.
 Each computer has a finite computing precision. This is normally 7 digits in case of 32 bits per word, and 15 digits in case of double precision. It is naturally meaningless to want to discuss about the 7. decimal digit of a final result. The danger however is that for FE-analyses, as in most cases in real life, it is not the absolute size of a displacement that is of interest, but the differences.
 Because of that, all numerical calculations are sensitive to large variations in stiffnesses or small variations of element dimensions, and sometimes with a large number of elements be- tween two boundary conditions (supports).

The program SOFiMSHA generates the basic structural system for plane or three-dimensional structures. On one hand the system consists of the nodes, defined by a number, their coordi- nates and geometric support conditions. On the other hand there are the elements, which are connected to each other at these nodes.
 For a restart of the system element properties or boundary conditions may be changed, ele- ments may be deleted or added. Only the coordinates of any existing node may not be changed any more. The orientation of the gravity, the group divisor or any defined base number of a group may not be changed either. Thus all elements added to existing groups must fit in the assigned space of numbers.
 SOFiMSHA has a more element based input mode than its predecessor GENF. Nodes will be generated mostly automatically. Nearly all elements have a mesh generation option. The basic concept is either a regular subdivision or a non-regular nodal sequence called a FIT. For more details see NODE.
 Cross sections and materials have to be defined beforehand with the program AQUA.

Nodes are assigned with a number for identification. For generation facilities new nodes will be automatically introduced or existing nodes identified with an effective octree search. Node numbers need not be in a consecutive order. The maximum value of these numbers is limited to 999999, due to the output format. The node numbering has normally no influence on the band width of the system of equations, because subsequent to the system’s generation an optimisation of the profile takes place. Undefined nodes do not have any influence.
 With nearly all element definitions it is possible to insert intermediate nodes automatically. This has either to be defined with the number of subdivision segments and an optional mid node, or a already defined sequence of nodes (FIT) may be used. In both cases new nodes will be compared against already existing ones and created only if necessary.

Elements are also identified by an arbitrary number within the selected element group. If the number is not specified, the element number is automatically assigned. Although an element number may only be used once for each element type. Elements can only be defined once.
 The element number contains the group number. The latter is for example the integer part of the element number divided by a freely defined divisor. The default value of this divisor GDIV of the record SYST is 0, i.e. all elements are assigned to group 0. If the elements are subdivided into groups with a different value for GDIV, any elements of the group 0 that follow a group initiation with the record GRP are assigned to that group by their element number, i.e. the program changes the element numbers so that they fit into the active group.
 Groups can be used to select a particular structural system or to define partial regions for post- processing or graphical representation. A sensible partitioning of a structure into such groups can be very helpful when evaluating the internal forces and moments at nodes. In case of
 folded structures, one should arrange the elements of each disk into separate groups.
 It is advantageous to number the elements in such a way, so that one can make use of the generation options during the system selection (groups) and the loading input (refer to STAR2, beam groups).
 The theoretical principals of the elements are described in the calculation programs.

The created structure is stored in the database (project file) and it can be represented graph- ically by the program WinGRAF; this can even be done for faulty systems, as long as the pro- gram has not terminated prematurely. Further processing of the analysis with other programs is only possible when the structure is free of errors.
 When no errors are detected, a profile optimisation is performed on the stiffness matrix, in order to minimise the cost of solving the system of equations for the structure.

At any time boundary conditions can be modified or new elements may be added with a Restart. However, existing elements and nodal coordinates remain unchanged. A restart takes place with the explicit input SYST REST. The following can be included in a Restart input:
 - Change support conditions and constraints for existing nodes
 - Add New nodes and new elements
 - Change element properties
 - Delete Elements

The fragment shown is taken from the CADINP “Basics” manual (SOFiSTiK) and forms part of a multi-page table that exhaustively lists all the “record items” (i.e. keyword fields) available in CADINP input records.  In RAG-vector terms, this table is a catalog of the atomic input-field identifiers you will find in any CADINP data file.  Below is a structured description of its contents and purpose:

1. Context and Units  
  • CADINP input uses three unit-categories for any numeric field:  
    – mm (fixed unit): every value is interpreted in millimetres, no override.  
    – [mm] (explicit unit): default = mm, but may be overridden by specifying a different length unit in square brackets (e.g. 2.5[m]).  
    – [mm]1011 (implicit unit): semantically tagged (by code 1011, etc.) to cover specialized length measures (geodetic elevation, section thickness, etc.). These use a default length unit defined by the active code-specific unit set (here Norm Unit 5 = Eurocodes).  

2. Table Structure  
  • Two principal columns:  
    – Record: name of a CADINP record type.  
    – Items: the list of keyword fields (“record items”) that that record type will accept.  
  • The table scrolls across multiple pages; only a subset is visible in the screenshot.  

3. Visible Item Groups (alphabetical slice)  
  A. Geometry, Grouping and Fixities  
    • SYST – system designation  
    • TYPE – classification code  
    • GDIV, GDIR – group division and direction  
    • FIX – fixed‐end / boundary specification  
    • XREF, YREF, ZREF – reference‐point coordinates  

  B. Contact and Interface Parameters  
    • COH – cohesion  
    • DIL – dilation angle  
    • GAPT – gap thickness  

  C. Displacement or Penetration Limits  
    • DP, DT, DM – normal, tangential and moment penetration limits  

  D. Export/Import Flags  
    • EXPP, EXPT, EXPM – export flags for penetration, tangential or moment data  

  E. Meshing and Numbering  
    • MNO – mesh numbering option  
    • AR – area or aspect‐ratio control  
    • DIV – division count (appears more than once, for different contexts)  
    • NM, NARE, NERE, NMRE – node‐related counters or lists  
    • KR – key‐release or stiffness ratio  

  F. Element or Local‐Axis Rotations  
    • DRX, DRY, DRZ – rotation about X, Y, Z axes  
    • DROT – composite rotation angle  

  G. Support/Boundary Sets  
    • BOUN – boundary set identifier  
    • NA, NE, NM – set names for nodes, elements, etc.  
    • TYPE – reuse of TYPE for set classification  

  H. Coordinate or Reference Frames  
    • CA, CE – coordinate axes or element axes flags  
    • REF – reference system index  
    • RX, RY, RZ – offset or rotation references  

  I. Control, Program and Output Options  
    • PROG – program or subroutine name  
    • TITL – title string  
    • EXPO – export option block  
    • OPT – general‐purpose option flag (occurs multiple times)  
    • TO, FROM – range specifiers for node/element pass or import  
    • PASS – pass or step identifier  
    • IMPO – import option  
    • ECHO – echo control for printing input  
    • VAL – generic value field  

4. Notes on Usage  
  • Many item names recur in different record types but may have slightly different meanings or defaults.  
  • Because CADINP is keyword‐driven, each record type only recognizes a fixed subset of these items; invalid keywords produce parsing errors.  
  • Together, the table serves as the definitive index for every field you can specify in a CADINP file, so it is a natural candidate for RAG-vector embedding when building a retrieval layer for CADINP grammar and schema lookups.

The table is a concise reference for CADINP record commands (first column) and the keyword-items each command accepts (second column). It is intended to drive a RAG vector store’s semantic understanding of CADINP input, so that queries about e.g. “what parameters does TRAN accept?” can be answered directly. Below is a structured description.

1. Units context  
  • Fixed units (“mm”): always interpreted in millimeters.  
  • Explicit units (“[mm]”): default in mm, but may be overridden by attaching another unit specifier in brackets (e.g. 2.5[m]).  
  • Implicit units (“[mm]1011”): semantic categories (e.g. geodetic elevation or thickness) whose default is determined by the active Eurocode unit set (NORM UNIT 5). The bracketed unit is the default for that set.

2. Record Groups  
  A. Data Addition & Properties  
   • ADDM: ADD material or property to element(s)  
     – Items: NO (element IDs), TYPE, PER, NO1/NO2 (node ranges), P (parameter), UX/UY/UZ (translations), UXX/UYY/UZZ (rotations), UW (warping)  
   • MASS: Assign mass properties  
     – Items: NO (element IDs), MX/MY/MZ (moments), MXX/MYY/MZZ (products of inertia), MXY/MXZ/MYZ, MB (mass), REF (reference point), LC (load case), PRZ (reaction zone), SELE (selection flag)  

  B. Geometry Creation  
   • SBOX: Create solid box by corner coordinates  
     – Items: A1X–A3Z, B1X–B3Z (two sets of three defining opposite corners), R, T (radii and thickness)

  C. Element Removal & Modification  
   • DEL: Delete elements in ID ranges or by coordinate window  
     – Items: TYPE, FROM/TO/INC, XMIN/XMAX, YMIN/YMAX, ZMIN/ZMAX  
   • MOD: Modify element properties similarly  
     – Items: TYPE, FROM/TO/INC, DNO (division number), XMIN/XMAX, YMIN/YMAX, ZMIN/ZMAX, FIX (lock flag)  

  D. Transformation (TRAN)  
   • TRAN: Rigid‐body transforms of selected entities  
     – Items: TYPE, FROM/TO/INC, DNO, WIDE (window width), XMIN/XMAX, YMIN/YMAX, ZMIN/ZMAX, PROP (proportion flag), FIX  
     – Translation deltas: DX, DY, DZ  
     – Rotation about axis: PHIX, PHIY, PHIZ  
     – Rotation center orientation: ALPH, BETA, THET  
     – Reference coords: REFX, REFY, REFZ  
     – Optional shift factors: FAKX, FAKY, FAKZ  

  E. Extrusion & Lofting  
   • EXTR: Extrude a planar profile into solids  
     – Items: TYPE, FROM/TO/INC, PATH, V1–V3 (direction vectors), DIV (divisions), SREF (section refs), OPT (options), SNAP  
   • LOFT: Loft between cross sections  
     – Items: TYPE, IDSC (start section ID), IDTG (target section ID), REFS/REFT (reference curves), DIV, OPT  

  F. Mirroring (MIRR)  
   • MIRR: Mirror elements about a plane or surface  
     – Items: TYPE, FROM/TO/INC, DNO, WIDE, XMIN/XMAX, YMIN/YMAX, ZMIN/ZMAX, PROP, FIX  
     – Mirror plane definition: A, B, C (plane equation), DIST (offset)  
     – Mapping of material properties: MP1, MP2, MP3, FAC  

  G. Mesh & Boundaries  
   • UMSH: User‐defined mesh parameters  
     – Items: TYPE, HMAX (maximum element size), PROG (grading), SAR  
   • UBND: Apply boundary conditions  
     – Items: TYP, SEL (selection flag), X/Y/Z (directions), N1–N32 (node IDs or flags)  

  H. Intersection & Reset  
   • INTF: Define or modify intersections  
     – Items: OPT, TYPE, REFT (reference type), NO (ID), D, MNO (master ID), CP (connection point), CT  
   • RSET: Reset or report settings  
     – Items: NO, SET, ITEM, UNIT, NG, NGS, TITL, X (user‐defined value)
