As SOFIMSHA follows a completely new and much more powerful concept for the generation of data, we have the situation that simple input data may be converted easily, but that depending on the complexity of the definition a rather expensive redefinition might be necessary which is beyond the scope of any automatic conversion. In many cases the input with an old GENF- version and the following export with AQUA/SOFIMSHA might be the most economically way to do the transition.
 Here following steps should be de noted or done:
 • Add the now mandatory group divisor in record SYST
 • Move all material and sectional definitions to AQUA
 Insert the item FIX for nodes of a planar system (there was no Z in GENF).
 •
 • Change of a few item names (e.g. KR instead of NR for BEAM)
 • Sections for haunched beams have now to be defined as a single string in the form 10.11. There are some minor restrictions of this format for generations.
 • Hinges of beams are defined with the beam itself. Beam sections are only defined with SECT.
 For other cases the following hints might be helpful:
 • Polar or spherical coordinates are defined with new special items. There is no longer the negative node number available for this effect.
 • Generation of bodes along a line is dound with NODE instead of BOUN or MESH. MESH and CUBE have been integrated as QUAD MESH/IMSH and BRIC MESH/IMSH. IMES has to be described with a QUAD FIT/IFIT now.
 • ALIN and SECT have been integrated in the record NODE. ALIN 101 100 102 0.5 becomes now NODE 101 0.5 NR1 100 102 "SS", and SECT 100 101 102 103 104 becomes NODE 100 NR1 101 102 103 104.
 • All implicit element generators (ENO/DNO/KNO) have to be replaced either with CADINP loops or by MESH or FIT Options.

The table shown is the definition reference for the SYST record in SOFiSTiK’s input deck. It lays out the four fields you can specify—Item name, Description, Unit and Default—and documents the global‐system parameters you may set once at the start of any model. Below is a structured description of each row in the table:

1. Columns  
   • Item  
     – The keyword or parameter name you supply in the SYST record.  
   • Description  
     – A brief explanation of what the parameter controls and, where applicable, a list of valid literal options.  
   • Unit  
     – The expected data type (for example LIT for literal text entries, or “–” if no unit applies).  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed when the keyword is omitted or when you expressly use the REST literal to retain existing settings.

2. TYPE  
   • Purpose: Defines the overall system type (dimensionality and special‐purpose modes).  
   • Valid Literals (unit = LIT; default = “!” which forces a prompt if missing):  
     – 3D: spatial (general 3-dimensional) structures.  
     – 2D: plane frame or panel.  
     – 2DSS: plane stress.  
     – 2DSN: plane strain.  
     – 2DAX: axisymmetric system (rotational geometry about X).  
     – 2DSL: plane girder or plate bending.  
     – 2DPS: prestressed plate system.  
     – SECT: sectional‐analysis system.  
     – REST: keep the existing system type.  
     – INIT: delete the system but preserve basic system information.  
   • Notes: TYPE combined with the gravity direction (GDIR) fully defines axis orientation. Former SPAC/SPAC etc. conventions are still valid but now superseded.

3. GDIV  
   • Purpose: Group divisor. Used internally when assigning elements to groups (see GRP record).  
   • Unit: none (“–”).  
   • Default: 0.

4. GDIR  
   • Purpose: Sets the global gravity direction, which in turn fixes which axis is “vertical” and how the two horizontal axes are permuted. This influences local coordinate‐system definitions, special load‐types, boundary conditions, and default graphical orientation.  
   • Unit: LIT.  
   • Valid Literals: POSX, POSY, POSZ, NEGX, NEGY, NEGZ.  
   • Default: “*” (must be specified or inherited from previous SYST).  
   • Mapping rules in 3D (for each choice of GDIR):  
     – POSZ/NEGZ: X = first horizontal axis, Y = second horizontal axis.  
     – POSX/NEGX: Y = first horizontal axis, Z = second.  
     – POSY/NEGY: Z = first horizontal axis, X = second.  
   • Special restriction: In axis‐symmetric analyses only POSX/NEGX is allowed.

5. FIX  
   • Purpose: Global default constraints (boundary‐condition template) applied to all nodes unless overridden.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal, see SOFiSTiK load‐case documentation).  
   • Default: “—” (none imposed).

6. LT  
   • Purpose: Title text for the system record—used in listings and graphical output.  
   • Unit: none (“–”).  
   • Default: “–” (no title).

Overall, this table is the cornerstone for initializing an analysis in SOFiSTiK: you must place a single SYST record at the very top of your input to define dimensionality, axis orientation, default restraints and so forth. Omitting or changing TYPE via a non-REST record will delete all previous system settings (and typically all intermediate results), so careful planning of these four fields is critical for reproducible and stable analyses.

The table provides a compact overview of the SOFiSTiK global “SYST” system types for two-dimensional and axis-symmetric analyses, distinguishing between two coordinate-system conventions (SCS vs. WCS) and listing the associated gravity‐direction settings and code identifiers. Below is a structured, row-by-row breakdown:

1. Common Header Information  
   • Two coordinate‐system conventions  
     – SCS (SOFiSTiK Coordinate System): z-axis points in the view direction; follows the DIN 1080 X-Y plane orientation.  
     – WCS (World Coordinate System): z-axis is opposed to the view direction; follows the international X-Y plane.  
   • Each convention entry specifies:  
     – GDIR setting (global gravity direction)  
     – Four-letter system code (in parentheses)

2. Column Definitions  
   • First column: System type code (e.g. “2D,” “2DSN,” etc.)  
   • Second column: English description of the model type  
   • Third column: Under SCS, the gravity‐direction option (GDIR) plus the SOFiSTiK system code  
   • Fourth column: Under WCS, the gravity‐direction option plus the World system code

3. Row-by-Row Description

a) 2D – Plane Frame  
   • Description: General planar frame analysis (beams, columns in a single plane).  
   • SCS: GDIR NEGX/POSY; system code = (FRAM)  
   • WCS: GDIR POSX/NEGY; system code = (WFRA)

b) 2DSN – Plane Strain  
   • Description: Two‐dimensional plane strain conditions (out‐of‐plane displacements suppressed).  
   • SCS: GDIR NEGX/POSY; system code = (PAIN)  
   • WCS: GDIR POSX/NEGY; system code = (WPAI)

c) 2DSS – Plane Stress  
   • Description: Two‐dimensional plane stress conditions (out‐of‐plane stresses zero).  
   • SCS: GDIR NEGX/POSY; system code = (PESS)  
   • WCS: GDIR POSX/NEGY; system code = (WPES)

d) 2DAX – Axially Symmetric System  
   • Description: Axisymmetric analysis about a rotation axis (X‐axis is rotational axis).  
   • SCS: GDIR NEGX; system code = (AXIA)  
   • WCS: GDIR POSX; system code = (WAXI)

e) 2DSL – Girder/Slab System  
   • Description: Plate‐and‐girder models combining slab behavior with beam elements.  
   • SCS: GDIR POSZ; system code = (GIRD)  
   • WCS: GDIR NEGZ; system code = (SLAB)

f) 2DPS – Pre‐stressed Plate System  
   • Description: Plate models including pre‐stress or tendon elements.  
   • SCS: (PGIR) — implies the same gravity direction convention as 2DSL but with code PGIR  
   • WCS: (PSLA) — implies the same WCS convention as 2DSL but with code PSLA

4. How It Fits Into the “SYST” Context  
   • The choice of system type (e.g. 2D, 2DAX) and the GDIR setting establishes the orientation of the global coordinate axes for analysis, loads, boundary conditions, and graphical output.  
   • Under “SYST,” only one global definition is active. Changing TYPE from REST deletes prior results unless controlled with CTRL REST.  
   • These 2D and axis‐symmetric variants replace older SPAC‐based definitions (FRAM, PAIN, etc.) by decoupling “system type” and “gravity direction” into two separate inputs.

By indexing each row as a separate document in your RAG vector store—capturing the four key fields (type code, description, SCS GDIR/code, WCS GDIR/code)—you ensure that downstream retrieval can precisely match user queries about model type, gravity direction, or coordinate‐system convention.

The table in question defines the structure of a “CTRL” or control–input record used by the SOFiSTiK RAG pre-processor to govern mesh generation, element numbering, solver configuration and result deletion. It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and lists four distinct entries (OPT, VAL, V2 and V3). Below is a detailed breakdown of its contents and intended use:

1. Columns  
   • Item: The mnemonic or keyword for each part of the control record.  
   • Description: A concise explanation of what each record field controls or holds.  
   • Unit: The physical unit or data type expected. In this table most entries are either literal tokens (LIT) or dimensionless “–”.  
   • Default: The factory-preset value if the field is omitted.

2. Record OPT  
   • Unit = LIT (literal string)  
   • Default = ‘*’ (asterisk)  
   • Purpose: Selects which internal control parameter to modify or query. One OPT record may carry exactly one literal drawn from the following list. Subsequent table rows define each literal and its semantic role:  
     – NODE  
       • Automatic node numbering start threshold. Defines the smallest node number assigned during automatic generation (default 1000).  
     – CONT  
       • Continuous-beam grouping logic. Determines when a new span in a multi-span beam is started, based on nodal or support changes. Default bit-pattern = 15, which includes: change of node ID, coordinate mismatch, support in gravity direction, group number change.  
     – EXTR  
       • Extrusion behavior for TRAN/MIRR commands. Governs how new element numbers derive from originals:  
         · EXTR=0 → use GRP record definition  
         · EXTR=1 → new elements inherit group’s element index  
         · EXTR=2 → explicit element number (if <262144)  
     – FIT  
       • Shortest-path factor for “FIT” operations. Defines the maximum multiplier by which a routed path may exceed the straight-line distance (default 1.571). FIT=0 disables path-finding to speed generation.  
     – GTOL  
       • Gap tolerance for merging nearly coincident nodes (in meters).  
     – SNAP  
       • Relative distance tolerance for snapping nodes inside QUAD elements (dimensionless).  
     – LOCA  
       • Local coordinate system definition for beam elements. Integer codes (0–3) select whether local z-axis aligns with gravity, first horizontal axis, or global Z/X/Y, including IFC and GENF conventions.  
     – LOOP  
       • Generation process mode. If present, triggers two-pass generation (first nodes, then elements), mimicking legacy GENF behavior.  
     – SUB  
       • Number of subdomains for domain decomposition (integer). Activates mesh partitioning.  
     – PART  
       • Mesh-partitioning flags (bit-pattern). Controls use of PMETIS or KMETIS, random matching (RM), heavy edge matching (HEM), sorted HEM, nodal bisection, or group-based partitioning.  
     – OPTI  
       • Equation-renumbering optimization (bit-pattern). Options range from no reordering to best local/global reorder, with skyline optimization, Metis RM/HEM variants.  
     – REST  
       • Deletion of elemental loads or results upon model regeneration or restart. Codes:  
         · 0 = always delete  
         · 1 = delete only if new elements are generated  
         · 2 = delete only if elements are explicitly deleted  

3. Record VAL  
   • Unit = –  
   • Default = ‘–’ (none)  
   • Purpose: Holds the primary numeric or bit-pattern value associated with the selected OPT literal (for example, the integer threshold for NODE, the bit-pattern for PART/OPTI, or the tolerance value for GTOL).

4. Record V2  
   • Unit = –  
   • Default = ‘–’  
   • Purpose: Provides a secondary numeric control value when OPT requires two parameters. For instance, CONT uses V2 to set the maximum allowed beam bend angle in degrees (default 45°).

5. Record V3  
   • Unit = –  
   • Default = ‘–’  
   • Purpose: Provides a tertiary numeric control value for options that need three parameters. Rarely used; available for future extensions.

Usage Note  
All OPT/VAL/V2/V3 records persist until overridden by a subsequent CTRL record or reset by OPT=REST (asterisk resets back to factory defaults). In looped generation (CTRL LOOP) these records are re-evaluated in each pass. Carefully combining bit-patterns for PART and OPTI can significantly affect parallel performance and solver efficiency.

The table under discussion defines the parameter structure for the SOFiSTiK “GRP” (Group) entity. In SOFiSTiK, all finite‐element entities—beams, shell panels, springs, cables, trusses, etc.—can be assigned to a “primary” or “secondary” group. Primary groups are addressed by an integer index from 1 to 999; secondary groups use a text identifier up to four characters long. A small reference number (REF) can be used to distinguish elements that share the same group geometry but differ in sequence, span, or other subdividing criteria. This table specifies the allowable fields when defining or editing a group, along with each field’s meaning, its unit or data type, and its default value when omitted.

Columns  
• Item  
  – The short tag used in the input deck.  
• Description  
  – A concise explanation of what the field represents.  
• Unit  
  – The expected unit or data type for the field’s value.  
• Default  
  – The value automatically assumed if the field is not explicitly provided.

Fields

1. NO  
   • Description: Group number or identifier.  
   • Unit/Data Type: “– / LIT”  
      – A hyphen (–) denotes a numeric index if digits are provided; “LIT” indicates a literal text string up to four characters.  
   • Default: “!”  
      – An exclamation mark tells SOFiSTiK to auto–assign the next available primary group number if none is specified.

2. REF  
   • Description: Span, reference or sequence number.  
   • Unit/Data Type: “–” (pure integer)  
   • Default: 0  
      – Zero means no extra subdivision or referencing is applied.

3. BASE  
   • Description: Base number for this group.  
   • Unit/Data Type: “–”  
   • Default: “*”  
      – An asterisk instructs the program to derive the base number from a higher‐level setting or to use a default grouping base.

4. ICS  
   • Description: Construction stage number of activation.  
   • Unit/Data Type: “–” (integer stage index)  
   • Default: “–” (blank)  
      – If left blank, the group is considered active from the first construction stage.

5. ICE  
   • Description: Construction stage number of deactivation.  
   • Unit/Data Type: “–”  
   • Default: “–” (blank)  
      – Blank indicates the group remains active through all subsequent stages unless otherwise overridden.

6. TITL  
   • Description: Title of the group.  
   • Unit/Data Type: Lit32  
      – A text string up to 32 characters.  
   • Default: “–” (blank)  
      – If omitted, no descriptive title is stored; the group is identified solely by its NO and REF fields.

Contextual Notes  
• Secondary groups (string identifiers) are especially useful when you need to classify elements according to architectural levels, material types, or custom naming conventions that go beyond simple numeric indices.  
• The REF field is optional but often used by automated mesh generators to tag elements in a repeated pattern (e.g., spans of a bridge deck or panels in a façade). If left at 0, no subdivision is assumed.  
• ICS/ICE enable staged construction modeling. By specifying the activation and deactivation stages, you can simulate the sequential installation and removal of structural components.  
• The BASE field can link a secondary group to a primary grouping logic, ensuring consistency in load combination or result extraction when you later assemble or post‐process analysis results.  
• See also related group‐oriented keywords: SYST (system definition), BEAM, QUAD, BRIC, SPRI, TRUS, CABL—each of which can reference GRP entries for organizing element sets.

Below is a detailed, step-by-step description of the input table in the context of SYST GDIV (the “group divisor”) and primary group number assignment. It explains how each “Group number” is computed from the given “Element number” using integer division by the specified divisor, and ties back to the broader rules on group bases, primary group 0, and recommended base values.

1. Table structure  
   • Columns:  
     – Group divisor (GDIV)  
     – Element number (the identifier to be grouped)  
     – Group number (the result of integer division: element number ÷ GDIV)  

2. Computation rule  
   – The primary group number is obtained by taking the integer part (floor) of (Element number ÷ GDIV).  
   – Allowed group numbers range from 0 up to 999.  
   – If the quotient is zero, the element is assigned to group 0 (“none”), which is reserved historically and generally avoided for deactivated elements.  

3. Row-by-row breakdown  
   a. GDIV = 1000, Element number = 1  
      • Calculation: 1 ÷ 1000 = 0.001 → integer part = 0  
      • Resulting group number = 0 (“none”).  
      • Interpretation: A very small element number falls below the first GDIV interval, so it ends up in the “group 0” bucket.  

   b. GDIV = 1000, Element number = 3569  
      • Calculation: 3569 ÷ 1000 = 3.569 → integer part = 3  
      • Resulting group number = 3.  
      • Interpretation: Element 3569 lies in the interval 3000–3999 when using a divisor of 1000, hence group 3.  

   c. GDIV = 2000, Element number = 3569  
      • Calculation: 3569 ÷ 2000 = 1.7845 → integer part = 1  
      • Resulting group number = 1.  
      • Interpretation: Now the grouping spans 2000 per bucket, so 3569 falls into the 2000–3999 range → group 1.  

   d. GDIV = 5, Element number = 3569  
      • Calculation: 3569 ÷ 5 = 713.8 → integer part = 713  
      • Resulting group number = 713.  
      • Interpretation: Very fine-grained grouping (five elements per group) drives the high group index.  

4. Contextual rules and recommendations  
   – If no explicit element-number is supplied (or it is given as 0), the system auto-assigns the “next free” number within the current primary group.  
   – When a GRP record is active (not “*”), any manually given element numbers are adjusted to fit the group’s base and divisor constraints.  
   – Base numbers for each group (when GDIV > 0) are chosen once all elements are generated; they must be multiples of the divisor to maintain non-overlapping, evenly spaced intervals.  
   – It is recommended to pick base values that are multiples of 100, 1 000, or 10 000, to keep printed element numbers readable and grouped logically.  
   – Primary group 0 should not be used for deactivation steps, and kinematic constraints without a valid group number cannot be turned off.  

By examining these four examples, one sees clearly how the SYST GDIV parameter partitions the full range of element numbers into contiguous, evenly sized intervals—each interval carrying its own group index from 0 up to a practical maximum of 999.

The sample table below illustrates how element numbers are partitioned into primary groups via explicit base offsets. Each row defines one group’s identifier (“Group”), its associated base‐number (“Base”), and the valid range of element numbers that belong to that group (“Element number”).  

1. Columns and Their Meanings  
- Group  
  • An integer between 0 and 999 that uniquely identifies a primary group.  
  • Group 0 is reserved as “none” (historic context) and should not be used for deactivation or kinematic‐constraint control.  
- Base  
  • A nonnegative integer that serves as the starting offset for element numbers in that group.  
  • Recommended to choose multiples of 100, 1 000, or 10 000, to simplify human‐readable numbering and avoid collisions.  
  • If GDIV (group divisor) = 0, base numbers are not used for element generation; they only provide a printing offset.  
- Element number  
  • The actual numeric identifier assigned to each element in the construction sequence.  
  • Must fall strictly between (Base + 1) and the upper limit determined by the next group’s base or the group‐specific cap.  
  • The default maximum count per group is one million elements.  

2. How Element Numbers Are Derived  
- Without a GRP record or immediately after a “GRP *” reset, the group is inferred by integer division of the element number by SYST GDIV (if GDIV > 0) or by checking which base‐range the number lies in (if GDIV = 0).  
- If a group’s base is defined and the element number specified is ≤ 999 999, that number is added to the base to produce the final element number—unless the provided value already exceeds the base, in which case it is taken as final (subject to range‐check).  
- If no explicit element number is given (or it is set to zero), the next free number in the current group is automatically chosen.  

3. Sample Rows Explained  
• Group 0 (none)  
  – Base = 0  
  – Element numbers 1 – 99 999  
  – Default “no‐group” interval; used only if no grouping is to be applied.  
• Group 1  
  – Base = 100 000  
  – Element numbers 100 001 – 199 999  
  – All new elements in group 1 are numbered by adding their sequential ID (1 – 99 999) to 100 000.  
• Group 2  
  – Base = 200 000  
  – Element numbers 200 001 – 249 999  
  – Allows up to 49 999 elements before approaching the next group’s region.  
• Group 3  
  – Base = 250 000  
  – Element numbers 250 001 – 259 999  
  – Small interval (10 000 elements), illustrating that intervals need not be uniform.  

4. Practical Considerations  
- The maximum group number is 999; all groups share the same base‐numbering scheme regardless of element type.  
- If GDIV ≠ 0, group membership can alternatively be computed by integer dividing the element number by GDIV. In that mode, base offsets are enforced to be multiples of GDIV.  
- Users must avoid assigning element numbers equal to the base exactly, since they can collide with the group’s start marker, although the system will still accept them.  
- Large element numbers may be defined “relative to base” purely for printing; internally, numbering always respects the group interval and GDIV rules.

Beneath the diagram, a caption reads:

Interpretation in context of a secondary‐group selection rule: the shaded (gray) area marks the elements that satisfy the logical condition  
  (group A1) OR (NOT group A2).  

Concretely:

 •  Every element in A1 is included, whether or not it also belongs to A2 (hence the entire left circle and the overlapping region are gray).  
 •  Every element outside of A2 is also included—even if it is not in A1—so the entire area of the rectangle that lies outside the right circle is gray.  
 •  Only the elements that lie exclusively in A2 (the right-only circle) are excluded from the selection and appear white.  

This mirrors the command sequence in an input deck such as:  
  grp 'B?' quad 'grp' 'A1' quad '~grp' 'A2'  
which builds a secondary group by taking all quads in A1 plus all quads not already in A2. The Venn diagram neatly illustrates that union of A1 with the complement of A2, highlighting in gray every region except the right-only slice of A2.

 A secondary group is defined by a leading GRP record, with the group identifier at NO consist- ing of maximum four characters (Text Lit*4), and following selection records. For selecting the elements within the secondary group, the following possibilities exist:
 • Element records without an element number select all elements of that type.
 • Element records with a single element number, or a pattern matching multiple numbers. Ranges of element numbers may be defined by two numbers, where the second number has a negative sign, thus 101,-109 will select all elements from 101 to 109. Patterns are literals where ’?’ matches any digit, ’*’ matches all digits to the left, ’E’ matches any even digit and ’O’ matches any odd digit.
 • Element records, followed by the literal ’GRP’ and a primary or secondary group ID. Mul- tiple groups may be combined in one secondary group, by applying the following logical operations:
 ’GRP’ selection with option OR
 ’&GRP’ selection with option AND
 ’!GRP’ selection with option AND NOT
 ’~GRP’ selection with option NOT
 – Option OR results in the union of the specified groups:
 grp 'B1'
 grp 'B1'
 quad 'grp' 'A1'
 quad 'grp' 'A2'
 quad ‘grp' 'A2'
 – Option AND results in the intersection of the specified groups:
 grp 'B2'
 grp 'B2'
 quad 'grp' 'A1'
 quad '&grp' 'A2'
 – Option AND NOT results in the difference of the specified groups:
 grp 'B3'
 quad 'grp' 'A1'
 quad '!grp' 'A2'
 – Option NOT results in the complement of the specified groups:

quad 'grp' 'A1'. quad '&grp' 'A2'. – Option AND NOT results in the difference of the specified groups:. grp 'B3'. quad 'grp' 'A1'. quad '!grp' 'A2'. – Option NOT results in the complement of the specified groups:.
 grp 'B4'
 quad 'grp' 'A1'
 quad '~grp' 'A2'
 • Selection of elements within a geometric body defined by SBOX: An element will be as- signed to the secondary group if at least one of its nodes lies within the given volume. Multiple selection bodies can be given to further specify the selection. If records of element types are added, the selection is limited to those given types, if no such selection is made, all element types are addressed.
 • Selection by element properties: By specifying one of the following special literals at the number, all elements having one of the further specified properties are selected:
 ’==’ elements having these properties
 elements not having these properties
 elements having properties above the given values
 elements having properties below the given values
 The following example creates a secondary group identified by ’GRS1’ and assigns all quad elements with material number 1:
 grp 'GRS1' quad '==' mno 1
 A preceding ampersand ’&’ changes the logical operation from ”or” to ”and”, i.e. the first case will select elements having any of the specified selections, while the second will select only elements having all of the specified conditions of this type.

Below is a structured, prose-style description of the “NODE” input table and its fields. It is organized by functional group—identification, positioning, constraints, kinematic/polar definitions, mesh parameters, and geometric projections—and includes each item’s unit and default behavior.

1. Node Identification  
   • NO  
     – The unique node number.  
     – Unit: not applicable (“–/”).  
     – Default: unspecified (!) forces the system to generate numbers automatically during MESH or IMSH.  
     – FIT/FITL sequences and SBOX selection allow grouping of nodes.  

2. Cartesian Coordinates  
   • X, Y, Z  
     – The nodal position in global space.  
     – Unit: meters (m), using length unit code [m]₁₀₀₁.  
     – Default: 0.0 in each direction.  

3. Boundary Constraints  
   • FIX  
     – A 16-bit literal (Lit16) mask prescribing which degrees of freedom are held fixed.  
     – Default: “*” (undefined until set).  
   • NR1, NR2, NR3, NR4  
     – Node numbers of up to four reference nodes used to define relative constraints or boundary couplings.  
     – Unit: none.  
     – Default: “–” (no reference).  

4. Kinematic or Polar Constraints  
   • DX, DY, DZ  
     – Directional offsets or kinematic constraint vectors (for moving constraints, linkages, etc.).  
     – Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁.  
     – Default: “*” (undefined until specified).  
   • PHIX, PHIY, PHIZ  
     – Rotation angles about the X, Y, Z axes respectively, for polar or spherical coordinate definitions.  
     – Unit: degrees (°) with angle unit code [°]₅.  
     – Default: 0.0°.  
   • PHIG  
     – Inclination angle in spherical coordinates.  
     – Unit: [°]₅.  
     – Default: 0.0°.  

5. Mesh Subdivision Parameters  
   • DIV  
     – The number of subdivisions along a line segment when using MESH or IMSH.  
     – Unit: none.  
     – Default: “–” (inherits global settings).  
   • PROG  
     – Progression factor for subdivision spacing (controls grading of element sizes).  
     – Unit: none.  
     – Default: 1.0 (uniform spacing).  

6. Geometric Projection and Primitive Definitions  
   • SLN  
     – Projection onto a structural line or axis (GAX).  
     – Unit: none or literal (Lit4).  
     – Default: “–” (no projection).  
   • SAR  
     – Projection onto a structural area (GAR).  
     – Unit: none or Lit4.  
     – Default: “–”.  
   • RC  
     – Radius of a sphere or cylinder for projection or constraint surfaces.  
     – Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁.  
     – Default: “–”.  
   • XC, YC, ZC  
     – Coordinates of the center of a sphere or a point on the axis of a cylinder.  
     – Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁.  
     – Default: 0.0.  
   • DXC, DYC, DZC  
     – Direction cosines defining the axis of a cylinder.  
     – Unit: none.  
     – Default: 0.0 for each component (requires normalization if used).  

Contextual Notes  
- All node definitions (coordinates, constraints, references) may be repeated or modified up until any element is defined. The last occurrence takes effect.  
- A RESTART command can be used to append or adjust nodes and boundary conditions without regenerating the mesh.  
- If automatic mesh generators (MESH/IMSH) are employed, user-defined nodes must be declared beforehand to reserve their numbers and locations.  
- Polar and spherical definitions allow complex boundary or coupling behaviors in TRAN (translational) and KINE (kinematic) analyses under the broader SYST control module.

See also: SYST, TRAN, KINE
 NODE
 The nodes are those points defining a mechanical connection between elements. They are
 addressed via unique node numbers which do not need to be in a consecutive order.
 Coordinates or constraints of all the nodes can be defined multiple times as long as no el- ements have been defined. The last input is valid at any time. With a RESTART nodes or boundary conditions may be added or changed. If only the constraints or certain coordinates are to be modified, then only those values should be defined. This feature will allow the use of different reference nodes.
 During the mesh generation nodes will be created automatically. If the user wants to have a special node with a fixed number at a certain location, he has to define that node explicitly before generating the mesh.

The user can choose among three coordinate systems for the input:
 For the spherical coordinates (X,PHIZ,PHIG) the angle PHIG is evaluated in advance as the angle between the gravity direction and the radius of the sphere. The angles PHIX to PHIZ define the rotations about the global coordinate axis. If more than one angle is defined, the transformation matrix used is that of the simultaneous incremental rotation (see Theoretical Principles). The definition of PHIG NORM a normalization based on the tangent values is selected which is easier to use in most cases.
 If only one reference node is defined, all coordinates are considered to be relative to this reference node. A node should not be defined relative to itself.
 If two or three reference nodes are given, the new node will be on the line defined by the first two points. Depending on the definition of coordinates there will be different projection rules applied. In the case of two reference nodes the coordinates are taken as absolute, in the case of three coordinates, they are taken relative to the third node NR3:
 If only one coordinate is given, the node will be on the line with that absolute or refered to NR3 coordinate value. (X 0.0 with NR3 is thus equivalent to the REF XX in ALIN of GENF)
 •
 • In case of two defined coordinates, the point NR3 as well as the straight line NR1-NR2 are projected onto the respective plane of the two defined coordinates. In this plane the perpendicular point from the projection of NR3 is then calculated onto the projected line.
 The point NO lies exactly on the connecting line, having the same projection in the direction of the missing coordinate onto this perpendicular point.
 •
 If there are three coordinates given or only the third reference NR3, then the projection is perpendicular in space on the line between those two nodes.
 • The definition of a literals S or SS at position NR3 will take the X-value as an absolute (S) or relative (SS) measure along the line from NR1 to NR2.

If there are three coordinates given or only the third reference NR3, then the projection is perpendicular in space on the line between those two nodes.. • The definition of a literals S or SS at position NR3 will take the X-value as an absolute (S) or relative (SS) measure along the line from NR1 to NR2..
 • The definition of a literal PERP at position NR3 will create the new node as a projection of (x,y,z) on a plane perpendicular to NR1-NR2 at point NR1. Thus (x,y,z), NR, NR1 and NR2 are coplanar.
 The base of the projection may be also given as a NR1 FIT node1 node2, the definitions to NR3 are then given with item NR4.
 If four references are given, the node is the intersection of the lines NR1-NR2 and NR3-NR4 or the point with the smallest distance on NR1-NR2 if the lines are skewed in three dimensions.
 As it is impossible to define kinematic constraints for a reference node and absolute coor- dinates in the same record, it is advantageous to define first all the nodal coordinates and subsequently all the support conditions and kinematic constraints (then without coordinates) in a separate record.
 There is also the possibility to project the coordinates on to a general surface or axis. Similar to the option of the hanging nodes, this may be specified as one time option with the nodal definition or with NODE PROP as a default for all following direct or generated node definitions. The default will remain active until a new NODE PROP record is defined. As projection targets we have all lines and areas defined with SOFIMSHC (Items SLN and SAR), as well as explicit definitions of a sphere (R,XC,YC,ZC) or a cylinder.  elements after an automatic mesh generation from SOFIMSHC.

Nodes may be generated with the following possibilities:
 • Definition of literal MESH at position NO for a generation with automatic node numbers not yet used. All generated nodes are compared against already existent nodes and created only if necessary (see CTRL FIT).
 • Definition of literal IMSH at position NO for a generation with interpolated node numbers. All nodes already defined within the selected sequence are retained, the interpolation will be in between those nodes only.
 In both cases the following positions X and Y are used to specify two node numbers NA and NE. The number of subdivisions may be specified with DIV either as integer value n or as real factor 1/N. For IMSH it is also possible to specify at position Z an increment:
 NODE IMSH 101 181 10
 generates 111,121 .. 171
 NODE IMSH 101 181 DIV 8 dito NODE IMSH 101 181 DIV 1/8 dito
 At position Z a third node NM may be specified for MESH to define curved edges:
 •
 a positive number NM generates quadratic interpolated nodes based on the geometry de- fined by the three nodes NA, NM, NE. Node NM does not need to coincide with one of the final generated nodes.
 • a negative value NM generates circular interpolated nodes based on the geometry defined by the three nodes NA, NM, NE. Node NM does not need to coincide with one of the final generated nodes.
 With PROG one can define edges with a subdivision as geometric progressions. Starting at NA, each segment is PROG times the previous one. If PROG is negative, a symmetric partitioning takes place (length of the first segment equal to that of the last one).
 For the reference nodes it is possible to specify starting at item NR1 the definitions FIT k1 k2 or MESH/IMSH k1 k2 km. The divisions have to match of course.

Any Generation of nodes according to the preceding paragraph will save the list of generated node numbers to be reused for other generations. However it is also possible to generate a sequence of existing node numbers. Thus we have the following possibilities:
 •
 a literal FIT for NO will search for an already defined nodal sequence between start and end node. If a node sequence is found with a geometric length not longer than a certain threshold value of the direct connection (CTRL FIT) this will be used and DIV will be set to the subdivision found.
 • a literal FITL will search for all nodes which are located within the tolerance specified with CTRL GTOL on the straight line between start and end node, sort them according to their relative distance and create a FIT from that, thus also defining the default value of DIV.
 Again in both cases the following positions X and Y are used to specify two node numbers NA and NE.
 For the generation of elements, it is also possible to generate nodes or nodal fits onn the fly automatically. This has to be defined with the number of subdivision segments DIV or M and N for QUAD or M and N and K for BRIC and optional mid nodes NMi.

Support conditions can also be defined in relation to another node (reference node). Coupling conditions describe infinitely stiff elements and special boundary conditions, which are numeri- cally stable. They are used for the formulation of boundary conditions for plates and shells and the modeling of very stiff structural parts. General coupling conditions can be defined using the record KINE.
 The following inputs are therefore only allowed in conjunction with the parameter NR1 in most cases. Combinations with other types of literals are not allowed. All constraints will have a group assigned to, but there are special rules described at the end of this paragraph. The formulas of the kinematic constraints are mostly given as the depending degree of freedom on the left side of the equation sign, while the referenced degrees are on the right side. The index 0 is always a degree of the reference node.
 Coupling conditions, as linear relations, can not be used for any non-linear geometric analysis (they can not describe 2nd or 3rd order theory effects).

The figure, labeled “Figure 3.9: INTE-couplings,” is composed of two separate schematic drawings, side by side, that illustrate how a middle “dependent” node (N0) can be interpolated from two adjacent “independent” nodes (N1 and N2) in a finite-element mesh.

Left-hand panel (oblique mesh with three top nodes):

• Overall shape  
  – A slanted, three-sided patch of quadrilateral (and a couple of triangular) elements  
  – The top edge is nearly horizontal but drawn at a slight tilt, connecting three distinct nodes in a row.  
  – The left and right slanted edges converge downwards but are not labeled.  

• Mesh interior  
  – Several quadrilateral elements filling the patch, each subdivided by diagonal lines that form smaller quads/triangles  
  – Diagonal subdivision lines run roughly parallel to the top edge.  

• Top‐edge nodes and supports  
  – Node N1 at the left end of the top edge, marked with the label “N1”  
    · Directly beneath N1 is a classic pinned-support symbol (an equilateral triangle resting on a short horizontal line), indicating that all translational degrees of freedom are fixed at that node.  
  – Node N0 at the midpoint of the top edge, labeled “N0”  
    · No support symbol beneath it—this is the “dependent” node whose displacements/rotations will be interpolated from N1 and N2.  
  – Node N2 at the right end, labeled “N2”

Right-hand panel (simple two-element stack):

• A single vertical rectangle, twice as tall as it is wide, divided into two equal subrectangles by a horizontal line running across the exact mid‐height.  
• No node markers or labels are shown, but the implication is that the top subrectangle corresponds to the region attached to node N1, the bottom to node N2, and the mid‐height interface line represents the location of the dependent node N0.  
• The rectangle’s outline and the interior midline are drawn with uniform, thin stroke weight.  

Interpretation in context of INTE-couplings:

• Left panel shows a practical mesh‐refinement scenario (“TALPA” application) in which a new node N0 must lie between two existing nodes N1 and N2 on a sloping mesh boundary, and its translational degrees of freedom are defined by linear interpolation from the adjacent nodes without introducing spurious stiffness.  
• Support symbols at N1 and N2 emphasize that those are fully constrained (fixed) reference nodes, while N0 is “floating” and fully dependent.  
• Right panel abstracts the same idea for a one-dimensional, two-element stack: three colinear points, with the midpoint’s displacements and rotations (where applicable) interpolated from the two end-points.  

Together, the two sketches visually reinforce the concept of an INTE-constraint: one “middle” node interpolated from two “reference” nodes, usable in mesh refinement of beams, plates, shells or stiff cross-girder connections, and ensuring no artificial stiffness is introduced into the finite-element system.

In case of mesh refinements, anchor points or in cases of stiff cross-girders there may arise a need for nodes that lie between others and depend on them. A rather general interpolation is available with KINE INTE, simpler cases may be defined with an explicit constraints INT? and special reference literals QGRP/BGRP.
 The INTE-coupling is a constraint with special attributes (see also remarks for KINE). Herein, opposite to node couplings, one node (the middle node) becomes dependent on two other nodes. The displacements and rotations of the middle node are interpolated from the corre- sponding ones of the adjacent nodes. Thus no artificial stiffness is introduced in the system. A more general formulation may be obtained via KINE. A rigid body with three nodes must be described by means of two KP/KF couplings; the INTE-coupling can not be used in that case.

The table shown defines the syntax and semantics of an “EDGE” input record, which is used to assemble a one‐dimensional list of nodes in a structural model (typically for defining boundary lines, loads, or mesh edges). Below is a structured, field‐by‐field description suitable for inclusion in a Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store:

1. Overall Record Purpose  
   - An EDGE record groups together node numbers that lie along a structural line or boundary.  
   - Only the sequence of node IDs is stored—no geometric coordinates or additional properties.  
   - Multiple EDGE records may share the same edge number if you wish to break a long line into subsections.  
   - Literal identifiers (strings) can also be used for edges, which is especially useful for specifying boundary conditions or loading sets.  
   - Upstream pre‐processors (e.g., SOFIMSHC or SOFiPLUS) will automatically generate EDGE records for each structural line when creating mesh connectivity.

2. Column Breakdown  
   The table has four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default:

   • Item  
     - The name of each field in the input line.  
     - Main entries: NO, TYPE, N1–N36 (nodes 1 through 36).

   • Description  
     - “NO”: the edge number or literal edge identifier.  
     - “TYPE”: the strategy for inserting intermediate nodes between the listed nodes. Valid keywords are:  
         • NONE  (no intermediate nodes)  
         • FIT   (automatic fitting/interpolation of nodes)  
         • FITL  (fitting with additional control on distribution)  
     - “N1” through “N36”: the first, second, third … up to thirty-sixth node numbers defining the path along the edge.

   • Unit  
     - NO: unit “–/Lit4” indicates either a numeric ID or up to four-character literal string.  
     - TYPE: “LIT” indicates a literal keyword.  
     - N1–N36: no unit (plain integer node identifiers).

   • Default  
     - NO: “!” marks that this field is required—no default is permitted.  
     - TYPE: “–” means no default; if omitted, no special fitting instruction is applied.  
     - N1–N36: “–” indicates that additional node positions are optional; you may list anywhere from one up to thirty-six nodes.

3. Special Notes and Usage Tips  
   - Range Selection Shortcut: To quickly include a regularly spaced list, you can specify two node entries with a negative second element. For example, “101  −191” expands to 101, 111, 121, …, 191.  
   - Multiple Records: If an edge is long or if you wish to apply different TYPE settings to different segments, define multiple EDGE records with the same NO or literal identifier.  
   - Boundary Conditions: Literal NO values (e.g., ‘WALL_LEFT’) make it easy to refer to specific edge sets in loading or support definitions.  
   - Interoperability: Upstream mesh tools automatically generate matching EDGE records—users typically only supply additional custom edges for special boundary or load cases.

4. See Also  
   - SPRI (spring elements)  
   - FLEX (flexible connection sets)  
   - GRP  (node or element grouping)  
   - NODE (point definitions)  

This description captures the purpose, field definitions, units, defaults, and advanced shortcuts of the EDGE record, making it straightforward to store, index, and retrieve in a RAG‐enhanced vector database.

See also: SPRI, FLEX, GRP, NODE
 EDGE
 This record allows the definition of edges, to be used for generations and boundary conditions. The created information in the database contains only a list of nodes along the edge, no other data. More than one record with the same edge number may be defined. Edges with a literal as identifier are primarily intended for boundary conditions and loading.
 SOFIMSHC resp. SOFiPLUS will generate an EDGE with the same number for every structural line used for mesh generation. To simplify the input of regular numbers it is possible to combine two entries of the list to a range with a negative element. A sequence of 101 -191 selects all defined nodes within that intervall, e.g. 101,111,121,...,191.

The table you see is the “parameter‐definition” for a single KINE constraint record.  In a SOFiMSHA input file the KINE record ties one or more degrees of freedom (DOFs) at a “dependent” node to a linear combination of DOFs at one or more “reference” nodes.  Each table row defines one of the pieces of that constraint.  Here is a field‐by‐field breakdown:

1. ND  
   • Description: Dependent node number. This is the global node ID whose motion you wish to constrain.  
   • Unit: — (an integer index, no physical units)  
   • Default: “!” (mandatory)  

2. FIX  
   • Description: Which DOF(s) at the dependent node are being constrained.  You supply a “support‐condition literal” (for example P = x‐translation fixed, Z = z‐translation fixed, PP = all translations, etc.).  You may also append a colon and specify a subset of DOFs (e.g. “INTE:PXPYMZ” to couple only Px, Py, Mz for an inertia‐distribution constraint).  
   • Unit: Lit16 (a 16‐character literal string)  
   • Default: “!” (mandatory)  

3. ND1, FD1  
   • ND1: Reference‐DOF specification #1.  You give a node number plus a “local DOF” index coded as 0.1×(local DOF).  Local DOFs are numbered:  
     1 = ux, 2 = uy, 3 = uz, 4 = φx, 5 = φy, 6 = φz, 7 = φb, and 0 = “same or corresponding DOF as FIX.”  
   • FD1: Weight (factor) multiplying the selected reference DOF.  By default FD defaults to 1.0 (unless you override).  
   • Unit: —  
   • Default: “–” (optional)  

4. ND2, FD2  
   • Same as ND1/FD1 but for a second term in the linear combination.  

…  

5. ND21, FD21  
   • You may chain up to 21 reference‐DOF terms in a single KINE record.  

Defaulting and optionality:  
• ND and FIX are mandatory (“!”).  
• Each NDk/FDk pair is optional; if you omit further NDk’s the record ends.  
• Any FDk you omit is assumed to be 1.0.  
• The record thus builds an equation of the form  
    Dependent-DOF(ND, FIX)  =  Σ[k=1→N]  FDk × Reference-DOF(NDk, local DOF)  

Key points of context (from the surrounding text):  
• Kinematic constraints define rigid coupling, hanging‐node behavior, or distributed inertia loads (“INTE”) among nodes.  
• When FDk are treated as weights W, SOFiMSHA uses them to distribute forces/moments back onto the reference nodes if FIX begins with “INTE.”  
• A classic example:  
    KINE 100 PZ 1.3 1.0 2.5 0.5  
    → uz at node 100 equals uz at node 1 plus 0.5·φy at node 2.  
• Hanging‐node example: averaging all three translations at node 200 from nodes 201 and 202 by setting FIX = PP and FD1=FD2=0.5.  

By structuring your KINE record according to this table you can flexibly enforce linear relationships among any combination of translational and rotational DOFs.

The table shown defines the input parameters for the GETN record (used to retrieve node or element numbers by spatial location) in a SOFiMSHA‐style preprocessor.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown of its structure, meaning and defaults, together with relevant contextual notes from the surrounding documentation.

1. Overall Structure  
   • Four columns:  
     – Item: the keyword or parameter name.  
     – Description: semantic role of that parameter.  
     – Unit: physical unit or data type expected.  
     – Default: value assumed if the field is omitted.  

2. Coordinate Fields (X, Y, Z)  
   • Item: X, Y, Z  
   • Description: Cartesian coordinates of the search point (in the global system).  These define the location around which GETN will look for nodes or elements.  
   • Unit: [m]_1001 (meters, unit code 1001).  
   • Default: 0.0—in other words, if X, Y or Z is omitted, its value is assumed zero.  

3. VAR (CADINP Variable Name)  
   • Item: VAR  
   • Description: Name of the CADINP array variable (without the leading “#”) in which matching node/element numbers will be stored.  This is a literal string up to 8 characters (Lit8).  
   • Unit/Data type: Lit8 (eight‐character literal).  
   • Default: “!” (an exclamation mark), signifying that the user must supply a valid variable name.  

4. IND (Base Index)  
   • Item: IND  
   • Description: An integer offset that determines the starting index within the CADINP variable array where the first found object is written.  Subsequent matches populate IND+1, IND+2, etc.  
   • Unit/Data type: — (no unit).  
   • Default: “–” (i.e. no offset; default behavior typically writes from index 1).  

5. TOL (Search Tolerance)  
   • Item: TOL  
   • Description: Radial tolerance (in meters) around (X,Y,Z) within which nodes/elements qualify as matches.  If TOL is negative, GETN saves only the single closest object rather than all within the sphere.  
   • Unit: [m]_1001.  
   • Default: “*” (asterisk), meaning use the program’s internal default tolerance.  

6. TYP (Object Type)  
   • Item: TYP  
   • Description: Specifies whether GETN should return:  
      – NODE: point‐type objects (nodes)  
      – QUAD: 4‐node shell elements  
      – BRIC: 8‐node solid elements  
   • Unit/Data type: — (enumeration).  
   • Default: NODE  

7. GRP (Primary Group Number)  
   • Item: GRP  
   • Description: For TYP=QUAD or BRIC, restricts the search to elements assigned to a particular group number.  Overlapping elements should be disambiguated by assigning a positive primary group in the GRP field.  
   • Unit/Data type: — (integer).  
   • Default: “–” (no group filter).  

Additional Context from Documentation  
• GETN locates existing or program‐generated nodes/elements by matching spatial coordinates after all geometry has been read. If you need up‐to‐date coordinates, a restart (SYST REST) may be required.  
• Once nodes are identified, you can reference their coordinates in subsequent input via CADINP macros:  
     #COOR_X(idx), #COOR_Y(idx), #COOR_Z(idx)  
• The GETN record is often used in tandem with KINE definitions (see NODE KINE entries) to establish kinematic constraints or mass‐lumping distributions by first retrieving the relevant node IDs into a CADINP array.

The table shown is the definition of the TRUS record—i.e. the input fields you supply whenever you create a truss‐element in the finite‐element model.  It lays out, column by column, the parameter name (“Item”), its meaning (“Description”), the physical unit in which you must supply a numeric value (“Unit”), and what value the program will assume if you omit it (“Default”).  Below is a structured, detailed walkthrough:

1. NO  (Number of truss member or option)  
   - Primary purpose: either the unique identifier of the new truss element, or an option keyword that changes the way following records are interpreted.  
   - Valid option keywords:
     • PROP — declare default values for subsequent TRUS records  
     • MESH — auto‐generate intermediate nodes along the element  
     • IMSH — alternate auto‐meshing routine  
     • FIT — project the element ends onto existing nodes  
     • FITL — linear version of FIT  
   - Unit: n/a  
   - Default: “*” (an asterisk means “repeat last used element number” when adding new ones)

2. NA (Start node)  
   - Node number at the “A” end of the truss element  
   - Unit: n/a  
   - Default: “!” (mandatory—no default, you must supply a node ID)

3. NE (End node)  
   - Node number at the “B” end of the truss element  
   - Unit: n/a  
   - Default: “!” (mandatory)

4. NCS (Cross‐section number)  
   - Reference to a cross‐section property defined elsewhere (e.g., in a CSA or CSY record)  
   - Unit: n/a  
   - Default: 1

5. PRE (Prestress force)  
   - Axial force to be “built in” at zero‐load; treated as a constant offset in all load cases  
   - Unit: kN  
   - Default: 0.0  
   - Note: Since PRE is active in every load case, it can’t be used for superposition in the MAXIMA postprocessor—if you need treat prestress as a standalone load case, define it separately with a LOAD record.

6. GAP (Gap of contact)  
   - Initial clearance before the element “contacts,” used in non‐linear analyses  
   - Unit: m  
   - Default: 0.0  
   - Note: Only effective if your solver supports non‐linear gap elements.

7. CRAC (Tensile rupture force)  
   - Maximum tension force beyond which the element “breaks”  
   - Unit: kN  
   - Default: “–” (no limit)

8. YIEL (Yield force, tension & compression)  
   - Elastic‐plastic threshold force in either direction  
   - Unit: kN  
   - Default: “–” (elastic only unless otherwise specified)

9. DIV (Subdivision in elements)  
   - Number of equal sub‐segments into which this truss is split for meshing or plotting  
   - Unit: n/a  
   - Default: “–” (no subdivision)

10. NM (Optional 3rd subdivision node)  
    - If you need to insert one additional node between NA and NE at a non‐uniform location, this parameter gives its node ID.  
    - Unit: n/a  
    - Default: “–”

Additional Usage Notes  
• PROP mode: “TRUS PROP NCS 1” will force every subsequent TRUS record to default to NCS=1 unless you override it.  
• Importing from an external database (IMPO): “TRUS PROP NA 500” will preload all following TRUS records with the same property set as element #500 in your import file.  
• The TRUS element only carries axial force—no bending or shear. It cannot be used with grid or slab‐type plates (SYST GIRD/SLAB). For non‐linear GAP, CRAC, and YIEL behavior the analysis program must explicitly support those features; check your solver’s documentation.  
• For uniform mesh spacing along the length, use the combined DIV + NM approach; see the NODE chapter for full details on mesh generation.

This table defines the syntax and semantics of the CABL record, which introduces a straight‐element “cable” into a linear‐elastic finite‐element model.  It is structured in four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and lists all parameters (and sub‐options) that govern geometry, sectioning, prestress, contact behaviour and optional mesh refinement.  The accompanying notes clarify that, although modeled as truss‐type members under linear‐elastic (eigenvalue or static) analysis, true cable‐only behaviour (sagging, tension‐only, contact gaps, rupture or yield limits) requires a non‐linear solver in ASE.  Geometric stiffness due to prestress is included, but contact/gap, yield and rupture definitions (GAP, CRAC, YIEL) become effective only in non‐linear runs.  Prestress is always “on,” so it cannot be superposed via MAXIMA—if superposition is needed, it should instead be defined as an explicit load case.  Uniform partitioning of a cable into sub‐elements is achieved with DIV and NM; default values of any parameter can be set globally via the PROP option (or inherited from an IMPO database entry).

1. NO (––, Default “!”)  
   • Primary selector: the cable element number or keyword.  
   • If NO = PROP, the following entries set default values for all subsequent CABL lines.  
   • If NO = MESH or IMSH, a regular mesh of nodes is generated along the eventual cable path.  
   • If NO = FIT, existing nodes are fitted to the defined cable curve.  
   • If NO = FITL, a linear fit is performed in the existing “Nodest” data structure.  

2. NA (––, Default “!”)  
   • Start node ID.  Mandatory unless using a mesh‐generation keyword (MESH, IMSH).

3. NE (––, Default “!”)  
   • End node ID.  Also mandatory.

4. NCS (––, Default = 1)  
   • Cross‐section number.  Links to a predefined section property.

5. PRE ([kN]_1101, Default = 0.0)  
   • Applied prestress (axial) force.  Contributes to geometric stiffness but is not superposed by MAXIMA.

6. GAP ([m]_1001, Default = 0.0)  
   • Contact gap size.  Only enforced in non‐linear analysis.

7. CRAC ([kN]_1101, Default = – )  
   • Tensile rupture limit.  Defines the maximum load before cable failure; activated in non‐linear runs.

8. YIEL ([kN]_1101, Default = – )  
   • Yield force threshold.  Used to simulate plastic behavior in non‐linear analysis.

9. DIV (––, Default = – )  
   • Number of equal subdivisions of the element between NA and NE.  Facilitates mesh refinement.

10. NM (––, Default = – )  
   • Optional third node index for irregular subdivision (see “NODE” record comments).

Additional usage notes:  
- Enter “CABL PROP NCS 1” to set cross‐section number = 1 as the default for all following CABL records.  
- If PROP is followed by an existing element number (at the NA field), all properties are inherited from that element in the current import database (IMPO).  
- For true cable‐only behaviour (sag, tension‐only, yielding, rupture) switch to the ASE non‐linear procedure; linear‐elastic (eigenvalue/static) runs will treat cables as two‐force trusses capable of compression.  
- The geometric stiffness effect of PRE is retained even in eigenvalue (buckling) analysis.  
- DIV and NM support uniform or controlled subdivision; see the NODE record for advanced meshing rules.

The table defines every input field (“Item”) you can specify on a BEAM record, together with a brief English description, its unit or literal type, and the default value assumed when you omit it. In practice you use BEAM to link two finite-element nodes into a beam element with a given cross‐section, partitioning, hinge behavior, local orientation and eccentricity. Below is a walk-through of each parameter in the order shown:

1. NO (Element number or option)  
   – Unit: “–” or LIT  
   – Default: “*”  
   You normally supply the beam’s ID number. You may also substitute a literal keyword (e.g. PROP) to set or modify property defaults.

2. NA, NE (Start and end beam node numbers)  
   – Unit: “–”  
   – Default: “!” (mandatory)  
   These two fields identify the FEM nodes that bracket the beam. Both are required unless you’re using special commands (e.g. mesh generators).

3. NCS (Cross-section number)  
   – Unit: “–”  
   – Default: 1  
   You can supply one section ID for a uniform beam or two IDs (`start,end`) if you want a tapered or varying profile. You may also use a formula beginning with “=”.

4. DIV (Equal partitioning)  
   – Unit: “–”  
   – Default: “–” (none)  
   When you input DIV > 0, the beam between NA and NE will be subdivided into that many equal‐length elements. DIV = 0 or DIV < 0 has special meanings (inherit or suppress default subdivision).

5. NM (Optional 3rd subdivision node)  
   – Unit: “–”  
   – Default: “–”  
   If you wish to force an additional node at some fraction of the beam, supply its node number here (see NODE).

6. AHIN, EHIN (Beam‐start and beam‐end hinges)  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: “–”  
   You can impose classical hinge conditions by concatenating any of N, VY, VZ, MT, MY, MZ, MB (unconstrained sectional force or moment). Literal PP or MM frees all forces or all moments. To reference an implicit hinge (i.e. a spring‐law hinge), give the working‐law number defined via SFLA.

7. NP (Bedding or reference‐axis profile)  
   – Unit: “–”  
   – Default: “–”  
   NP = –1 generates a “reference‐axis beam” whose axis coincides with the cross‐section origin. NP > 0 attaches the beam to profile BORE NP (for piles or eccentrically loaded beams).

8. BETY, BETZ (Buckling‐length coefficients)  
   – Unit: “–”  
   – Default: BETY=0; BETZ=BETY  
   Specify the effective length factor for global buckling about the major (Y) or minor (Z) axis. If you omit BETZ, it copies BETY.

9. ALFY, ALFZ (Span‐length coefficients)  
   – Unit: “–”  
   – Default: ALFY=“–”; ALFZ=ALFY  
   Similar to buckling factors but for elastic‐span length in bending. Omitted ALFZ defaults to ALFY.

10. KR (Local coordinate orientation)  
    – Unit: LIT or “–”  
    – Default: 0  
    A literal (e.g. “X”, “Y”, “Z”, “ANNOT”) or an index into a pre‐defined local‐axis system controls the rotation of the beam’s 2-axis about its longitudinal axis.

11. DRX, DRY, DRZ (Direction vector)  
    – Unit: “–”  
    – Default: “*” (use global system)  
    If you need an arbitrary local‐axis orientation, supply a nonzero direction vector here. Omitting forces the FEM program to choose one automatically.

12. DROT (Additional rotation about beam axis)  
    – Unit: degree  
    – Default: 0  
    Applies a final twist (in degrees) to the local cross‐section after the DR* orientation is set.

13. XA, YA, ZA (Eccentricities at beam start)  
    – Unit: [m]  
    – Default: 0  
    Offsets of the cross‐section centroid relative to the start node, given in global X, Y, Z.

14. XE, YE, ZE (Eccentricities at beam end)  
    – Unit: [m]  
    – Default: 0  
    Analogous offsets at the end node. Nonzero values introduce initial crookedness or pre-load eccentricity.

By combining these fields judiciously you can define a wide variety of beam behaviors—constant or varying sections, hinged or rigid‐joint ends, special buckling/span factors, tilted local axes, and even piles or reference beams—using a single standardized input record.

A uniform partitioning can be defined with DIV. With the definition of a literal MESH/IMSH/FIT/FITL for NO, individual beam elements will be created (see also NODE, CTRL FIT. In this case, DIV is the number of elements. With the input of the literal PROP for NO it is possible to define values, becoming default for following records BEAM and especially for the import or modification. With following input

In that case the section definitions and subdivisions will be also predefined unless an explicit definition of DIV 0 or DIV -n or explicit BSEC records are specified. DIV +n has here the special function to define a different subdivision, while maintaining the explicit section definitions.

A corresponding set of working laws (at the most, one for every single sectional force) can be defined by means of the input record SFLA (AQUA). A corresponding set of working laws (at the most, one for every single sectional force) can be defined by means of the input record SFLA (AQUA). Provision of an implicit beam hinge is then simply achieved by referencing the appropriate working law number. Example:.

If a single beam element is transformed to a truss element by hinges, it looses all its bending properties, thus the buckling is no longer possible within a pure FE analysis. A correct model has to include all degrees of freedom in the global system matrix, thus the effects have to be described by duplicate nodes, kinematic constraints and spring elements.

The image, labeled “Figure 3.18: Small cantilevers,” is a schematic side-view of a straight, prismatic beam element illustrating the distinction between three different span measures (Free Span, Effective Span and Total Span) in the presence of a small cantilever. The beam itself is drawn as a long, narrow, horizontal rectangle with uniform depth. Toward the left end of this rectangle there is a red, filled‐in triangular support symbol (a classic pinned support). Directly above that support, and cutting the beam cross‐section, is a single dashed vertical line; this line indicates the beam station or section location where a reference axis (e.g. the shear‐centre or centroidal axis) is taken.

Below the beam, three parallel horizontal lines—each extended beyond the beam’s left and right ends—are used to show how the three span definitions differ when the beam sticks out past its support. Each of these lines carries on its left and right ends a short, perpendicular “T” marker. The topmost of these is labeled “Free Span”; its left “T” is located exactly at the dashed vertical line under the beam (i.e. at the support location), and its right “T” coincides with an implied support at the opposite end of the beam (not drawn in the figure but understood as the far-right support). This Free Span thus measures the clear distance between the beam’s supports, ignoring any small overhang.

The middle line, labeled “Effective Span,” shifts the left “T” to the very tip of the beam’s small cantilever on the left side. In effect, the left end of the Effective Span falls at the beam’s actual left physical end, while the right “T” again sits at the far support line (or wherever the program defines the boundary of the beam element). This Effective Span therefore includes any minor overhangs beyond the support up to the first support centerline, as is often required for design codes that take end constraints into account.

The bottom line, labeled “Total Span,” extends even beyond the leftmost end of the beam rectangle (i.e. it includes the full cantilever plus any extra stub beyond), and similarly may extend past the right-hand support if there is a cantilever there. Its “T”‐markers bracket the absolute end-to-end nodal distance of the element. In other words, Total Span is the nodal length defined in the finite‐element input (sum of the cantilever stub and the clear span plus any other overhang), Free Span is the net support‐to‐support clearance, and Effective Span lies somewhere in between.

This drawing vividly demonstrates how in SOFiSTiK (and other structural analysis programs), small cantilever sections (often defined with a BSEC record) lead to multiple ways of interpreting the “length” of a beam element. Software that automatically stitches beam segments into a continuous element (via CTRL CONT) must recognize these subtle differences—especially when cross‐section interpolation (INTE ALL) or virtual elements (for infinite rigidity eccentrics) come into play—as noted in the surrounding text.

Both sub-figures share a basic horizontal beam rendered as a long, pale-gray rectangle with a thin black outline; however, the support conditions and the depiction of the “virtual” section differ between left and right.  

Left sub-figure  
• The beam spans from left to right.  
• Near the left end of the beam, a small solid black rectangle is inset halfway up the beam’s height; this represents the actual cross-section location of the beam element.  
• Directly below that black rectangle, a solid red triangle sits on the baseline, indicating a pinned support or hinge support under the beam.  
• A thin vertical dashed line runs upward through the center of the black rectangle and the apex of the red triangle; this dotted axis denotes the geometric reference axis of the beam element (i.e. the “design” or neutral axis) when no additional eccentricity is applied.  

Right sub-figure

• Above the beam, but horizontally aligned with the black rectangle, there is now a solid red circle—this marks the location of a “virtual” section of infinite rigidity that SOFiSTiK will insert to account for eccentricity along the beam axis.  
• A thin vertical dashed line continues to pass through the original cross-section (the black rectangle).

Overall composition and context  
• Both subfigures appear on a white background, aligned side by side, with some horizontal separation.  
• Underneath, centered, is the caption “Figure 3.19: Virtual sections.”  
• The drawing style is schematic and minimalist, using only rectangles, basic geometric shapes, and standard line types (solid, dashed, dash-dot) to communicate beam geometry, support conditions, and introduced offsets.  
• Color coding is consistent: black for actual beam cross-sections and outlines; red for added elements—supports (triangle), virtual sections (circle), and the eccentric reference axis (dash-dot line).  

By comparing the two schematics, one immediately sees how a “virtual” section (red circle) of infinite rigidity is inserted in the beam element model to shift the local beam axis away from the nominal geometric centerline, thereby enabling the software to capture additional eccentric effects (e.g. applied loads not aligned with the centroidal axis) without altering the physical beam geometry itself.

Beams can have segments and variable cross sections. Although not all of the programs can consider all the effects resulting from this. One must occasionally settle with an average value (e.g. rotation of the principal axes or shear centre).

 On the other side it is possible to combine several beam elements to a single continuous beam for the design or detailing. This will be detected automatically if the beams are defined in the correct sequence and none of the break conditions defined with CTRL CONT is encountered.

The table presented defines the parameters used to subdivide a beam element into individual “sections” for internal‐force evaluation in a finite‐element model (often invoked via a “BSEC” or similar beam‐section record).  In nonlinear or haunched‐beam analyses, several intermediate sections are required to capture geometry changes (inclination of the centerline) and stiffness variation between end‐sections.  Below is a detailed breakdown of each column and row in the table, together with the governing philosophy and any default behaviors.

Columns  
• Item: The keyword or parameter name.  
• Description: A brief explanation of the parameter’s purpose.  
• Unit: The physical unit or datatype.  
• Default: The value assumed if the user omits this field.

Rows / Parameters

1.  X  (Section location)  
   ­- Description: The position along the beam’s reference axis where this section is defined.  
   ­- Unit: meters [m] (code‐internal unit index 1001).  
   ­- Default: Required (there is no implicit default; you must specify X to place a section).  
   ­- Notes:  
     • X is measured from a reference point attached to the beam (by default, the start node unless “A” or “E” SPEC flags are used).  
     • Positive X directs toward the beam midpoint; negative X indicates cantilever portions.  
     • The same reference point controls how section forces are smoothed at supports.  

2.  NCS  (Cross‐section number)  
   ­- Description: Index into the predefined cross‐section library (PROP definitions or previously introduced sections).  
   ­- Unit: integer (no physical units).  
   ­- Default: “*” (none); you must supply a valid section number or else inherit from a default PROP.  

3.  SPEC  (Special options of section placement)  
   ­- Description: A literal‐8 string of single‐character flags that modify how X is interpreted or how the section behaves.  
   ­- Unit: Lit8 (eight‐character literal).  
   ­- Default: “*” (no special options).  
   ­- Flags (each may appear once in the string):  
     • N: Print this section’s results only if explicitly requested.  
     • D: Do not include self‐weight for this section.  
     • A: Treat X relative to the beam’s start (override default reference).  
     • E: Treat X relative to the beam’s end.  
     • S: Interpret X as a fraction (0–1) of the effective beam length.  
     • I: Interpolate section properties linearly between adjacent sections.  
     • V: Virtual section (infinite stiffness; used for certain boundary conditions).  
     • B: Section governs bending‐member design.  
     • C: Section governs compression‐member design.  

4.  TYPM / TYPT  (Section‐type qualifiers)  
   ­- Description: Define how this section is used in design checks and output:  
     • TYPM: Type for the main bending plane.  
     • TYPT: Type for the transverse bending plane.  
   ­- Unit: Literal token (LIT).  
   ­- Default: “SECT” (regular section).  
   ­- Possible values:  
     • SECT: Ordinary section.  
     • FACE: Section at the face of a clamped support (fully fixed).  
     • HFAC: Masonry‐type hinge support (face with articulated connection).  
     • IFAC: Indirect support face (e.g., pinned or spring support).  
     • SHEA: Critical section for shear design (shear‐control check).  

5.  NO  (Beam number)  
   ­- Description: Identifier of the beam element to which these subsections apply.  
   ­- Unit: integer (no physical units).  
   ­- Default: “*” (if omitted, sections are attached to the most recently defined beam).  

Additional Context and Modeling Philosophy  
- Finite‐element theory typically breaks a beam into many small elements, each with constant cross‐section.  As an alternate approach, large beam elements may carry one or more “subsections” defined via BSEC records.  Which method is preferable depends on the implementation of the beam element in the software and on convergence/performance considerations.  
- Haunched beams (i.e. beams with variable depth) require:  
  • Accurate representation of the center‐line inclination, and  
  • A model for how stiffness changes between adjacent subsections.  
- All subsections of a continuous beam should appear immediately after the beam’s definition, unless you explicitly re-reference an existing beam number (NO).  
- When neither SPEC flags “A” nor “E” are set, all X‐coordinates default to the beam’s start node.  

Together, these items allow precise control over where internal forces are computed, how section properties transition along the span, and which sections participate in specific design checks.

The image is a two‐part technical illustration (labelled “Figure 3.21: Jump or smooth transition of section”) showing how beam cross‐sections can be modeled either with abrupt (“jump”) changes or with a gradual (“smooth”) taper in a finite‐element mesh. Both halves of the figure depict a straight, horizontal beam rendered in a uniform light‐blue color against a pale background. Fine black lines indicate the element edges and mesh divisions along the beam’s length and around its perimeter.  

Left half – Jump of section:  
• The beam is partitioned by two rectangular “collar” regions where the cross‐section suddenly enlarges. These collars are wider and thicker than the nominal beam segments on either side.  
• Mesh divisions remain regular within each segment but do not blend between section sizes. Element boundaries line up exactly at the abrupt section interfaces, so that at each interface the element geometry and node locations change discontinuously.  
• The central collars are drawn as solid blocks with the same mesh density as the rest of the beam (uniform grid of quadrilateral elements), highlighting that the section properties change instantaneously at the interfaces.  

Right half – Smooth transition of section:  
• The beam cross‐section swells gradually from the nominal size at either end toward a maximum midspan section, creating a symmetrical, tapered profile.  
• Mesh lines are slanted and curved in the transition zones, illustrating how element shapes stretch and align to follow the evolving geometry. The density of mesh lines remains comparable to the jump case, but the elements themselves become trapezoidal or wedge‐shaped to accommodate the continuously varying section.  
• There are no sharp edges or discrete collars; instead, the progressive change in width and depth is captured by smoothly varying nodal positions across several element layers.  

Overall caption and context:
