The table shown defines the syntax, units and default values of the “QUAD” record in ASE’s finite‐element input.  A QUAD record creates one four‐node shell/plate element (or, in mesh‐generation mode, a block of many such elements).  Each row in the table corresponds to one keyword or parameter (Item), gives a brief Description, the physical Unit (if any), and the Default behavior or value when the field is omitted.  Below is a breakdown of every field and how it is used:

1. Identification and Connectivity  
  • NO  
    – Element number, or a mesh‐generation option (see M,N mesh discussion below).  
    – No units.  
    – Default “*!”: if you omit NO, the program picks the next free element number in the current group.  
  • N1, N2, N3, N4  
    – The node numbers at the four corners, ordered so that the element is non‐re-entrant and its local normal is consistent.  
    – No units.  
    – Mandatory (!): you must supply all four or use mesh-generation modes.  

2. Material Assignment  
  • MNO  
    – Material (section) number for the plate.  
    – No units.  
    – Default “*”: inherits from a preceding PROP or from the last used MNO.  
  • MRF  
    – Alternate material number used if the element contains reinforcements.  
    – No units.  
    – Default “*”: inherits similarly to MNO.

3. Stiffness Formulation  
  • NRA  
    – Bit‐mask selecting which stiffness terms are active:  
      0 = geometry only  
      1 = plate (bending)  
      2 = membrane (in‐plane)  
      4 = in‐plane rotation  
    – No units.  
    – Default = 7 (i.e. 1+2+4 → full plate + membrane + in‐plane rotation).

4. Vertical Position  
  • POSI (literal)  
    – CENT: element geometry is centered on the plane of nodes (default)  
    – ABOV: element lies above the nodal plane  
    – BELO: element lies below the nodal plane (useful for eccentric T‐beams)  
    – Default = CENT.

5. Thickness Definitions  
   You may define a scalar thickness or orthotropic thickness parameters.  
  • T   
    – Uniform thickness t in mm.  
    – Unit = [mm].  
    – Default = “*” (inherited via PROP or last QUAD).  
  • T1, T2, T3, T4  
    – Nodal thicknesses at each corner (mm). Not allowed simultaneously with orthotropy TX…TD.  
    – Unit = [mm].  
    – Default = T (i.e. the uniform T).  

6. Elastic Bedding (Winkler Foundation)  
  • C    
    – Normal bedding stiffness (kN/m³).  
    – Unit = [kN/m³].  
    – Default = –1: interpreted as a factor multiplying the global foundation coefficient on the BMAT record.  
  • CT   
    – Tangential (in‐plane) bedding stiffness (kN/m³).  
    – Unit = [kN/m³].  
    – Default = –1: same signification as C.

7. Local Coordinate Orientation  
  • KR (literal)  
    – Predefined local‐x axis: POSX,POSY,POSZ, NEGX,NEGY,NEGZ, XY,YZ,ZX, YX,ZY,XZ, or LOCX,LOCY.  
    – You may also point local x at a particular node number.  
    – Default = “*” (global coordinate system).  
  • DRX, DRY, DRZ  
    – Components of a user‐supplied direction vector for the local x–axis.  
    – No units. Default = – (none).  
  • DROT  
    – Additional rotation about the local z–axis (degrees).  
    – Unit = [°].  
    – Default = 0°.

8. Orthotropic Thickness (Alternate Section Definition)  
  • TX, TY  
    – Effective thickness in local x, y (mm).  
    – Unit = [mm].  
    – Default = – (no orthotropy).  
  • TXY  
    – Effective thickness for lateral bending coupling (mm).  
    – Unit = [mm].  
    – Default = –.  
  • TD  
    – Effective thickness for torsion (mm).  
    – Unit = [mm].  
    – Default = –.

Mesh-Generation Notes  
  – Using the M and N parameters or the literal NO=“M×N” invokes a structured Coons‐type interpolation mesh between edges.  
  – Mid-edge subdivisions: positive “mid‐node” numbers → quadratic interpolation, negative → circular arc, zero → straight.  
  – QUAD FIT subdivides each parent quad into up to six sub-quads, subject to parity (even‐odd count) and triangle‐inequality rules on subdivisions.  
  – Pure triangular meshes require the “:T1” / “:T2” specifier or the QUAD MESH command with explicit N.  
  – PROP may be used to preset defaults (thickness, material, orthotropy) for subsequent QUAD entries.

       –  FIT — automatic subdivision into 1–6 internal quads (odd subdivisions must be even)  
       –  FITS — surface mesh on existing BRIC structures (special-case use)  
       –  MESH — pure triangle mesh by explicit N divisions or “:T” literal  

2.  Element Identification  
   •  NO (integer ≥ 1)  
     –  Unique element number (if omitted, next free in current group is taken; duplicates prohibited)  
   •  GRP (integer)  
     –  Optional group number, see GRP record  

3.  Corner Nodes  
   •  N1, N2, N3, N4 (integers)  
     –  Node numbers in counter-clockwise order.  The software checks for correct ordering and disallows self-intersecting or re-entrant shapes.  

4.  Edge Subdivision Controls  
   •  M subdivides edges N1-N2, N3-N4  
   •  N subdivides edges N2-N3, N4-N1  
     –  Values:  
       > 0  →  number of straight segments (linear interpolation)  
       <0  →  number and type of curved segments (negative = circular interpolation)  
       =0  →  single straight edge  

5.  Element Actions (NRA)  
   •  NRA (integer bitmask)  
     –  0 = geometry only  
     –  1 = plate bending  
     –  2 = membrane (in-plane)  
     –  4 = in-plane rotation  
     –  Combined actions via sum (e.g. NRA = 3 for plate + membrane)  
     –  Typically only used in 3D models  

6.  Foundation Coefficients  
   •  C, CT (real)  
     –  Negative ⇒ scale factor applied to BMAT foundation coefficient  
     –  Positive ⇒ absolute coefficient for this element  

7.  Local Coordinate System Orientation (KR, DROT)  
   •  KR (literal or integer)  
     –  POSX, POSY, POSZ, NEGX, NEGY, NEGZ: align local x ± global axes  
     –  XY, YZ, ZX (positive projected), YX, ZY, XZ (negative projected)  
     –  LOCX, LOCY + node number: explicit local-x direction toward a node  
   •  DROT (real)  
     –  Rotation in degrees about local z-axis from default orientation  

8.  Plate Eccentricity (POSI)  
   •  POSI = BELO  
     –  Elevate or drop QUAD around its nodes to model T-beam action  
     –  Requires SYST SPAC in ASE for axial-force effects  

9.  Thickness & Orthotropy  
   •  T (real)  
     –  Uniform thickness (m)  
   •  TX, TY, TXY, TD (reals)  
     –  Effective orthotropic thicknesses: normal/horizontal, orthogonal, in-plane shear, diagonal bending  
     –  Can’t mix node-wise T1–T4 variations with TX–TD definitions  
     –  Negative section number = normalize section area & I_y to 1 m width  

10.  Mesh Generation  
   •  COON interpolation (with M, N, or NO literal)  
     –  Generates M×N structured block with curved edges  
   •  KMSH (legacy irregular structured mesh)  
     –  Uses only N1, N2, N3 to seed parallel edge copying  
   •  “:T” (triangular override)  
     –  Forces pure triangular subdivision along short diagonal  

11.  PROP Defaults  
   •  After “QUAD PROP …” any fields set become defaults for all following QUAD records  
     –  e.g. “QUAD PROP T 0.2 MNO 1” sets thickness = 0.2 m and material = 1 by default  
     –  Supplying any new thickness or orthotropy resets that portion of defaults  

12.  Examples  
   1.  QUAD NO 1 N1 1 N2 2 N3 3 N4 4  
       M 2 N 2 NRA 3 T 0.4  
       → Quadrilateral element 1, 2×2 subdivision, plate+membrane, thickness 0.4 m  
   2.  QUAD PROP T 0.5 TX 0.3 TY 0.2 TXY 0.1 TD 0.1  
       QUAD NO 2 N1 4 N2 5 N3 6 N4 7  
       → Element 2 uses PROP’s orthotropic thickness unless locally overridden

The snippet shown is the “mid‐edge node” portion of a QUAD‐element definition. In a full QUAD record you normally supply four corner node numbers (N1…N4) plus, if desired, up to four intermediate or “middle” nodes (M12, M23, M34, M41), one on each edge. Below is a breakdown of what each column and row means, how these fields interact with the rest of the QUAD input, and when and why you would supply them:

1. Table Structure  
   • Item  
     – M12, M23, M34, M41. These are the literal keywords in the input record.  
   • Description  
     – Specifies which edge the middle node belongs to:  
       • M12 → edge between corner nodes N1 and N2  
       • M23 → edge between N2 and N3  
       • M34 → edge between N3 and N4  
       • M41 → edge between N4 and N1  
   • Unit  
     – “—” (no physical units). You supply an integer node number.  
   • Default  
     – “–” (blank). If you do not supply an Mij entry, the element edge remains “straight” with no mid‐edge node.

2. Purpose and When to Use  
   • Quadratic (isoparametric) vs. Linear Edges  
     – By default QUAD elements are bilinear (straight edges). To introduce curvature or higher‐order shape functions, you can insert a mid‐edge node.  
     – A positive integer for Mij references an existing node ID. The program then treats that edge as a quadratic segment passing exactly through the mid‐edge node.  
     – A value of zero or omission of the Mij field → the edge is straight.  
     – A negative value for Mij can be used to indicate a circular arc interpolation for that edge (depending on the mesh‐generation routine in use).  
   • Mesh Fitting and Structured Blocks  
     – When using QUAD FIT, FITS or KMSH (structured mesh generation), specifying M‐nodes allows the creation of up to six sub-elements per original quad, or the enforcement of a particular curved‐edge shape.  
     – Under COONS‐type or edge‐by‐edge subdivision (M and N parameters), mid-edge nodes control how curved edges interpolate between corner and subdivision nodes.  

3. Interactions with Other Input Parameters  
   • Subdivision Parameters M and N  
     – In the context of QUAD MESH or COONs interpolation, M12…M41 supplement the M,N counts by fixing a single node per edge instead of a full uniform subdivision.  
   • Default Propagation (PROP keyword)  
     – If you use “QUAD PROP M12 100” in a PROP record, then every subsequent QUAD defined will automatically pick node #100 as the mid-point on edge N1-N2 unless overridden by an explicit M12 in that QUAD.  
   • Coordinate System and Orientation  
     – In 3D systems, the actual location of M-nodes must be consistent with the local coordinate orientation (KR and DROT) so that curved edges interpolate correctly in space.  

4. Practical Example  
   Suppose you have a quad with corners 1,2,3,4 and you wish to introduce a single mid-edge node #10 on the edge between nodes 2 and 3 and keep the other edges straight. Your record might read:  
     QUAD NO 5 N1 1 N2 2 N3 3 N4 4 M23 10  
   – Edges 1–2, 3–4 and 4–1 remain linear.  
   – Edge 2–3 is interpolated through node 10, giving a quadratic curve or higher‐order bending behavior on that side.

5. Best Practices and Recommendations  
   • Use mid‐edge nodes sparingly to control element distortion and to avoid extreme aspect ratios.  
   • Avoid subdividing only one edge of a quad if the overall element warpage or Jacobian check might fail (the program flags highly skewed or “re-entrant” quads).  
   • When building structured meshes (COON or KMSH), define all mid-edge nodes consistently so that adjoining quads share the same M-node along common edges and maintain mesh conformity.  

By understanding M12 through M41 as optional node references rather than physical properties, you gain fine control over element order (linear vs. quadratic), curved‐edge representation, and advanced mesh‐generation strategies in your QUAD definitions.

The table below defines eight distinct mesh‐generation modes (the “NO” column) that may be specified on a QUAD record to control how quadrilateral elements are built, how their edges are subdivided, and how new node numbers are assigned. The third column (“Default for K”) indicates which mode is invoked if you simply supply a generic K= setting without naming one of these literals explicitly.

1. NO = MESH  
   • Effect: All new node numbers are assigned sequentially (“with new node numbers”), and no interpolation along edges is performed.  
   • Default for K: – (no default; you must request it explicitly)

2. NO = IMSH  
   • Effect: Edges are subdivided according to the subdivision counts you supply, and intermediate nodes are interpolated along each edge (“with interpolated node numbers”). After edge‐node interpolation, the interior nodes are automatically created to form a structured mesh.  
   • Default for K: IMSH

3. NO = MMSH  
   • Effect: Like IMSH but interpolation is applied only in the M‐direction (i.e. along the pair of edges you designate as M‐edges). The N‐direction edges remain untouched.  
   • Default for K: FIT/IMSH

4. NO = NMSH  
   • Effect: Mirror of MMSH—interpolate only along the N‐direction edges.  
   • Default for K: FIT/IMSH

5. NO = KMSH  
   • Effect: Edges are subdivided and interpolated, then copied “in parallel” onto the opposite edge so as to form a totally structured block mesh even if the original edges were irregular. This is a legacy “GENF” approach to structured meshes.  
   • Default for K: IMSH

6. NO = FIT  
   • Effect: Use the exact pre‐defined edges you supply (no additional interpolation). Interior node placement is determined by a default fitting algorithm between those edges.  
   • Default for K: FIT

7. NO = FITL  
   • Effect: Generate linearized versions of any curved or higher‐order edges first, then apply the FIT algorithm. In other words, curves are approximated by straight segments before mesh fitting.  
   • Default for K: FITL

8. NO = IFIT  
   • Effect: Employ the full Coons‐patch (bilinear surface) algorithm to assign node numbers and interior nodes; this yields the most geometrically accurate mapping between all four edges.  
   • Default for K: FIT

Additional remarks:  
- You may suffix FIT (or any of these) with “:T”, “:T1” or “:T2” to force a triangular subdivision (pure triangle mesh) by splitting each quad along its shorter or specified diagonal.  
- When using MSH modes (IMSH, MMSH, NMSH, KMSH), you normally supply up to four subdivision integers (one per edge). They must satisfy the triangular inequality if you end up creating triangular sub‐areas (for any three subdivisions a, b, c, a + b ≥ c).  
- FIT and FIT variants rely on your input edges being “compatible” (odd subdivision counts must remain even in total), otherwise automatic refinement may fail.  
- These modes can be combined with other QUAD input options (PROP, T/TX/TY, KR orientation, NRA actions, eccentricity POSI=BELO, etc.) to fully control element thickness, orthotropy, local axes, and plate‐action behavior.

Below is a structured, field-by-field description of the “BRIC” input table, suitable for use in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store. It captures each column’s meaning, the interplay with automatic meshing, default behaviors, and relevant commands mentioned in the surrounding documentation.

1. Record Overview  
   • Purpose: Defines 3D solid elements (primarily hexahedra, with tetrahedra as a special case).  
   • Related Commands:  
     – GRP: grouping of elements  
     – PROP: set default property values for subsequent BRIC records  
     – FIT, FITL: surface‐interpolation qualifiers for curved mesh edges  
     – “:T” suffix: generate pentahedra with a triangular face  
   • Element Numbering:  
     – NO may be specified arbitrarily; if omitted, the next free number in the current group is used.  
     – Duplicate NO values are disallowed.

2. Mandatory Fields (cannot be defaulted)  
   These entries appear in columns NO, N1–N8, and MNO with default indicator “!”.  
   • NO (Element number)  
     – Unit: integer (LITERAL allowed)  
     – Default: next available (auto‐assigned if blank)  
     – Role: uniquely identifies each element.  
   • N1–N8 (Node indices)  
     – Unit: integer  
     – Default: none (must be provided or auto‐created via block‐generation literal)  
     – Role: specify the eight corner nodes of a hexahedron.  
       * Tetrahedron mode: set N4=0; N1–N3 define a counter-clockwise base, N5 the apex.  
   • MNO (Material number)  
     – Unit: integer  
     – Default: 1  
     – Role: links the element to material properties.

3. Mesh Subdivision Parameters  
   These control structured block or curved surface meshing; columns M, N, K each default to 1:  
   • M: number of subdivisions along edge N1–N2 and N3–N4  
   • N: subdivisions along N2–N3 and N4–N1  
   • K: subdivisions along any edge from N1–N5, N2–N6, etc.  
   – Unit: integer  
   – Default: 1 (single, first‐order element)

   Subdivision qualifiers: for each edge one may:  
   – use a positive value >1 to invoke quadratic interpolation  
   – use 0 for straight‐line, linear mesh  
   – use a negative value to approximate circular geometry  
   – apply FIT (search existing nodal sequence) or FITL (generate linearized sequence) for non-uniform subdivisions.  
   – ensure matching FIT/FITL settings on adjacent edges to allow surface creation.

4. Optional Middle-Node Fields  
   These columns define midside nodes (serendipity or quadratic elements). Defaults are blank (“–”), meaning no midside node. Applicable only if M, N or K >1 or if a curved/serendipity element is desired.  
   • M12: node on edge N1–N2  
   • M23: node on edge N2–N3  
   • M34: node on edge N3–N4  
   • M41: node on edge N4–N1  
   • M56: node on edge N5–N6  
   • M67: node on edge N6–N7  
   • M78: node on edge N7–N8  
   • M85: node on edge N8–N5  
   • M15, M26, M37, M48: mid-nodes on “vertical” edges N1–N5, N2–N6, N3–N7, N4–N8

5. Property Presets via PROP  
   • “BRIC PROP MNO <value>” sets material number <value> as the default for following BRIC entries.  
   • “BRIC PROP <ElementID>” will copy all property settings from that existing element in the current import database (IMPO) into subsequent records.

6. Special Cases & Recommendations  
   • Tetrahedral Mode: Use only for automatic meshing or highly distorted elements; hexahedra are preferred for accuracy.  
   • Surface Mesh Control: After specifying FIT or FITL on an edge, sub-division counts on adjacent edges must match to allow the program’s surface‐creation algorithm to succeed.  
   • Pentahedra (“:T”): Appending “:T” to the BRIC keyword generates special five-node elements with one triangular face.

4. Contextual Notes on SPRI Usage  
   – All SPRI parameters are referenced to an “influence area” AR. By default AR = 1.0, so a single spring constant in [kN/m] behaves as expected. Internally, however, the system always generates “per-point” springs.  
   – You may define a spring either as a support (single node) or as a coupling between two nodes.  
     • Single-node SPRI: omit the second node number.  
     • Coupling SPRI: supply both node numbers.  
   – To generate chains of springs along node sequences, set NO = MESH/IMSH or FIT/FITL and supply NARE/NERE as start/end nodes.  
   – Axisymmetric support: If AR > 0, AR is automatically set to each node’s current radius. To disable this, set AR = 0.0.

     • CTRL SNAP: threshold for collapsing nodes to the nearest quad‐element node when using shape‐function integration.  
   – PROP literal at NO allows you to import default SPRI properties from an existing element; e.g.  
       SPRI 10 PROP CRAC 0  
     will fix the spring-failure load to zero for all following SPRI records.  
   – For QGRP/QREF/QBOX definitions you can also use LOCX, LOCY, LOCZ to align spring directions with the mean local axes of the generating quads.  
   – Optional +R or –R flags on DX align the spring radially toward (or away from) the reference point given in DY. For circular arc (FIT NM < 0), the arc center is used automatically.

The table shown is the parameter‐definition block for the SPRI record (elastic spring support) in your CAE model import. It is arranged in four logical groups, each with four columns:

 1. Item  
 2. Description  
 3. Unit  
 4. Default value  

Below is a walkthrough of each group, its members and how they tie back to the SPRI‐record usage described in your additional notes:

Group 1: Non‐linear damping exponents  
– EXPP: Exponent for non-linear damping in the translational (DP) direction (DP^expp). Unitless. Default = 1.0.  
– EXPT: Exponent for non-linear damping in the tangential (DT) direction (DT^expt). Unitless. Default = 1.0.  
– EXPM: Exponent for non-linear damping in rotation (DM^expm). Unitless. Default = 1.0.  

These three set how force or moment scales with relative velocity or rotation rate. When you supply a non-linear law instead of a constant damping coefficient, each exponent modifies the rate-dependency.

Group 2: Geometry, subdivision and reference nodes  
– MNO: Index of stress–strain curve or material law. Unitless. No default (must be supplied if you reference a material).  
– AR: Reference area. The area over which the spring stiffness is normalized (see “All Values are thus referred to an area AR…”). Unit shows “[∗]” because AR inherits units from the stiffness (e.g. kN/m divided by AR gives kN/m²). Default = 1.0.  
– DIV: Number of subdivisions for element generation along an edge or in an area. Unitless. No default – if omitted, no subdivision.  
– NM: Optional midpoint control node. Unitless. Default = – (not used).  
– NARE, NERE: Start and end node IDs of the reference edge. Define a line segment on which multiple SPRI springs can be meshed. Unitless. No default.  
– NMRE: Optional midpoint node of the reference edge. If you need a third node for curved or segmented definition. Unitless. No default.  

Use these fields when you want the system to generate springs along an edge (between NARE and NERE) or over a region (in conjunction with QUAD groups or SBOX).

Group 3: Moment‐axis orientation and rotational spring properties  
– KR: Literal or index defining direction data of the spring’s moment axis. Can be a reference to a predefined axis (LIT/–). Default = 0 (global coordinate z).  
– DRX, DRY, DRZ: Optional explicit vector components that define the moment axis if KR=0. Unitless. Default = “∗” (use KR).  
– DROT: Additional constant rotation about the spring axis. Unit = degrees; default = 0°.  
– MPRE: Prestress moment within the spring. Unit = kNm/m². Default = 0.  
– MGAP: Rotational spring gap (slip angle before engagement). Unit = rad. Default = 0.  
– MCRA: Rotational failure moment. Unit = kNm/m². No default (– means unlimited or undefined).  
– MYIE: Yield moment. Unit = kNm/m². No default.  

These parameters let you define pre-moments, gaps, failure and yield thresholds for rotational springs.

Group 4: Search directions for coupling springs  
– DXSQ, DYSQ, DZSQ: Components of an explicit search direction vector used when generating coupling springs between two node sets (QGRP, QREF, QBOX operations). Units = meters. Defaults = 0.  

In practice you would choose one of the following modes for SPRI record generation:  
• Single‐node support: omit second node fields (NARE etc.) and directly assign stiffness to one node.  
• Edge/area distribution: supply NARE/NERE or use QGRP/QBOX literals to auto-generate springs on a set of QUAD elements or within an SBOX.  
• Coupling mode: enter two node ranges (NA … NE and NARE … NERE) and your DXSQ/DYSQ/DZSQ search vector to match pairs.

The table defaults ensure a rigid spring (if no damping or moment properties are supplied) and a unit reference area, so that a simple input of “SPR NO stiff =1000” will yield a 1000 kN/m spring at each targeted node.

In the context of the SPRI (spring) record described in your excerpt, CT and CP would correspond to spring‐constant entries (fields DX, DY or DM, depending on whether they carry a translational or rotational stiffness).  For instance:

Because all SPRI values are referenced to an influence area AR (default = 1.0), a single‐point definition behaves exactly as a conventional lumped spring.  If one instead uses QGRP, QREF or QBOX for NO, the software automatically generates springs at every node of the specified QUAD elements, integrating their influence areas and collapsing any nodes whose shape‐function-threshold exceeds CTRL SNAP.  Likewise, supplying PROP in item NO lets you preset default values (for instance SPRI NO PROP CRAC 0 sets failure load = 0 for all subsequent SPRI records).  

Visually, the diagram makes clear that two independent stiffnesses—CT in the horizontal direction and CP in the vertical—have been placed in series between a fixed support (the wall and the rigid bar) and the single node NE.  In an actual input file, one might simply write two SPRI records:

  SPRI NO 1 DX = CT  
  SPRI NO 1 DY = CP  

or, if CP were a coupling between node 1 and node 2:

  SPRI NO 1 NE = 2 DY = CP  

Either way, the sketch in Figure 3.30 provides a graphic shorthand for any series or branching spring assembly you wish to impose at a node.

The table summarizes how the input field NO in an SPRI record controls the way the reference area AR is interpreted and what geometric quantity the code actually represents when the program generates spring–support elements. In practice you choose NO to be either a simple numeric node, one of several literals that trigger “meshing,” or one of the area‐based selectors. The three columns in the table mean:  
• NO (the code you type)  
• specified AR (what physical dimension your AR value carries when you use that NO)  
• Calculated dimension (what the code actually computes from the finite‐element model to scale each spring)  

Details by row:  

1. NO = numerical / SBOX  
 – specified AR: “Area of support [m²]”  
  • Here you give AR explicitly as an area in square meters. You are defining a single spring or support whose “influence surface” is AR.  
  • If you use the literal SBOX in place of a node number, AR still means total area, but the program will collect all nodes inside the named box region (SBOX) and assign one spring per node; each spring’s stiffness is scaled by (AR ÷ number_of_nodes).  
 – Calculated dimension: 1.0  
  • Because you are supplying AR directly, no additional sizing is done by the software: it takes AR as is (unit factor 1).  

2. NO = MESH / IMSH  
 – specified AR: “width of support [m]”  
  • You request generation of springs along an edge or line between node NA and NE; the program will subdivide (“mesh”) that line into individual spring connections. AR then represents a linear measure—the width of the support line in meters—over which you want the total stiffness distributed.  
 – Calculated dimension: Length of support  
  • The software computes the actual length of the NA–NE line (based on nodal coordinates and mesh density), then scales each incremental spring’s stiffness by (AR ÷ total_length).  

3. NO = FIT / FITL  
 – specified AR: width of support [m] (same as MESH/IMSH)  
  • Like MESH, FIT/FITL generates a sequence of springs along a curve or straight segment. FITL meshes by arc length if you supply a negative FIT parameter (circular arcs), otherwise it meshes by straight‐line segments. AR again is the effective width over which you distribute stiffness.  
 – Calculated dimension: Length of support (same as MESH).  

4. NO = QGRP / QREF / QBOX  
 – specified AR: 1.0 [–]  
  • These codes trigger area‐based generation of springs for QUAD elements.  
  • QGRP: All QUAD elements belonging to group NA; QREF: all QUADs in region NA; QBOX: all QUAD elements whose centroids fall inside the spatial box named NE.  
  • AR is preset to unity (1.0) because the program will internally compute the actual QUAD surface areas and multiply by 1.  
 – Calculated dimension: Area of QUAD elements  
  • The software integrates the influence areas of the selected QUADs and assigns each node a share of the total area; spring stiffnesses are scaled accordingly by the element areas.  

Key points and contextual notes:  
• Default AR = 1.0 means that a single “spring constant” you enter in kN/m will be assigned per node without additional scaling.  
• When using area‐based codes (QGRP/QREF/QBOX), you can also specify CTRL SNAP: a threshold for collapsing nodes that are very close to a QUAD corner into that corner, preventing duplicate springs.  
• The literal PROP at NO copies properties from an existing SPRI record or element, establishing defaults (e.g. failure loads) for subsequent SPRI entries.  
• You may orient springs radially by appending +R or –R to DX (and supplying a reference point in DY), or align them with local QUAD element axes via LOCX/LOCY/LOCZ.  

By selecting the appropriate NO code and AR interpretation, you control whether your support springs behave as point supports, line supports, or distributed area supports, and the software automatically computes the necessary geometric measures (lengths or areas) to scale stiffness values consistently.

The image is labeled “Figure 3.31: Spring characteristic curves” and consists of three side-by-side P–V plots (vertical axis P, horizontal axis V) illustrating the three types of non-linear axial spring behavior discussed in the text: gap, failure load (CRAC), and yield load (YIEL).

1. Gap characteristic (leftmost plot)  
   • Axes: vertical P (force), horizontal V (displacement or deformation)  
   • A horizontal zero-force segment spans a finite interval of V around the origin, representing the “gap.” No axial force is transmitted while the deformation remains within ±gap.  
   • This gap region is annotated by a double-headed arrow labeled “GAP” straddling V=0.  
   • Beyond the positive gap limit, the curve departs the zero line at an oblique angle, rising linearly with slope equal to the axial stiffness CP. Equivalently, for V smaller than the negative gap limit, the force branch slopes downward linearly (same stiffness).  
   • In effect, the spring is “loose” until it closes the gap, then it behaves like an ordinary linear spring.

2. Failure load (middle plot)  
   • Same P–V axes. From V=0 the curve rises linearly with the principal spring constant CP.  
   • At a certain critical displacement the spring force would reach the prescribed failure load CRAC. At exactly that point the spring “breaks,” so the force abruptly drops to zero.  
   • This is rendered by a straight line from the origin up to the failure point, then a vertical downward line (force collapse) back to zero, and the force remains zero for any further increase in V.  
   • The vertical arrow adjacent to the P-axis is labeled “CRA,” indicating the magnitude of the tensile failure load. Negative (compressive) failure is not permitted, so only the positive branch is shown breaking.

3. Yield load (rightmost plot)  
   • Again P vs. V. Initially identical to the failure‐type spring: linear stiff response from the origin with slope CP.  
   • Once the force reaches the prescribed yield load YIEL, the curve transitions to a horizontal plateau at P = YIEL. Further deformation occurs at constant force (plastic or slip behavior), i.e. the spring “yields.”  
   • A small double-headed arrow next to the P-axis marks the distance from the origin up to “+ YIEL.”  
   • In compression (negative V) one would have a symmetric plateau at – YIEL, though only the positive side is explicitly drawn.

Across all three subplots, the vertical dotted line marks V=0 (the undeformed reference), and the small center cross indicates the origin (P=0, V=0). Together these three curves encapsulate the simple non-linear spring options available: an elastic gap, a brittle failure threshold, or an elastic–perfectly-plastic yield threshold.

The sketch in Figure 3.32 illustrates a generic viscous‐type damping element as it might be used in a finite‐element, dynamic (DYNA/ASE) analysis.  It is drawn in a simplified, one‐dimensional form, showing how two separate dashpots (“dampers”) are arranged between a fixed structural frame and two nodes, NA and NE:

1. Overall layout  
   - On the left, a large, rigid rectangular outline represents the stationary structural reference (for example, part of a foundation or large body to which the damping element is attached).  
   - On the right, two nodes, NA (top) and NE (bottom), are shown as small open circles on a vertical “backbone” line.  These nodes correspond to the degrees of freedom in the dynamic model.

2. Vertical damper D  
   - Between NA and NE the main damping path is a single viscous damper symbol, drawn as two parallel plates with a thin gap, and labelled “D.”  
   - This damper connects directly in series along the vertical line, so any relative motion between NA and NE generates a resisting force FD = D · v, where v is the relative velocity.

3. Horizontal dashpot DT  
   - In addition to the vertical damper, a secondary dashpot (labelled “DT”) is attached between the lower node NE and the rigid frame.  
   - A short horizontal line runs from node NE to the right side of the DT symbol (also rendered as two sliding plates in a rectangular housing).  The left side of DT is fastened to the frame.  
   - This branch provides an extra shear‐wave damping path, controlled by the coefficient DT.

4. Functional interpretation  
   - Together, D and DT form a composite “radiation boundary” damping element.  Under compressive (normal) motion between NA and the frame, the vertical damper D dominates; under transverse (shear) motion at NE, DT provides supplemental damping.  
   - By selecting DT and DP (the analogous normal‐wave damping coefficient, not shown but defined in the accompanying text) one can mimic an absorbing boundary for both shear and compressive wave propagation in material MNO over some influence area AR.

5. Context from the surrounding text  
   - The manual notes that all remarks for spring elements (directions, influence width) equally apply to these dampers.  
   - The prescribed formulas  
        DP := V J (p–K) – AR  
        DT := J (p–G) – AR  
     allow the analyst to calculate appropriate damping constants (with units carefully kept in m and s to ensure consistency).  
   - Non-linear damping laws (P = D·v^e_p, or combined spring-plus-damper force sums) can also be implemented, provided exponents use the same base units.

In sum, Figure 3.32 is a schematic representation of a two-branch damping element used to absorb both compressive and shear energy at a model boundary.  It combines a vertical dashpot D (between the two nodes NA–NE) with a horizontal dashpot DT (from NE back to a fixed frame), enabling the user to preset DP and DT so as to approximate the desired radiation conditions for material MNO over area AR.

The table displayed above defines the syntax and parameters available when you issue a BOUN (boundary‐element) record in SOFiPLUS or SOFIMSHC.  BOUN elements are used to impose elastic support or post‐processing constraints along line segments in a finite‐element model.  Every BOUN definition consists of an initial “header” record—where only the element number (NA) and its title (TITL) may be entered—followed by one or more “segment” records that enumerate the individual line spans making up that boundary.  In each segment record the first node (NA) must match the last node (NE) of the preceding segment to enforce continuity.

Columns  
• Item:  The keyword or parameter name.  
• Description:  What the parameter specifies.  
• Unit:  The physical or literal type expected (if any).  
• Default:  The value assumed when the field is omitted.

1. NA  
   – “Starting node or element number.”  Required for every record.  
   – Unit: none.  
   – No default (must be supplied).

2. NE  
   – “End node number” of the segment.  
   – Unit: none.  
   – No default (must be supplied).

3. NM  
   – “Increment of numbers or the literal FIT / FITL.”  Instead of listing every intermediate node, you can supply an increment (e.g. 5) or use FIT/FITL to invoke a nodal‐fit generator (see NODE).  
   – Unit: “–” or LIT for literal.  
   – Default: “*” (no intermediate nodes).

4. TYPE  
   – “Direction of support.”  A required literal (LIT) that specifies which degree of freedom is spring‐supported.  No default.  
     • CX, CY, CZ: global X, Y, Z translations  
     • CN: longitudinal translation (along the line)  
     • CT: both transverse translations (perpendicular to line)  
     • DX, DY, DZ: rotations about global X, Y, Z  
     • DN: rotation about the longitudinal axis  
     • DT: both transverse rotations  
     • MNNN: material number for SBFEM‐based foundation elements

5. CA  
   – “Bedding constant at the beginning” of the segment.  Enter one or more numeric spring‐stiffness values ([KN/m], [KN·m–1], [KN·m/rad], etc.) in the order dictated by TYPE.  
   – Unit: [*].* (vector of real numbers).  
   – No default (must be supplied).

6. CE  
   – “Bedding constant at the end” of the segment.  Same format as CA.  
   – Unit: [*].*  
   – Default: equals CA (implies uniform stiffness if CE is omitted).

7. REF  
   – “Reference axis for linear variation if CA ≠ CE.”  Optional literal of XX, YY or ZZ to indicate whether the interpolation between CA and CE should use the true segment length (default) or project along a global axis.  
   – Unit: LIT.  
   – Default: “*” (use real length).

8. RX, RY, RZ  
   – If you select TYPE = CN or DN (longitudinal support only), these three fields let you define the actual direction vector N in global XYZ coordinates.  
   – Units: none (direction cosines).  
   – Default for each: “*” (automatically uses the vector from NA→NE).

9. DIV  
   – “Equal partitioning of edge segment.”  Enter a positive integer if you want to subdivide the segment into equally spaced springs.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: “–” (no equal partitioning).

10. PROG  
   – “Geometric progression of created nodes.”  Instead of equal subsegments, you may define a ratio to generate a geometric series of springs.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: “–”.

11. TITL  
   – “Boundary‐element designation” (up to 24 characters).  Only allowed on the first (header) record.  
   – Unit: LT24.  
   – Default: “–” (no title).

Notes and Best Practices  
– All segments must connect end-to-start for continuity.  
– In 3D, a “transverse” support (CT/DT) automatically places two orthogonal springs perpendicular to the line; if you want only one, choose CN/DN plus RX,RY,RZ.  
– The BOUN element uses the Winkler foundation assumption; it ignores shear in the supporting medium and can be less accurate if the characteristic length Lc (function of stiffness and spring constants) is violated.  
– For nonlinear support behavior only “single‐spring” models (DIV or PROG) are allowed.  
– See also SPRI, FLEX, GRP, NODE for related spring, flexible linking, group‐definition, and automatic node‐fit utilities.

The illustration shows a schematic “BOUN” boundary element composed of a broken line passing through a series of nodes (points) and carrying directional support annotations.  Visually, the element consists of four straight-line segments joined end-to-end:

 1. A sloping segment rising gently from left to right, whose left end is marked “FROM.”  
 2. A second, slightly steeper upward segment.  
 3. A horizontal segment in the middle of the figure.  
 4. A final, downward-sloping segment on the right.  

Each segment represents a span between two finite-element nodes.  The rule for constructing a multi-segment BOUN element is that the start node number of each new segment coincides with the end node number of the previous segment.  Thus the polyline as drawn could correspond to a sequence of node pairs (NA → NE, NA → NE, etc.) in the input data.

Two arrows indicate the local coordinate directions for elastic support behavior:

 • Underneath the second segment, an arrow points downward into the figure and is labeled “DT, CT.”  This denotes the tangential direction (T) of the boundary element and the associated tangential stiffness coefficient.  
 • Above the third (horizontal) segment, an arrow points to the right and is labeled “DN, CN.”  This marks the normal direction (N) of the boundary element and its corresponding normal stiffness coefficient.  

These two orthogonal directions (T and N) define the elastic supports that the BOUN element applies perpendicular to each segment’s axis.  In a three-dimensional model the program automatically resolves those into two mutually perpendicular supports in the plane normal to the local segment axis.  If only one direction is to be supported, the user can select N and define its exact orientation via RX, RY, RZ.

Below the graphic is the caption “Figure 3.33: BOUN boundary element.”  Together with the accompanying text, the image conveys how a continuous line of boundary supports is assembled in SOFIMSHC/SOFIPLUS input: by chaining segment definitions, specifying start node (NA), end node (NE), and optionally a node increment (KM) or literal keywords to capture intermediate nodes.  The BOUN element adheres to a Winkler-type foundation assumption, modeling the soil or elastic medium as a series of independent springs distributed continuously along the line.  Although shear deformations of the supporting medium are neglected, the formulation provides a compromise between single‐spring supports and an exact differential solution, and it integrates seamlessly with standard beam (QUAD, BRIC) elements without creating gaps at the interface.

The image is a schematic, labeled “Figure 3.34: Foundation models,” showing two alternative ways to represent an elastically supported (founded) beam in a finite-element context. Both renderings share the same top element—a straight horizontal line representing the beam or structural line to which elastic supports are attached—but differ in how the supporting medium (the “foundation”) is idealized beneath it. Beneath the drawings is the title “Modules for elastic founded beam.”

Left-hand model (continuous foundation)  
- The beam’s entire underside is drawn as a single continuous zig-zag line.  
- This illustrates a Winkler-type continuous foundation, in which the reaction to any vertical displacement along the beam is modeled by a distributed stiffness per unit length (a foundation modulus, typically in [kN/m²], [kN/m^1.5], or [kN·m/rad·m] depending on the support type).  
- In practice this corresponds to a spring matrix assembled by energy equivalence under the assumption that deflections between nodes vary linearly.  
- Such a model enforces support “everywhere” along the beam, eliminating gaps between structural element and foundation (fully compatible with quad and brick elements).  

Right-hand model (discrete spring supports)  
- The beam is supported by a series of individual zig-zag springs attached only at specific points (nodes), rather than continuously.  
- Springs vary slightly in drawing style and spacing to indicate that each can have its own stiffness coefficient; this is the “single-spring” or “nodal spring” approach.  
- Because loads and deflections are only tied in at the nodes, beam elements between two spring nodes see a constant shear distribution and a linearly varying moment, with no direct shear or moment contributions at mid-span except in the averaged Winkler sense.  
- A pair of horizontal arrows—one at each side, pointing toward the beam’s center—illustrates the case where only one elastic direction (the boundary normal N) is active. By selecting N and providing RX, RY, RZ values, the user can limit support to a single transverse direction instead of all directions perpendicular to the line.  

Key conceptual contrasts drawn by the figure  
1. Continuous vs. discrete foundation: continuous springs everywhere vs. lumped springs only at nodes.  
2. Compatibility with various element types: continuous model fits seamlessly under quad or brick meshes; discrete springs offer straightforward nonlinear options.  
3. Numerical behavior: continuous foundation better approximates true beam–foundation interaction, especially for elastically supported beams, whereas discrete springs can suffer local oscillations or “gaps” in shear/moment distributions.  
4. Practical guidance: element lengths should reflect the characteristic length L of the supported structure—beam and boundary element lengths roughly twice the beam’s shear depth, yet no shorter than the cross-section height, to avoid numerical artifacts.  

This dual-diagram therefore provides design and implementation guidance for the BOUN (boundary element) record in SOFiPLUS/SOFIMSHC: how to generate either a continuous spring matrix or individual nodal springs, how to select support directions, and what numerical considerations (characteristic length, spring distribution, load application) affect solution accuracy.

The table defines the ADDM record, which is used to supply element‐level or support‐level matrices (flexibility, stiffness, damping or mass) for up to six nodes in a structural model.  It is also employed to create impedance (frequency‐dependent) sub‐matrices when specifying a non‐zero period (PER).  The record is organized into named fields (“Item”), each with a clear role, a unit convention, and—where appropriate—a default or indication that the field is mandatory.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown:

1. NO (Element number)  
   – Description: Unique identifier for this matrix element or support.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: mandatory (indicated by “!”)  

2. TYP (Element type)  
   – Description: Selects which kind of matrix you are defining.  Valid literals are:
     • FLEX  → Flexibility matrix  
     • STIF  → Stiffness matrix  
     • DAMP  → Damping matrix  
     • MASS  → Mass matrix  
   – Unit: literal (LIT)  
   – Default: mandatory  

3. PER (Period for impedance)  
   – Description: When defining an impedance (frequency‐dependent) sub‐matrix, supply the oscillation period (in seconds). If omitted or zero, the record is treated as static.  
   – Unit: sec  
   – Default: optional  

4. NO1 (Node number 1)  
   – Description: First node index in the sub‐matrix.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: mandatory  

5. NO2 (Node number 2)  
   – Description: Second node index in the sub‐matrix.  When left blank (or zero), only the diagonal entries are assumed or a single‐node sub‐matrix is implied.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: optional  

6. P (Component of force or moment)  
   – Description: Direction or type of load component for which the matrix row/column is being defined.  Select one of:
     • PX, PY, PZ – Force components [kN]  
     • MX, MY, MZ – Moment components [kNm]  
     • MB – Bimoment component [kNm²]  
   – Unit: literal (LIT)  
   – Default: mandatory  

7. UX, UY, UZ (Displacement responses)  
   – Description: Entries in the matrix for translational displacements in the x, y or z direction respectively, induced by the unit load P.  
   – Unit: “*” (unit depends on the type of matrix and scaling rules; see below)  
   – Default: 0  

8. UXX, UYY, UZZ (Rotational responses)  
   – Description: Matrix entries for rotational directions xx, yy or zz responding to the component P.  
   – Unit: “*” (see scaling rules)  
   – Default: 0  

9. UW (Distortional response)  
   – Description: Matrix entry for the out‐of‐plane or warping distortion mode (denoted u‐w) under the unit load.  
   – Unit: “*”  
   – Default: 0  

Unit‐Scaling Rules (depending on TYP):  
- FLEX (flexibility matrix, NO2=0): UX–UW are pure deformations, but must be scaled by the implicit load unit (SUPP_POINT, SUPP_MOMENT or BEAM_BIMOMENT). Diagonal zeros are skipped; supports that are perfectly rigid should use nodal constraint records instead.  
- STIF (stiffness matrix): Each table line defines a full row or column for nodes NO1–NO2.  Values must be scaled by the chosen load unit (P-literal) and by geometric deformations (GEO_DEFORMATION, GEO_ROTATION, GEO_DISTORTION).  No positive‐definiteness check is performed.  
- DAMP (damping matrix): Same format as STIF, but values are scaled according to VELOCITY, A_VELOCITY or W_VELOCITY for damping forces.  
- MASS: Same row/column format, with scaling by ACCELERATION, A_ACCELERATION or W_ACCELERATION for inertial forces.  

Notes:  
• For matrices larger than six degrees of freedom, build the full matrix by linking multiple ADDM records via sub‐matrices.  
• Frequency‐dependent (impedance) definitions are only activated when PER is non‐zero; full impedance processing is not supported for all matrix types yet.

The table defines the layout of a single FLEX record, which is used to introduce a general elastic support (for example, a pile trestle) at one or two nodes in a finite‐element model.  Each FLEX record consists of several lines sharing the same element number (NO); each line corresponds to one “unit load” case P and the elastic response (displacements, rotations, warping) at the specified node(s).

1. Record header items  
   • NO   (Element number)  
     – Integer identifier of this elastic‐support element.  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: mandatory (“!”) – you must supply it.  
   • NO1  (Node number 1)  
     – The primary node where the unit load is applied and at which the elastic response is computed.  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: mandatory (“!”).  
   • NO2  (Node number 2)  
     – Optional second node. If specified (≠ 0), the record may define a stiffness coupling between NO1 and NO2.  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: 0 (no second node; i.e. pure single-node support).

2. Unit‐load identifier (“P”)  
   • Literal (LIT) text field selecting one of the seven loading directions or moments:  
       – PX, PY, PZ → force in kN along the global X, Y, Z axes  
       – MX, MY, MZ → moment in kNm about the global X, Y, Z axes  
       – MB        → bimoment in kNm^2  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: mandatory (“!”).  

   Each instance of P defines one “column” of the local stiffness (or compliance) submatrix for node NO1 (and NO2, if used).  Zero diagonal entries (e.g. specifying a zero for UX when P = PX) are not processed—use nodal constraints for fully rigid support.

3. Elastic‐response components (effects at NO1 due to the specified unit load P)  
   • UX, UY, UZ  (translations in mm)  
   • UXX, UYY, UZZ  (rotations in mrad)  
   • UW  (warp in 1/km)  

   For each component, you supply the displacement or rotation at NO1 when the single unit load P is applied.  
   – Units:  
       UX, UY, UZ → [mm]_1003  
       UXX, UYY, UZZ → [mrad]_1004  
       UW → [1/km]_1005  
   – Defaults: 0. If you omit the field or set it to zero, that coupling term is assumed zero (no elastic restraint in that component).

4. Notes on usage and context  
   – To build a complete 6×6 stiffness (or flexibility) submatrix at node NO1, you supply six FLEX lines (one for each P = PX, PY, PZ, MX, MY, MZ) plus an optional MB case if bimoments are relevant.  
   – Diagonal zeros are automatically skipped; rigid behavior must be enforced via BOUN/SPRI (nodal constraints) rather than zeroing FLEX diagonals.  
   – For general stiffness, mass or damping matrices—especially when cross‐coupling is complex—use the ADDM record rather than the deprecated NO2‐coupling option.  
   – Deprecated option: if NO2 is nonzero, each FLEX line defines one row or column of the stiffness submatrix between node NO1 and NO2. Units remain kN/m or matching units for each record; the solver does not check positive definiteness.  

See also:  
  ADDM (general matrices),  
  BOUN/SPRI (rigid supports),  
  GRP (element grouping).

 FLEX
 FLEX can be used for the input of general elastic supports (e.g. pile trestle) for a single node. An element or sub-element consists of several FLEX records with the same element number, where for each unit load ’P’ (in fixed units kn and m ), the displacements are input as affected components. Components with diagonal terms 0 are not processed, and rigid supports must be defined by means of nodal constraints.
 General stiffness, mass or damping matrices may be defined with record ADDM.
 However there is still an obsoleted option to define a stiffness matrix with FLEX: By defining NR2 with a second node number, the values for an explicit row or column of the submatrix of node NR1-NR2 may be defined as stiffness valkues in (kN,m) or a matching explicit unit for every single item. A check for ”positive definite” is not performed.

The table shown defines the keywords, parameters, units and default values for the MASS command used in dynamic analysis. Each row corresponds to one field of the input record.  Below is a detailed, field-by-field description:

1. Item “NO”  
   – Description: Identifies the node number (in the model’s nodal database) to which the mass entry applies. Alternatively, you may specify the literal FIT or FITL to apply masses along a Fit element.  
   – Unit: “–” or “LIT” (literal identifier)  
   – Default: 1  

2. Translational Masses (MX, MY, MZ)  
   – MX: Translatory mass in the X-direction  
   – MY, MZ: Same as MX but for Y and Z directions (defaults to the MX value if not explicitly set)  
   – Unit: [*] (see remarks on units below – typically [t] for a single mass or [t/m] for distributed masses)  
   – Default: MX = 0.0; MY = MX; MZ = MX  

3. Rotational Masses (MXX, MYY, MZZ)  
   – MXX: Rotational (moment of inertia) mass about the global X-axis  
   – MYY, MZZ: Rotational masses about the Y and Z axes (hints for dimensions provided below)  
   – Unit: [*] (usually [tm²] for a point moment of inertia or [tm²/m] for distributed)  
   – Default: all zero  

4. Off-Diagonal Mass Terms (MXY, MXZ, MYZ)  
   – Represent coupling terms in the 3×3 mass matrix when the rotation axis is inclined  
   – Unit: [*]  
   – Default: 0.0  

5. Warping Mass “MB”  
   – Captures the torsional warping inertia, used in special beam‐torsion analyses  
   – Unit: [tm⁴]  
   – Default: 0.0  

6. Reference & Persistence Flag “REF”  
   – Controls whether the mass is temporary or persistent, and in which coordinate system it is stored:  
     • TEMP: Temporary global mass (deleted on redefinition)  
     • GLOB: Persistent mass in the global coordinate system  
     • LOCA: Persistent mass in the element’s local coordinate system  
   – Unit: LIT (literal)  
   – Default: GLOB  

7. Load Case Identifier “LC”  
   – Specifies which load case in the central database (CDB) to convert into mass entries  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: “!” (the currently active load case)  

8. Permanent-Load Percentage “PRZ”  
   – Defines ψ-factors (PSI0, PSI1, PSI2) to scale nodal/element loading into additional mass entries (e.g., quasi-permanent combinations)  
   – Unit: LIT (literal combination identifier) or – (numeric factor)  
   – Default: 100  

9. Load Selection Filter “SELE”  
   – Selects which loading to convert to mass, and in which direction:  
     • PG: Nodal loads in gravity direction  
     • PGB: Beam loads in gravity direction  
     • PXX/PYY/PZZ: Nodal loads in global X/Y/Z  
     • PXXB/PYYB/PZZB: Beam loads in global directions  
     • PXB/PYB/PZB: Beam loads in local directions  
     • PGS/PGSB: Negative masses for holes (special)  
     – Further EXPLICIT factors via MX…MB may be supplied.  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: PG  

10. FIT Range Nodes (NA, NE)  
   – NA: Start node of the Fit element range  
   – NE: End node of the Fit element range  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: “–” (not used unless FIT/FITL is specified in NO)  

Remarks on Units and Usage  
• Single masses are entered in [t] (translational) or [tm²] (rotational); distributed masses use [t/m] or [tm²/m].  
• For axisymmetric models, values are specified per arc length ([t/m] or [tm²/m]), and internally multiplied by the radius.  
• Temporary masses (REF=TEMP) disappear on redefinition; global and local masses accumulate across restarts unless explicitly deleted via MASS DEL.  
• Self-weight of materials is automatically converted into mass entries—if unwanted, set material self-weight to zero.  
• To capture variable loading effects on natural frequencies, convert static load cases via ASE/DYNA or SOFiMSHA with appropriate ψ-factors.  
• Off-diagonal mass terms require a fully consistent mass matrix representation.  

This table-driven input format gives the user full control over translational, rotational and warping mass assignments—both pointwise and distributed—and how they persist, combine and align with load cases and coordinate systems.

MASS

 Temporary masses may be also created by ASE and DYNA, old values will automatically deleted with a redefinition. Persistent masses will be accumulated with a restart, but may be deleted with a MASS DEL command.
 A translatoric mass usually acts equally in all three coordinate directions, they should therefore be input for all three directions. Rotational masses however have a clear rotation axis and if
 this axis is inclined we get off diagonal terms for the mass matrix, which can be used only for a fully consistent mass matrix.
 For dynamic analysis the self-weight of the entire structure is always converted to masses. If this is not intended, the user has to define the self-weights of the materials as zero. Additional masses defined with MASS will also trigger additional loads for automatic self-weight loading of statical load cases unless defined as REF TEMP.
 For the correct Eigenvalues it is generally necessary to add masses from variable loading. It is recommended to define them based on static load cases within ASE / DYNA with their MASS command or with SOFiMSHA and a restart as additional masses. It is possible to convert nodal loads from any load case to mass entries with a given percentage of the loading. The most useful default is given by the quasi permanent combination value ψ2. The definition of a literal for PRZ will select the combination value from the imported load case, or if this value is pointing to the action, the value of the action of the main project is taken as factor.
 SELE defines a Filter on the loads to be converted. Other valid literals are: PXX, PYY, PZZ for nodal loads; PXXB, PYYB, PZZB for beam loads in global directions; PXB, PYB, PZB for beam loads in local directions. For nodal loads, all generated loads from other element load definitions will be included, if the load case has been analyzed before. For PG and PGB only those loads acting really in the direction of gravity will be converted. For beam loads, the defined excentricities will be squared to establish the rotational inertia for the torsion using the optional factor MXX.

For nodal loads, all generated loads from other element load definitions will be included, if the load case has been analyzed before. For PG and PGB only those loads acting really in the direction of gravity will be converted. For beam loads, the defined excentricities will be squared to establish the rotational inertia for the torsion using the optional factor MXX..
 For special cases it is possible to define explicit further factors via entries MX to MB with the unit [-]. If no unit is defined, the factor is taken as it is, but then the user has to take care of a correct SI-transformation factor from loads to masses or even rotational masses. A very special case is the generation of negative masses to account for holes. This may be accomplished with the Literal PGS or PGSB for SELE.
 For a FIT all masses are defined per length of the Fit, thus in [t/m] or [tm2/m]. For axis symmetric systems values are usually defined per arc length: Masses are in [t/m] or [tm2/m], distributed Masses in [t/m2] or [tm2/m2]. The table in question defines the keyword‐block “SBOX” used to carve out a geometric selection of nodes (and hence elements) for subsequent commands (DEL, MOD, TRAN, MIRR).  In essence, SBOX allows you to specify one or more volumetric or planar regions—boxes, spheres, cylinders, parallelepipeds, skewed slabs or arbitrary polygons with constant thickness—and to accumulate them with logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) before applying a delete, modify, translate or mirror operation.  Below is a structured description of each column and row in the table:

1. Columns  
   • Item: the parameter name or keyword to be supplied on the SBOX record.  
   • Description: a concise summary of what the parameter controls.  
   • Unit: the dimensional unit in which numeric values must be given; for all coordinates, radii and thicknesses it is meters [m] (internal code 1001).  
   • Default: the assumed value if the parameter is omitted; an asterisk (*) indicates “use current default or extreme global extent,” a dash (–) indicates “no default,” and for OPT the default selection logic is OR.

2. First Axis (A1–B1)  
   • A1X, A1Y, A1Z: the X, Y, Z coordinates of the first corner (start point) of the region or, alternatively, “GPT nnn” to refer to the coordinates of an existing node nnn.  
   • B1X, B1Y, B1Z: the X, Y, Z coordinates of the opposite corner (end point) along the first axis.  
   • All six parameters share unit [m] and default “*,” meaning if you omit them the software will fill in the minimum and maximum extents of the entire model in that coordinate direction (with Z tied to gravity in spatial systems or vertical in planar ones).

3. Second Axis (A2–B2)  
   • A2X, A2Y, A2Z: defines the second axis by its own start point.  
   • B2X, B2Y, B2Z: defines the end point of the second axis.  
   • Same unit [m] and default (“*”) behavior as the first axis.

4. Third Axis (A3–B3)  
   • A3X, A3Y, A3Z: start point for the third axis of selection.  
   • B3X, B3Y, B3Z: end point for that axis.  
   • Again, units are [m] and default is “*.”  When no explicit axes are given but a radius R is provided, the three axes will default to the global coordinate extremes.

5. Optional Scalar Parameters  
   • R: an optional radius [m].  If supplied, the selection becomes spherical (centered at A1) or cylindrical (along A1–B1) with that radius.  Default is “–” (no radius).  
   • T: an optional thickness [m].  For plane and polygon definitions this gives the half‐thickness perpendicular to the defined plane.  Default is “–.”

6. OPT (Selection Logic and Polygon Mode)  
   • OPT is a literal token that takes one of: AND, OR, NOT, POL, PAND, POR, PNOT.  
     – AND: every node/element must lie inside all currently defined SBOX regions.  
     – OR: a node/element is selected if it lies in at least one region (this is the default).  
     – NOT: invert selection for that region (exclude what lies inside).  
     – POL: this signals the start (or continuation) of a polygon vertex list (up to 10 coordinates per record) with constant thickness T.  
     – PAND/POR/PNOT: polygon definitions that combine the polygon region with AND, OR or NOT logic.  
   • Unit is “LIT” (literal).  
   • Default is OR.

Usage Notes  
– If you call SBOX with no parameters, the current SBOX definitions are cleared.  
– You can string together multiple SBOX records; they accumulate and only “reset” when you apply them with DEL/MOD/TRAN/MIRR or explicitly issue an empty SBOX.  
– Syntax variants allow defining polygons in one long list or across several SBOX lines, using OPT POL/PAND etc.  
– Coordinate keywords (A1X, B2Z, etc.) may be mixed with GPT node references for ease of selecting around existing mesh points.

The illustration is a three-dimensional, oblique-projection sketch of a “spar” selection box—that is, a general parallelepiped defined by three independent edge-vectors.  It corresponds to the third bullet under SBOX in the accompanying text: “A general parallelepiped (spar) defined by three independent axis.”

Key visual elements and labeling:

    - A1: A horizontal edge running straight to the right from the origin, labeled “A1.”  
    - A2: A receding edge running diagonally down and away into the plane of the page, labeled “A2.”  
    - A3: A slanted edge running diagonally down and forward (toward the viewer), labeled “A3.”  

   These three axes need not be orthogonal—they define a skewed box in space.

 3. Opposite Edges (B1, B2, B3)  
    - On the face reached by translating A1, A2, A3 to the “far” end of each vector, you see the three corresponding opposite edges:  
      • B1 runs upward-right from the far end of A1 (parallel to A3’s direction).  
      • B2 runs upward-right (but more steeply) from the far end of A2 (parallel to A1’s direction).  
      • B3 runs upward-right (yet at a slightly different angle) from the far end of A3 (parallel to A2’s direction).  

    These B-edges close off the top “face” of the spar, each being parallel to one of the original A-axes.

 4. Hidden or Dotted Edges  
    - To complete the box shape, some edges that lie behind the visible faces are drawn as dotted lines. These indicate the rearmost connections between vertices.

 5. Caption  
    - Beneath the figure is the legend: “Figure 3.35: A general parallelepiped (spar).”

How it ties into the SBOX command set:

  • In a CAD or mesh-editing context, defining an SBOX spar requires specifying six points (or three direction vectors):  
    – The starting node coordinates (implicit origin).  
    – The tip of A1 (A1X, A1Y, A1Z), the tip of A2 (A2X, A2Y, A2Z), and the tip of A3 (A3X, A3Y, A3Z).  
  • Once those three axis vectors are defined, the software constructs the six faces of the parallelepiped.  
  • Any finite element mesh nodes that lie strictly inside that skewed volume are flagged as selected.  
  • The selection may then be passed to DEL (delete), MOD (modify), TRAN (translate), or MIRR (mirror) operations as described in the SBOX text.

The table summarizes the input parameters accepted by the DEL record, which is used to mark finite-element model components for deletion at the end of a program run. Unlike immediate removal commands, DEL only sets deletion markers; the elements remain in the active model (and continue to participate in all intermediate steps such as transformations or contact checks) until the very last processing pass. Because nodes cannot be deleted with DEL, only element types are supported. When complex selection logic or dynamic group manipulation with negative group divisors is required, the user must fall back on multiple DEL blocks combined with a SYST REST or use the explicit selection mechanisms described under TRAN (e.g. SBOX).

Column Layout  
• Item: the keyword specifying one of the eight recognized fields.  
• Description: human-readable summary of each field’s purpose.  
• Unit: engineering units (if any) in which values must be supplied. Square-bracket notation with subscript “1001” indicates the internal unit code. A dash (—) means “unitless.”  
• Default: the assumed value if the field is omitted or set to “*” (wildcard) in the command line.

Table Field Details  
1. TYPE  
  – Description: element category to delete. Must be one of the literal codes (LIT) listed below.  
  – Unit: LIT (literal string)  
  – Default: “!” (an exclamation point indicates no deletion type specified, so no elements are marked).  
  – Valid Codes:  
     • KINE – kinematic constraints on nodes (though nodes themselves cannot be removed, the constraints are marked deleted)  
     • BEAM – beam (1D bending) elements  
     • TRUS – truss elements  
     • CABL – cable elements  
     • SPRI – discrete spring elements  
     • QUAD – shell (2D plate/quad) elements  
     • BRIC – solid/brick (3D volume) elements  

2. FROM  
  – Description: the first element (or group) number in a sequential range to delete.  
  – Unit: unitless  
  – Default: 1

3. TO  
  – Description: the last element (or group) number in the range.  
  – Unit: unitless  
  – Default: * (all the way to the highest available number)

4. INC  
  – Description: increment for stepping through selection numbers or group IDs; a negative sign (–) may be used only in literal-type mode (LIT).  
  – Unit: —/LIT (unitless when numeric, literal when specifying groups)  
  – Default: 1

5–10. XMIN, YMIN, ZMIN, XMAX, YMAX, ZMAX  
  – Description: define a 3-D box. Only elements whose entire geometry lies within the axis-aligned bounding box are marked. Coordinates are interpreted in the global reference frame. If any of the six limits is set to “*,” that bound is considered unbounded (e.g. XMIN = * means no lower X bound).  
  – Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁ (meters, internal code 1001)  
  – Default: * (no bounding constraint)

Usage Notes and Limitations  
• All marked elements remain active until the end of execution. They will appear in dynamic groups (including negative group filters) and during all transformation (TRAN) steps unless manually excluded.  
• Since deletion is deferred, interactive selection tools such as SBOX or window-based picks only set markers; they do not remove elements immediately.  
• For complex deletion logic—particularly when mixing type-level selections with spatial filters or when dynamic group divisors are negative—users must orchestrate multiple DEL records interleaved with SYST REST calls to isolate the intended subsets.  
• Consult the records MOD, TRAN, MIRR, and SBOX for alternate or complementary methods of selection, manipulation, and eventual removal of model components.

See also: MOD, TRAN, MIRR, SBOX
 DEL
 With DEL it is possible to delete existing elements at the end of the program run. Nodes however may not be deleted.
 The following types are possible:
 KINE Kinematic Constraints of nodes
 BEAM Beam elements
 TRUS Truss elements
 CABL Cable elements
 SPRI Spring elements
 QUAD Shell elements
 BRIC Volume elements
 As a DEL sets only markers, which are processed at the end of the program run, the deleted elements remain active until then and will be active during all processing steps (e.g. TRAN). Even for a selection using a window or a SBOX, DEL sets only markers on the element num- bers. Thus the usage for dynamic groups with a negative group divisor is severely restricted. In all those cases, where these limitations become relevant, a definition with several blocks and a SYST REST has to be used.
 The element selection and definition of a selective box is done as described in record TRAN.

The MOD record’s input signature is summarized in a four-column table (Item, Description, Unit, Default). It defines which existing elements or nodes will be modified, and how. Below is a detailed walkthrough of each parameter:

1. Column Layout  
  • Item   – the keyword or literal you type into the input stream.  
  • Description   – a brief explanation of the parameter’s role.  
  • Unit   – the physical units expected (or “LIT” for literal values, “–” for unitless).  
  • Default   – the value assumed when you omit the field (“*” means “no limit/ignore,” “!” flags “not set,” a numeric default is used otherwise).

2. Row-by-Row Breakdown  
  2.1 TYPE  
    – Description: Specifies which element family or node type you wish to modify.  
    – Allowed values (LIT): NODE, BEAM, TRUS, CABL, SPRI, QUAD, BRIC  
    – Unit: LIT  
    – Default: ! (mandatory; must be supplied)  

  2.2 FROM  
    – Description: The starting ID (or group) number in your selection range.  
    – Unit: – (unitless integer)  
    – Default: 1  

  2.3 TO  
    – Description: The ending ID (or group) number in your selection range.  
    – Unit: – (unitless integer)  
    – Default: * (up to the last existing element/node)  

  2.4 INC  
    – Description: Step size between IDs in the range, or a literal GRP code.  
    – Unit: – / LIT  
    – Default: 1  

  2.5 XMIN, YMIN, ZMIN  
    – Description: Lower coordinate limits of a 3D selection box. Only elements whose centroids lie inside this box will be eligible for modification.  
    – Unit: [m] (unit code 1001)  
    – Default: * (no lower bound)  

  2.6 XMAX, YMAX, ZMAX  
    – Description: Upper coordinate limits of the selection box (complements XMIN–ZMIN). For more complex geometric selections, an SBOX may be defined beforehand via the SBOX record; see also the TRAN record for selective-box definition syntax.  
    – Unit: [m] (unit code 1001)  
    – Default: * (no upper bound)  

  2.7 FIX  
    – Description: Support condition keyword, allowed only when TYPE=NODE. This adds constraints to nodes without redefining them.  
    – Unit: LIT  
    – Default: – (no change to supports)

3. Usage Notes & Cross-References  
  • MOD cannot create new nodes or elements; it only adjusts properties (defined earlier via PROP) on existing IDs.  
  • To redefine beam subdivisions (DIV), you must first remove and re-insert beams via TRAN or MIRR—MOD cannot change the topology.  
  • Property groups (e.g. all thickness definitions or local coordinate‐system settings) update atomically. Supplying a single subgroup record (e.g. DROT alone) resets the entire group to default plus your rotate angle.  
  • See DEL (element deletion), TRAN (element/transformation records), MIRR (mirroring), and SBOX for detailed geometric and selection-box operations.

See also: DEL, TRAN, MIRR, SBOX
 MOD
 With MOD it is possible to change the support conditions of nodes or the properties of exist- ing elements. The properties of the elements selected will be modified according to the last element record with property attribute PROP.
 However for nodes only support conditions may be added with FIX. Compared with a direct definition with record NODE, the benefits of MOD are mainly the provision of geometric attribute volumes.
 The following types are possible:
 NODE support conditions for nodes
 BEAM Beam elements
 TRUS Truss elements
 CABL Cable elements
 SPRI Spring elements
 QUAD Shell elements
 BRIC Volume elements
 With following input for example the element thickness is modified to 22 cm only for the QUAD elements No. 1 till 155:
 QUAD PROP T 0.22
 MOD QUAD FROM 1 TO 155
 The element selection and definition of a selective box is done as described in record TRAN.
 Hints:
 • MOD may only change existing data, it is not possible to generate any new data structures. Thus a change of beam subdivisions (BEAM PROP DIV nn) is only possible with a TRAN or MIRR command.
 • Properties are organized in groups, which may be changed only in total. For example all thickness values or all definitions for the local coordinate system define a group each. A definition of DROT only will thus create a new standard orientation although rotated by DROT.

The table shown is the master input‐definition for the TRAN (transformation) command.  It is organized in four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and covers every keyword you can supply to TRAN (and, by extension, MIRR when used for mirroring).  Below is a breakdown of its structure, grouped by functionality.

1.  Selection of Entities  
   • TYPE  
     – defines which entity class to transform.  Literals (LIT) allowed: ALL, NODE, EDGE, BEAM, QUAD, etc.  
     – Default: ALL  
   • FROM / TO  
     – first and last ID in the numeric range of nodes or elements.  
     – No units.  
     – Default FROM=1, TO=* (all)  
   • INC  
     – increment for stepping through FROM…TO or FIT/GRP.  
     – Units: “–/LIT” (can be number or literal GRP, FIT).  
     – Default: 1  
   • WIDE  
     – linear‐interval selection in the chosen translation direction. Only entities fully within [REF + 0…WIDE] get copied.  
     – Default: 0.0 (disabled)  

2.  Geometric Box Selection (requires prior SBOX definition)  
   • XMIN, YMIN, ZMIN / XMAX, YMAX, ZMAX  
     – only elements completely inside the global‐coordinate box are selected.  
     – Units: [m] (global meters); tag “1001” points to a unit‐conversion reference.  
     – Defaults: all blank (no box filtering)  

3.  Property & Support Filters  
   • PROP  
     – choose which element‐property classes receive the “current” properties instead of inheriting OLD ones  
       · NEW: all types get new props  
       · OLD: none (delete defaults)  
       · B, T, C, Q, H: beam, truss, cable, quad, brick only  
     – Unit: LIT  
     – Default: OLD (inherit old)  
     – Exception: first TRAN after a new PROP implicitly activates it and then reverts to OLD.  
   • FIX  
     – logical‐AND support‐condition filter.  Any new node only inherits those supports that were common in the source node and FIX.  
     – Unit: LIT  
     – Default: blank  

4.  Translation & Rotation  
   • DX, DY, DZ  
     – translation distances in X, Y, Z global axes.  
     – Units: [m] (1001)  
     – Defaults: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0  
   • PHIX, PHIY, PHIZ  
     – incremental rotation about X, Y, Z axes.  
     – Units: [°] (tag 5: uses ALPH‐NORM convention)  
     – Defaults: 0, 0, 0  
   • ALPH, BETA, THET  
     – alternative rotation angles: precision (meridian), main rotation, nutation/descent.  
     – Units: [°]5  
     – Defaults: 0, 0, 0  

5.  Numbering & Reference Point  
   • DNO  
     – increment added to source ID to form new IDs (nodes or elements).  
     – “0” triggers automatic numbering above current maximum.  
     – “SELF” keeps identical IDs (import only; see restrictions).  
     – Unit: “–/LIT”  
     – Default: 0  
   • DNON  
     – increment for newly generated element‐node numbers (distinct offset).  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: 0  
   • REFX, REFY, REFZ  
     – reference point for all translations and rotations.  Default is global origin (0,0,0).  
     – Units: [m]1001  
     – Defaults: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0  

Key Notes from Context  
-  TRAN + MIRR can generate new copies by rotation, translation, or mirroring of selected nodes/elements.  
-  Sequence of operations (scale, rotate, translate) matters only if rotations are involved.  
-  New nodes are either mapped to existing ones or assigned fresh IDs; element group numbers remain unless overridden with GRP.  
-  Extrusion features (via PROP Xnnn or FIT) can combine original and transformed geometry into higher‐order elements (beams → quads → bricks).  

This table thus fully specifies how to select, filter, transform, number, and re-assign properties or supports when copying or mirroring geometry in the database.
