 With TRAN and MIRR it is possible to generate new nodes and/or elements by rotating and translating respective mirroring existing ones from any database (see IMPO) .
 The most simple transformation is a scaling and displacement only. If rotations are added, the sequence of the operations becomes important. A simple general rotation method is the simul- taneous incremental rotation by a rotation tensor (see theoretical principles). The definition of ALPH NORM a normalization based on the tangent values is selected which is easier to use in most cases, but is not unique for some angles with 90 degrees.
 The numbers of the nodes or elements to be transformed are selected via a range FROM TO INC. Without any definition all elements are selected, if a value for FROM is given, the default value for TO is the same number. With a definition of INC GRP the numbers are treated as group numbers.
 With the type EGDE an already defined sequence of nodes may be copied and will be mem- orized as a new sequence. If only the FROM value is given, the edge with that number is addressed, if both values are given, the sequence of the edge between those nodes is cho- sen.
 The number of a transformed element is the source number plus DNO. By entering DNO 0 the new numbers of elements or nodes are automatically assigned. With DNO SELF the node and element numbers will not be changed for an import. For a transformation within the project data base, option SELF is only allowed for a node selection, as long as no elements have been defined yet, and only before any system restart occurs.
 The group number of the elements remain unchanged if GRP 0 is selected, otherwise the elements will be reassigned to the currently selected group. Therefore it is not possible to shift elements to a different group with a DNO value.

For a transformation within the project data base, option SELF is only allowed for a node selection, as long as no elements have been defined yet, and only before any system restart occurs.. The group number of the elements remain unchanged if GRP 0 is selected, otherwise the elements will be reassigned to the currently selected group. Therefore it is not possible to shift elements to a different group with a DNO value..
 New nodes of the elements will be generated automatically. With an explicit definition of DNON the new nodes will have a distinct offset to their old node if the old node has been defined explicitly. Generated nodes will be either mapped to existing nodes or receive new generated node numbers aobove the current upper limit number (see CTRL NODE).
 For a translation it is possible to select the elements to be copied by defining a value for WIDE. Only those elements will be copied then, which are fully in the interval defined by the reference point and the distance wide in the translation direction. Positive values define a region behind the reference point, negative values define a region before the reference point.
 The properties of the elements will be kept in general from the original (OLD). However it is possible to select element classes which will receive the current defined element properties:
 NEW all element types
 OLD no element types, delete defaults
 B beam elements
 T truss elements
 C cable elements
 Q QUAD elements
 H BRIC elements
 To simplify the input definition there is one exception. If a PROP has not yet been used, it will be activated for the first following TRAN. For all other following TRAN the default will be OLD again.
 The local coordinate systems of the BEAM and QUAD elements will be transformed in the same way, however it is possible to specify with a BEAM or QUAD PROP-record an explicit direction via KR or a vector DRX to DRZ and an additional rotation which is applied on the newly generated coordinate system and NOT on the original coordinate system. Directions of springs will be recalculated in all cases, thus explicit directions have to be specified with a PROP-record.
 Support conditions are created via a filter, i.e. any new node will receive support conditions only which are common to the original node and the support filter FIX. (Logical AND)
 Last not least, it is also possible to use TRAN and MIRR to generate elements by an extru- sion, i.e. the original nodes and the transformed nodes will be combined to a higher type of element with the currently defined properties. If desired a subdivision of that extrusion may be performed. This is input via the item PROP and the input value Xnnn, where nnn is either an optional number for a uniform subdivision or the literal FIT. The latter case the Item FIX is used to define:

the original nodes and the transformed nodes will be combined to a higher type of element with the currently defined properties. If desired a subdivision of that extrusion may be performed. This is input via the item PROP and the input value Xnnn, where nnn is either an optional number for a uniform subdivision or the literal FIT. The latter case the Item FIX is used to define:.
 a number of an EDGE respective a structural line
 • a @ followed by the number of a structural line if the original coordinates should be taken as local coordinates.
 • a negative number of a structural line if the local coordinate system of the edge is not to be used.
 two nodes of a fit or an edge in the format node1:node2
 The FIT of those nodes defines than the position of the extruded nodes in the way that all elements are taken relative to the reference point (REFX,REFY,REFY, default is the origin for FIX, first node of the FIT for PROP YFIT) and copied and optionally rotated to each node of the nodal sequence. For a pure EDGE the software will detect circular arcs automatically if there are at least three points available within the fit. For TYPE there are then only four possibilities allowed with an extrusion:
 NODE each selected node triggers a beam element
 EDGE an edge yields QUAD elements
 BEAM Beam elements trigger QUAD elements
 QUAD QUAD-elements trigger BRIC-elements
 The geometric reference number of the extruded QUAD and BRIC elements will be created from the element number of the original element according to the settings of CTRL EXTR.
 When extruding a point, truss or cable elements will be created if a PROP record of TRUS or CABL type is preceding the TRAN record.

The table you provided defines the syntax and semantics of an “extrusion” record (often called EXTR) in a finite‐element preprocessing language.  This record lets you sweep or extrude an existing set of “source” entities (nodes, beams, shells, etc.) into higher‐dimensional elements (beams into quads, quads into bricks, etc.).  Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter breakdown:

1.  TYPE  (unit = LIT, mandatory)  
    •  Specifies what kind of source entities you are extruding.  Common literal values include:  
       –  NODE: single nodes → beam elements  
       –  NODT: nodes → trusses  
       –  NODC: nodes → cables  
       –  BEAM, SLN, EDGE: line‐types → quad shells  
       –  QUAD: shell elements → brick (3D solid) elements  
       –  SAR: surface areas → bricks  
       –  FIX, KINE, SPRI: various constraint or spring templates → layers of new constraint or spring elements  
    •  No default—must be specified.

2.  FROM, TO, INC  (unit = integer selector, FROM mandatory)  
    •  FROM: start index, or selector type if a group or structural entity is used (e.g. “GRP”, “EDGE”, “SLN”, “SAR”).  
    •  TO: end index or ID.  If FROM is a literal index range, TO is the last index; if FROM names a selector, TO is the selector ID and INC is ignored.  
    •  INC: increment between successive entity IDs.  Default INC = 1 when a numeric range is used.  
    •  Together these parameters define exactly which source entities are picked for extrusion.  Valid combinations depend on TYPE (e.g. for TYPE = SPRI, you must select by EDGE).

3.  PATH  (unit = LIT, mandatory)  
    Defines along what geometric or parametric path your entities will sweep.  Options:  
    •  DIR: straight‐line extrusion by a vector (see V1–V3).  
    •  EDGE: follow an existing nodal sequence (EDGE ID = V1).  
    •  FIT: sweep between two spatial points (V1, V2, V3 define endpoints).  
    •  SLN: along a structural line (line ID = V1, can prefix with “–” to invert orientation).  
    Default: none—one form of PATH must be given.

4.  V1, V2, V3  (unit = * or m)  
    •  When PATH = DIR, V1–V3 are the X–Y–Z components of the extrusion vector.  
    •  When PATH = EDGE/FIT/SLN, V1 carries the ID of the edge or line; V2 and V3 are unused for EDGE/SLN and for FIT they supply the second point coordinates.  
    •  V1 is mandatory; V2 and V3 default to “–” when not required.

5.  DIV  (unit = integer subdivisions, optional)  
    •  Number of segments or layers to create along the path.  
    •  For DIR‐type paths, DIV is required.  
    •  For EDGE/FIT/SLN, if omitted the mesh will automatically subdivide at existing nodes along the geometry.

6.  SREF  (unit = node ID, optional)  
    •  Reference node on the source geometry.  
    •  When set, the chosen source nodes or elements are first translated so that SREF coincides with the start of the PATH.  
    •  If not provided, extrusion always begins “in‐place,” and the source stays put.

7.  OPT  (unit = LIT2, optional)  
    •  Only applicable with PATH = SLN (a structural line).  
    •  “R” rotates each source entity to align with the local coordinate system along the line (instead of preserving its original orientation).

8.  SNAP  (unit = LIT, default = YES)  
    Controls nodal connectivity at each subdivision:  
    •  YES: snap new nodes to any existing nodes lying on the path.  
    •  NO: always create fresh nodes.  
    •  TOPO: attempt to match only topologically related nodes when possible.

9.  FLIP  (unit = LIT, default = NO)  
    •  For 3D QUAD extrusions, inverts the local “Z‐axis” orientation of the generated element before filling with brick elements.  
    •  YES to flip; NO to preserve the original shell‐normal direction.

Hints & Cross‐References  
•  Temporary “template” elements (springs, couplings, kinematic links) can be used to define an extrusion but should typically be deleted (via a DEL command) before analysis.  
•  See also: TRAN (translate), LOFT (loft between multiple cross‐sections) for alternative shape‐generation records.

See also: TRAN, LOFT
 EXTR
 NO
 This record allows to create elements by extruding or sweeping a set of selected source ele- ments to new elements of a higher dimension. For example, nodes can be extruded to beam elements, beams or nodal sequences can be extruded to quad elements and quads to bric ele- ments. The properties of the elements generated during extrusion can be defined by preceding property initialization records, e.g. GRP NO 1 REF 10, QUAD PROP MNO 2.
 The type of the source elements is defined at parameter TYPE. The following table summarizes all available options as well as the resulting type of elements:
 Option Type of source element will be extruded to NODE Nodes Beam elements NODT Nodes Truss elements NODC Nodes Cable elements FIX Nodal constraints Layers of nodal constraints KINE Kinematic dependencies Layers of kinematic dependencies SPRI Spring elements Layers of spring elements EDGE Nodal sequence Quad elements BEAM Beam elements Quad elements SLN Structural line Quad elements QUAD Shell elements Bric elements
 SAR
 Structural area
 Bric elements
 The source elements can be selected using parameters FROM, TO and INC, by a range of element numbers, a group number or the ID of the hosting structural element, if applicable. Especially for spring elements, it is enough that only one of the spring nodes belongs to a nodal sequence or structural line, in order to be selected. Whenever parameter FROM is a literal, then the selection ID is given in parameter TO and parameter INC is not taken into consideration. The following table summarizes the valid selection combinations for each source element type:
 TYPE FROM TO NODE − − FIX − / EDGE / SLN − / −, LT4 / − KINE − / EDGE / SLN − / −, LT4 / − SPRI EDGE − / LT4 − SLN − − QUAD − / GRP / SGRP / SAR − / − / LT4 / − SAR − −

 Hint
 Temporary source elements, such as spring elements or couplings, acting only as a tem- plate for the extrusion, should be deleted after the extrusion with a separate DEL com- mand, or excluded from a subsequent analysis.
 A linear extrusion path can be defined using PATH DIR. In this case, the direction and length of the extrusion is entered as a vector in parameters V1, V2 and V3. Alternatively, an extrusion path definition using an existing nodal sequence or structural line is possible, with the use of PATH EDGE / FIT / SLN and an ID at V1. The extrusion start- and end-node depend on the orientation of the path, as it has been defined. It is possible to invert this orientation using a minus (-) symbol at the value of V1.
 Parameter DIV defines the number of subdivisions or layers along the extrusion path. In the case that the extrusion path is defined by EDGE / FIT / SLN, parameter DIV is optional, while for PATH DIR it is required. In the first case, if DIV is not provided, the number of subdivisions is defined by the sequence of nodes along the line or the edge.
 By default, the extrusion starts at the position of the source elements, even if the extrusion path is not connected to the source elements. This behavior can be changed by setting the number of a reference node on the source, at parameter SREF. In this case, the elements of the source are first copied to the start-point of the extrusion path, such that the reference point coincides with the start-point.
 The orientation of the source elements is kept along the extrusion by default. For an extrusion along a structural line, this can be changed by setting parameter OPT to R. In this case, the source elements are rotated according to the local coordinate system along the structural line.

metadata.sections: 3.29 EXTR – Extrusion and sweeping of elements

content:
Finally, parameter SNAP offers the possibility to control whether the generated elements will be attached to existing nodes of the system, in case the node positions coincide. Otherwise, this parameter has no effect.
 Option YES will use a detected node at the computed coordinates, giving priority to the one most recently created. However, if a path with explicitly specified node numbers is given, e.g. EDGE, SLN, then a coinciding path node is prefered, so that the new elements are attached to the nodes of the path.
 Option NO will unconditionally force the generation of new nodes.
 Option TOPO will give priority to a node which, in the existing system, is directly connected, i.e. through a finite element, with the corresponding node used in the previous extrusion layer. If no such a node exists, then the behaviour is the same as with SNAP YES.
 This option may be useful when extruding unconnected elements, with coinciding nodes, and it is desirable that the new extruded elements remain unconnected. Or in a similar case where, however, 0-length spring elements are extruded inbetween. Depending on the overall system size, option TOPO may be computationally demanding and, thus, should be reserved only for special cases.

The properties of the generated spring elements can be defined in a preceding SPRI PROP record. In case such a definition does not exist, every new spring will inherit the properties of its corresponding source spring. The Reference Area AR is an exception, as it will always be automatically computed for every spring, based on the type (linear / areal) and geometry of the extrusion.
 Hint
 IMPORTANT: Selecting source springs FROM EDGE / SLN will result to an areal bedding, while selecting springs by number or by group will result to a separate linear bedding for every source spring. The correct computation of the Reference Area depends on that. It is recommended that the properties of the generated spring elements are always validated, to ensure they are the intended ones.

The following example shows an extrusion of the quad elements of group 1 to brics along a straight path defined by a vector:
 GRP 10
 BRIC PROP MNO 1 EXTR TYPE QUAD GRP 1 PATH DIR 0 0 5.0 DIV 10
 Ten layers of bric elements will be generated along the extrusion path. The group number as well as the properties of the new bric elements are defined in advance.
 Extrusion of all quad elements in group 1 to brics along structural line no 5.
 EXTR TYPE QUAD GRP 1 PATH SLN 5 OPT R
 The structural line has been defined in a previous SOFiMSHC run (see SOFIMSHC: SLN). The subdivision of the extrusion matches the sequence of nodes generated along the structural line. Each extrusion layer will be rotated according to the local coordinate system of the line.
 Extrusion of spring elements on a linear support, along structural line 1, to 10 layers of spring elements in vertical direction:
 EXTR TYPE SPRI SLN 1 PATH DIR 0 0 5.0 DIV 10
 The spring elements will automatically be connected with already existing nodes of quad, bric or beam elements. The reference area of the resulting springs is taken by the corresponding source springs and will be scaled according to the path subdivision, yielding an areal support on the extrusion surface.

The table defines the LOFT record – a command that generates intermediate layers of quad or bric elements by “lofting” between a source and a target entity.  In what follows, we describe each parameter (Item), its purpose (Description), how it is specified (Unit), and its default or requirement status (Default).  Wherever relevant, we refer to the additional context on lofting (“See also: TRAN, EXTR”) and the detailed notes provided.

1.  TYPE  
    ‑ Description  
      • Specifies the kind of geometric entity at both the source and the target.  
      • Four permissible literal values (Unit = LIT):  
         – EDGE  : Loft between a sequence of nodes (i.e. a curve) → yields a quad mesh  
         – SLN   : Loft between a structural line → yields a quad mesh  
         – QGRP  : Loft between a group of existing quads → yields a bric mesh  
         – SAR   : Loft between a structural area → yields a bric mesh  
      • Quad-mesh loft only valid if source and target are EDGE or SLN; bric-mesh loft only if they are QGRP or SAR.  
    ‑ Default  
      • “!” denotes this parameter is mandatory  

2.  IDSC (ID of Source)  
    ‑ Description  
      • Numeric or alphanumeric identifier referencing the source curve/mesh or quad group/area.  
    ‑ Unit  
      • “*” indicates an entity reference  
    ‑ Default  
      • “!” mandatory  

3.  IDTG (ID of Target)  
    ‑ Description  
      • Identifier referencing the target curve/mesh or quad group/area for lofting  
    ‑ Unit  
      • “*” entity reference  
    ‑ Default  
      • “!” mandatory  

4.  REFS / REFT (Reference Nodes on Source/Target)  
    ‑ Description  
      • Optional node‐IDs used to manually establish correspondence between source and target if automatic detection fails.  
      • REFS applies to the source, REFT to the target.  
    ‑ Unit  
      • “–” (simple integer node number)  
    ‑ Default  
      • “–” (omitted unless needed)  

5.  DIV (Number of Subdivisions)  
    ‑ Description  
      • Explicitly set the number of intermediate layers between the source and target.  
      • When OPT includes E (edge/line detection), the program auto-sets DIV based on the first matching connecting edge or structural line.  
      • If multiple connecting edges/lines exist, only the first is used; user can override by supplying DIV.  
    ‑ Unit  
      • “–” (integer)  
    ‑ Default  
      • “–” (auto or user‐defined)  

6.  OPT (Interpolation Options)  
    ‑ Description  
      • Three‐character literal field (Unit = LIT3) combining any of:  
         – “–” (dash) : plain linear interpolation if no other guidance is given  
         – E          : detect and use existing connecting nodal sequences, edges or structural lines to guide lofting and subdivisions  
         – Q          : detect existing QUAD elements between source and target and attach new quads to them  
         – B          : detect adjacent BRIC faces between source and target and attach new bric faces  
      • Flags may be concatenated in any order (e.g. “EQ”, “EB”, “EQB”).  
      • Default = EQ, meaning:  
         – E: pick up connecting edges/lines and infer subdivisions  
         – Q: attach new elements to any intervening quads  
      • Note: B can be omitted to avoid the heavier cost of bric‐face searches, since any coincident nodes (even on existing bric faces) will automatically snap.  
    ‑ Default  
      • EQ  

Additional Context and Best Practices  
– Topological Similarity  
   • The loft operation requires that the source and target have the same topology (i.e. the same number of nodes or quads in corresponding sequences).  
   • You can enforce matching nodal sequences ahead of time by coupling lines (SLNS) or areas (SARS) in a prior SOFiMSHC run.  
– Automatic vs. Manual Correspondence  
   • With OPT E, the system looks for shared edges or structural lines; if it cannot find a unique match, supply REFS and REFT to force the pairing.  
– Subdivision Logic  
   • When OPT E detects one or more connecting lines, the subdivisions (DIV) are taken from the first match.  If no match or if a different DIV is wanted, specify DIV explicitly.  
– Node Snapping  
   • Regardless of interpolation mode, newly created nodes in intermediate layers will always snap to any existing node locations if they coincide, ensuring mesh conformity.  

By following the above definitions and guidelines, users can precisely control how quad and bric meshes are lofted between arbitrary source/target entities, leveraging both automated detection and manual overrides where needed.

See also: TRAN, EXTR
 LOFT
 This record allows the generation of quad or bric elements by lofting between a source (IDSC) and a target (IDTG) curve or area.
 A quad mesh can be created by lofting between a source and a target curve (TYPE EDGE / SLN).
 A bric mesh can be created by lofting between a source and a target quad mesh (TYPE QGRP / SAR). In both cases, the source and the target mesh must be topologically similar, such that each element on the source can be associated with an element on the target.
 The generation of topologically similar nodal sequences on curves or quad meshes can be enforced by coupling the respective structural entities in a previous SOFiMSHC run. See SOFIMSHC: SLNS and SOFIMSHC: SARS for further information. Parameters REFS and REFT can be optionally used to help auto-detect and establish such an association.
 By default, the nodes of the intermediate layers will be interpolated linearly between the source and the target mesh. The resulting elements will always snap to any existing elements with coinciding nodes.
 Parameter OPT can be any combination of E, Q and B. Option E enables the detection of con- necting nodal sequences or structural lines, the subdivision and geometry of which will be used as lofting guide curves. Accordingly, Q and B enable the detection of existing QUAD elements and faces of BRIC elements, between the source and the target, that the new elements will be attached to. The option can be deactivated by setting OPT -.
 When OPT E is enabled, the program will try to detect a correspondence between the nodes on the target and the nodes on the source mesh, based on the existence of connecting edges / structural lines. In case this is not possible, the user can always establish a correct association through REFS and REFT.
 The number of subdivisions between the source and target meshes is automatically set, when using OPT E and a connecting edge / structural line is detected. If more than one connecting edges exist, the subdivision of the first detected edge is considered, and the remaining edges are not used at all. The user may also specify an number of subdivisions manually, using parameter DIV. Once again, only detected edges that match the specified DIV will be used.

The number of subdivisions between the source and target meshes is automatically set, when using OPT E and a connecting edge / structural line is detected. If more than one connecting edges exist, the subdivision of the first detected edge is considered, and the remaining edges are not used at all. The user may also specify an number of subdivisions manually, using parameter DIV. Once again, only detected edges that match the specified DIV will be used..
 Note: OPT B may be computationally demanding and its use can in most cases be avoided: The resulting elements will always attach to coinciding existing nodes, including those of BRIC faces. The presence of connecting edges / structural lines and possibly quads, between the source and target meshes, is usually enough to guide the loft operation in the desired way.

Generation of bric elements between the two structural areas 1 and 2:
 GRP 10 BRIC PROP MNO 1 LOFT TYPE SAR 1 2 DIV 10 OPT E
 GRP 10
 The two structural areas 1 and 2 have been coupled in a previous SOFiMSHC run using com- mand SOFIMSHC: SARS, in order to enforce a topologically similar subdivision of quad ele- ments between the two surfaces. Ten layers of bric elements will be generated between the two surfaces. The group number as well as the properties of the new bric elements are defined in advance. Only structural lines with 10 segments will be used as guiding curves, if detected. No reference nodes are provided on the source and target surfaces, so a topological association may fail if no connecting structural lines of 10 segments are detected.

Below is a comprehensive, self-contained description of the MIRR input table. It is organized into functional groups—element selection, spatial filtering, property filtering, and mirror-plane definition—followed by the scaling parameter. Wherever a “Unit” is specified, it refers to either a literal flag (LIT) or metres [m] in global coordinates. Default values are noted in parentheses.  

1. Element-type and index selection  
 • TYPE (LIT; default: ALL)  
   – Specifies which entities to transform by literal name or type keyword. “ALL” applies to every supported item.  
 • FROM (–; default: 1)  
   – Starting index or label in the sequence to be mirrored.  
 • TO (–; default: *)  
   – Ending index or label; “*” means “up to the highest existing index.”  
 • INC (– / LIT; default: 1)  
   – Increment step between consecutive indices in the FROM–TO range.  
   – If “GRP” is specified, FROM and TO define groups; if “FIT,” a fresh sequence of nodes is generated.  
 • DNO (– / LIT; default: 0)  
   – Increment to be applied to newly created node numbers. Setting to “SELF” (0) continues numbering seamlessly.  
 • DNON (–; default: 0)  
   – Increment applied specifically to element-node numbering.  

2. Spatial-region selection  
 • WIDE ([m]; default: 0.0)  
   – A buffer distance from the mirror plane. Only elements whose entire volume lies outside the ±WIDE region about the plane are copied. A zero value prevents mirroring of any element intersecting the plane.  
 • XMIN, YMIN, ZMIN, XMAX, YMAX, ZMAX ([m]; default: –)  
   – Define an axis-aligned bounding box in global coordinates. Only those elements completely contained within the box will be candidates for mirroring.  

3. Property and support filtering  
 • PROP (LIT; default: OLD)  
   – Controls property-based filtering of elements. “OLD” retains existing properties on mirrored copies unless overridden.  
 • FIX (LIT; default: –)  
   – Applies a support (boundary-condition) filter; only elements satisfying the FIX condition are mirrored.  

4. Mirror-plane definition  
   The plane can be defined in one of two equivalent ways:  
 • Hessian form (recommended):  
   – A, B, C (–; default: 0.0 each)  
     · Components of the unit-length normal vector to the mirror plane.  
   – DIST ([m]; default: 0.0)  
     · Signed distance from the coordinate origin to the mirror plane along the normal direction.  
   Equation: A·x + B·y + C·z = DIST  
   Note: In older GENF conventions, this appears as A·x + B·y + C·z + D = 0 with D = –DIST.  
   
 • Three-point definition:  
   – MP1, MP2, MP3 (–; default: –)  
     · Coordinates or node labels of three noncolinear points lying on the mirror plane.  

5. Scaling factor  
 • FAC (–; default: 1.0)  
   – Uniform multiplier applied to the mirrored-point distances from the plane. A value other than 1.0 allows amplified or diminished mirror offsets.  

Additional notes  
– MIRR inherits all other transformation parameters (e.g., translation vectors or rotation angles) from the TRAN command specification.  
– By combining the region selectors (WIDE and the bounding-box limits) with Property/FIX filters, users can target a precise subset of elements for mirroring.  
– The choice between Hessian and three-point definitions offers flexibility: Hessian is compact and numerically stable when the normal is known; three-point input may be more intuitive when the plane is specified via geometry already in the model.

 MIRR
 With MIRR it is possible to generate new nodes or elements by mirroring existing ones from any data base. The mirroring uses a general plane in 3D (not an axis which is only valid in 2D). The equation is of general type, but we recommend to use the Hessian form where:
 (A,B,C) = Normal vector of the plane with length of 1.0
 DIST = Distance of the plane to the origin
 Hint: GENF used the general canonical equation of
 the mirror plane with D = -DIST.
 An other common definition is via the axis interceptions (D=1.0):
 The distance a of the mirrored point may be scaled with an additional factor FAC.
 For a mirroring it is possible to select the elements to be copied by defining a value for WIDE. Only those elements will be copied then, which are fully outside the interval defined by the distance WIDE to the mirroring plane reference point and the absolute distance WIDE. The default of 0.0 will therefore not mirror any elements intersecting the mirroring plane.
 All other parameters are identical to those at TRAN.

The table is a concise, four-column specification of the key input parameters (“Item”) available in the UMSH record for unstructured mesh generation.  It tells you, for each parameter: what it does (“Description”), which physical or literal units it carries (“Unit”), and what value is assumed if you don’t supply one (“Default”).  Taken together with preceding UBND records that define geometry, and following the UMSH header, this table guides you through selecting the right mesh type, controlling the element size, and—when working in 2D—focusing on a particular structural area (SAR).

1.  Item = TYPE  
    Description: “Type of mesh”  
      • QUAD: a 2D unstructured mesh of quadrilateral elements.  
      • TRI: a 2D unstructured mesh of triangular elements.  
      • TET: a 3D unstructured mesh of tetrahedral elements.  
    Unit: LIT (i.e. a literal keyword)  
    Default: none (you must explicitly choose one of QUAD, TRI or TET)

   Notes:  
   - In 2D, pick QUAD for four-sided elements or TRI for three-sided ones.  
   - In 3D, only TET is available, so before you ask for a volume mesh with tetrahedra you must have meshed the boundary surfaces (via UBND) in either quad or tri elements.

2.  Item = HMAX  
    Description: “maximum mesh size on edges (2D)”  
    Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁ (meters, code 1001)  
    Default: ‘*’  

   Notes:  
   - If you leave HMAX blank (asterisk), the code computes it automatically as the maximum edge length of the existing boundary curve (in 2D) or surface (in 3D).  
   - This parameter sets the largest permissible edge length for elements across the domain.

3.  Item = PROG  
    Description: “Progression factor”  
    Unit: none (–)  
    Default: 1.25  

   Notes:  
   - PROG is the growth ratio between neighboring element edges.  
   - A value >1.0 means elements may gradually increase in size moving away from a boundary or feature.  
   - The default 1.25 provides moderate grading; smaller values force more uniform sizing, larger values allow rapid expansion.

4.  Item = SAR  
    Description: “Identifier of a structural area to work on (2D)”  
    Unit: none (–)  
    Default: none (–)  

   Notes:  
   - SAR applies only to 2D mesh generation.  
   - You supply the ID of a previously defined structural area. The UMSH routine then automatically detects and meshes its entire boundary—no UBND records are needed in this path.  
   - This approach handles non-planar surfaces more robustly than the plain UBND-based approach, which assumes a planar domain.

Contextual summary:  
• Before calling UMSH you issue UBND records to lay out your curves (2D) or surfaces (3D).  
• You then specify TYPE to choose element shape and dimension.  
• You may tune element size explicitly with HMAX or leave it to the default auto-computed value.  
• PROG lets you control element size grading.  
• When meshing an existing structural area in 2D, use SAR to skip manual boundary definitions entirely.

See also: UBND
 UMSH
 With the use of UMSH, an unstructured mesh generation in 2D / 3D is possible. This record is followed by a set of UBND records that define the geometry of the domain to be meshed.
 The desired element type can be selected by setting TYPE to QUAD / TRI for a 2D mesh, con- sisting of quadrilateral / triangular elements, or TET for an unstructured 3D mesh generation, using tetrahedral elements. In the case of a volume mesh, the boundary surface of the domain must have been previously meshed, with quadrilateral or triangular elements.
 The maximum element size is controlled by parameter HMAX. If not input is provided, the default HMAX is computed as the maximum edge length of the boundary curve (2D) or surface (3D). The progression factor PROG controls the ratio of the edge length of neigboring elements.
 Finally, SAR is only applicable in 2D mesh generation and refers to a structural area that has been previously defined. With the use of SAR, the boundaries of the surface are automatically detected and, in this case, the use of UBND records is not necessary. This is the only suitable option for meshing non-planar surfaces, as the use of UBND records for 2D meshing assumes a planar geometry.

The table shown is the complete definition of the UBND (U-mesh boundary) record in LS-DYNA, which you must supply whenever you call the UMSH mesher (unless you’ve used UMSH SAR).  It tells DYNA how to pick off one or more closed loops (2D) or surfaces (3D) that form the outer and—optionally—inner boundaries (openings or constraints) of your meshing domain.  You may issue multiple UBND records; however at least one “outer” boundary (TYPE=OUT) record is required for every mesh generation run.

1.  Structure  
    •  Four columns:  
       –  Item: keyword or parameter name  
       –  Description: what that keyword or parameter does or accepts  
       –  Unit: the physical or data‐type unit (LIT for literal, [m] for metres)  
       –  Default: default value or “!” if mandatory  

2.  Fields  

  2.1 TYPE  (unit = LIT, default = ! )  
       –  REQUIRED literal specifying whether this boundary loop/surface is:  
         •  OUT  → external (outer) boundary  
         •  IN   → internal opening (hole)  
         •  CONS → constraining edge (only for 2D meshes)  

       Multiple UBND entries with TYPE=IN or TYPE=CONS are applied in addition to your primary TYPE=OUT record.

  2.2 SEL  (unit = LIT, default = ! )  
       –  REQUIRED literal controlling how “points” on that boundary are picked:  
         •  NODE → select by node IDs (2D only)  
         •  FIT  → select by FIT point IDs (2D only)  
         •  EDGE → select by EDGE set IDs (2D only)  
         •  QREF → select by QUAD reference orient. (3D)  
         •  QGRP → select by QUAD group IDs (3D)  
         •  COOR → select by specifying an interior point coordinate (3D)  
         •  AUTO → automatically detect internal boundaries (only valid with TYPE=IN in 3D)  

  2.3 X, Y, Z  (unit = [m], no default)  
       –  Only used when SEL=COOR  
       –  Define one point (X,Y,Z) that lies strictly inside the surface whose bounding loop you want  
       –  Mesher shoots rays from that point to find the closed loop of edges/faces  

  2.4 N1 … N32  (unit = *, no default)  
       –  List of up to 32 integer identifiers, whose meaning depends on SEL:  
         •  For SEL=NODE: node numbers on the boundary chain  
         •  For SEL=FIT: FIT IDs to follow the FIT‐defined path  
         •  For SEL=EDGE: EDGE set numbers  
         •  For QREF/QGRP: quad face reference or group numbers  
       –  You may use fewer than 32; extra positions are ignored.  

3.  Usage Notes  
   –  If SEL=COOR, you must supply X, Y, Z.  N-fields are then not used.  
   –  If SEL is anything else, X,Y,Z must be blank/dash and you list your boundary IDs in N1..N*.  
   –  In 3D, if you choose AUTO (and TYPE=IN), the mesher seeks all internal “voids” automatically.  
   –  At least one TYPE=OUT/SEL=… record is mandatory.  Additional TYPE=IN or TYPE=CONS are optional.  
   –  The UBND keyword works in concert with UMSH parameters (e.g. UMSH SAR) to define 2D or 3D domains.  

See also UMSH for more on how these boundaries are used to form the triangulation or tetrahedral mesh.

See also: UMSH
 UBND
 With UBND, the boundary of a surface or volume is defined, that forms a domain to be meshed using UMSH. Multiple records are possible, that act additionally to the previous ones. Unless parameter UMSH SAR has been used, at least one UBND record, defining the outer boundary of the domain, is required for every mesh generation.

For 2D meshing, all nodes on the boundary must be co-planar, otherwise the mesh generation may fail or result to a distorted mesh. For non-planar surface meshing, UMSH SAR is available.
 Option TYPE specifies whether it is an external (OUT) or internal (IN) boundary that is being defined. For 2D meshes, it is also possible to define constraining boundaries (CONS), for example prescribed nodes or edges.
 A definition of a boundary is possible in various ways, through parameter SEL. In order to
 define a 2D domain, a list of up to 32 nodes (per entry) on the periphery may be provided, by defining SEL NODE and providing the node numbers in the fields N1 – N32. Their input must be in the correct sequential order, while for TYPE OUT / IN it is assumed that they form a closed curve – no repetition of the first node at the end of the sequence is required. The boundary segments between the nodes are assumed to be linear. For constraining boundaries, TYPE CONS, individual nodes are considered, without forming a closed boundary.
 An alternative option is the use of SEL FIT, which behaves similarly to SEL NODE, with the addition that a nodal sequence will be followed, if detected, instead of assuming no subdivision between the nodes.
 Finally, with SEL EDGE a list of boundary edges may be provided, the identifiers of which – numbers or literals – are then specified via N1 – N32. In this case, the sequence of the edges is not important, as they are automatically sorted in a sequential node order. However they have to form a closed curve when defining an outer or inner boundary.
 It should be noted that the combination of different SEL options for a 2D outer boundary is not possible. Multiple TYPE OUT entries will be taken into consideration, however they must all refer to the same type of boundary description.
 GRP 10
 QUAD PROP MNO 1 UMSH TYPE QUAD HMAX 0.5 PROG 1.5 UBND TYPE OUT SEL NODE N1 1 2 3 4 $ Outer boundary $ UBND TYPE OUT SEL NODE N1 5 6 7 8 $ Outer boundary (continued) $ $ UBND TYPE OUT SEL EDGE N1 11 12 13 14 $ $ Not possible $ UBND TYPE IN SEL NODE N1 5 6 7 8 $ First Hole $ UBND TYPE IN SEL EDGE N1 15 16 17 18 $ Second Hole $

For a 3D domain, the boundary surface may be defined by a list of structural area numbers, using SEL QREF, or group numbers, using SEL QGRP. In both cases, the QUAD elements belonging to the specified selection are considered as boundary elements of the volume. The QUAD elements may be triangular or quadrilateral and must form a closed surface. As opposed to 2D, different SEL options may be combined in order to define a 3D outer boundary.
 If SEL QREF is used and only N1 is provided, an automatic volume detection will be attempted on the positive direction of the specified structural area, or to the negative one if the value of N1 is negative (SOFIMSHC: SAR). The detected boundary surface will be the one that encloses the minimum volume at the specified direction.
 In a similar way, using SEL COOR, an automatic detection of a boundary surface is possible by providing the coordinates of a point that is internal to the defined volume (TYPE OUT) or void (TYPE IN). In this case, X, Y and Z must be defined. The detected volume is, again, the minimum possible.
 All of the above options apply both in defining an outer (TYPE OUT) or an inner boundary (TYPE IN). Additionally, the automatic detection of all internal voids is also possible, after an external boundary has been defined, using TYPE IN SEL AUTO.
 Hint
 With the use of options COOR or AUTO, BRIC faces on the boundary of an existing adjacent volume are automatically detected. Therefore, the presence of QUAD elements at this region is not necessary.
 Definition of a volume with inner voids:
 GRUP 10
 BRIC PROP MNR 1 UMSH TYPE TET UBND TYPE OUT SEL QREF N1 21 22 23 24 $ Outer boundary $ UBND TYPE OUT SEL QGRP N1 1 2 3 4 $ Outer boundary (continued) $ UBND TYPE IN SEL AUTO $ Detect inner voids automatically $

BRIC PROP MNR 1 UMSH TYPE TET UBND TYPE OUT SEL QREF N1 21 22 23 24 $ Outer boundary $ UBND TYPE OUT SEL QGRP N1 1 2 3 4 $ Outer boundary (continued) $ UBND TYPE IN SEL AUTO $ Detect inner voids automatically $.
 Definition of a volume by internal coordinate:
 GRUP 11
 BRIC PROP MNR 1 UMSH TYPE TET UBND TYPE OUT SEL COOR X 0.1 0.1 0.1 $ Internal coordinate $

The table below defines the syntax and semantics of the INTF record used to generate interface elements (currently only spring‐type) between a specified structural area of QUAD elements and its surrounding mesh or adjacent element types. It is organized into four columns – Item (the keyword), Description (its purpose), Unit (physical units, if any) and Default (value assumed when the entry is omitted).

1.  OPT  
    •  Description: Option flags for controlling INTF command execution.  
    •  Allowed Value: CONT  
        – CONT: “Continuation record” – tells the parser to hold execution of the interface‐generation until one or more additional INTF lines (with OPT=CONT) have been read. Use when multiple areas share a common face and must be processed as a single interface.  
    •  Unit: –  
    •  Default: none  

2.  TYPE  
    •  Description: Specifies the kind of interface elements to create.  
    •  Allowed Values (literal): SPRI  
        – SPRI: spring elements (axial + lateral springs)  
    •  Unit: LIT (literal string)  
    •  Default: SPRI  

3.  REFT  
    •  Description: Defines how to select the reference QUAD elements that will be decoupled.  
    •  Allowed Values (literal):  
        – SAR   (select by structural area or region number)  
        – QREF  (select by explicit QUAD element list)  
        – QGRP  (select by QUAD element group)  
    •  Unit: LIT  
    •  Default: SAR  

4.  NO  
    •  Description: Identifier of the reference region, element set or group. A leading “+” or “–” specifies on which side of the QUAD layer the interface springs are generated.  
    •  Unit: –  
    •  Default: “!”  (no default; this field is mandatory)  

5.  D  
    •  Description: Thickness of the interface layer (gap) created by shrinking the reference QUAD elements inward. Primarily used for mesh‐connectivity checks; the gap is not intended as part of the physical model and may introduce distorted elements if nonzero.  
    •  Unit: [m]  
    •  Default: 0.0  

6.  MNO  
    •  Description: Material number assigned to the generated interface elements. This number must correspond to a predefined material record that supplies the non‐linear spring properties.  
    •  Unit: –  
    •  Default: none  

7.  CP  
    •  Description: Axial (normal) spring stiffness constant of the interface springs. The software automatically computes spring element geometry (direction and reference area).  
    •  Unit: [kN/m³]  
    •  Default: 0.0  

8.  CT  
    •  Description: Lateral (shear) spring stiffness constant of the interface springs.  
    •  Unit: [kN/m³]  
    •  Default: 0.0  

Usage Notes:  
- To build a continuous interface over adjacent areas, issue multiple INTF records with OPT=CONT. The command only executes once the final (no-CONT) record is read.  
- TYPE is currently limited to SPRI; future releases may support alternative interface element types.  
- REFT/NO define the “reference” QUAD face to decouple; the sign on NO determines whether the interface is generated on the outside (“+”) or inside (“–”) of that face.  
- D should remain zero for physical modeling; nonzero values serve only to reveal mesh connectivity.  
- CP and CT default to zero (a purely kinematic coupling). Nonzero values must be set to model stiffness or contact compliance.

The table below defines the syntax of the RSET record in the input deck. RSET records are used to group and label sets of results (forces, displacements, stresses, etc.) for later post‐processing. Each row in the table corresponds to one keyword or field that may appear in a single RSET record; the columns specify its name (“Item”), its meaning (“Description”), the kind of data it holds (“Unit”) and whether it has a default value or is mandatory (“Default”).

Columns  
• Item: the literal keyword that appears in the RSET record.  
• Description: a short, human‐readable explanation of what the keyword represents.  
• Unit: the data type or field width. “LITn” means a literal text field of up to n characters. For numeric fields there is either “–” (free format) or explicit physical units.  
• Default: “–” indicates no default (the field is optional and blank if unused); “!” indicates that the field is mandatory and must be supplied.

Rows  
1. ID  
   – Description: Identifier  
   – Unit: LIT4 (up to 4 characters)  
   – Default: none (this field must be provided to name the result set)  

2. SET  
   – Description: Primary type of results (e.g. NODE, BEAM, SPRI_RES)  
   – Unit: LIT8 (up to 8 characters)  
   – Default: “!” (mandatory)

3. ITEM  
   – Description: Specific item of results within the set (e.g. PZ, VZ, SIGX)  
   – Unit: LIT8  
   – Default: “!” (mandatory)

4. UNIT  
   – Description: Unit of the results (e.g. “kN”, “mm”)  
   – Unit: LIT8  
   – Default: “–” (optional but recommended for clarity)

5. NO  
   – Description: Element or node number that this result refers to  
   – Unit: free‐format integer (“–”)  
   – Default: “–” (optional in some contexts, but usually required to locate the result)

6. NG  
   – Description: Group or material number (optional qualifier)  
   – Unit: free format (“–”)  
   – Default: “–”

7. X  
   – Description: Abscissa along beam elements, if the set is BEAM (0 ≤ X ≤ 1)  
   – Unit: [m] (subscript “1001” indicates internal unit code)  
   – Default: “–” (only used for beam results)

8. OPT  
   – Description: Options (single‐letter flags or modifiers, e.g. S for new table line)  
   – Unit: Lit (single literal)  
   – Default: “–”

9. TITL  
   – Description: Designation or title for the result set block (a descriptive caption)  
   – Unit: LIT32 (up to 32 characters)  
   – Default: “–”

Notes on Usage  
• Any RSET definition begins with an ID field to name the set. Subsequent RSET lines may repeat the ID to append items.  
• SET and ITEM are required: they tell the solver both what type of result to extract (SET) and which component or stress (ITEM).  
• You may use the UNIT field to convert or label output in specific units; otherwise default global units apply.  
• The NO field ties each result item back to a specific node or element number.  
• Beam results often use the X field to specify a location along the element axis.  
• OPT S can be inserted to force a page break or new line in the results table (up to 29 lines per table).  
• TITL allows grouping several RSET definitions under a common heading in the output.  

By following this schema, you can build compound result sets, apply simple formulas (using ITEM names prefixed with “=”), and drive the post‐processing tools (MAXIMA, ELLA) to extract exactly the reactions, stresses, or internal forces you need.

See also: SPRI
 INTE
 INTF
 Using record INTF it is possible to generate elements with bedding or coupling properties, on a structural area, known as interface elements. Technically, the QUAD elements of the specified structural area are decoupled from the surrounding structure and a layer of spring elements is introduced, in order to bind the corresponding nodes with the specified type of kinematic coupling.
 This option is primarily intended for modeling contact conditions between or within volumes, such as the case of a retaining wall with its surrounding soil or the contact area between two materials. However, the cases of use are not limited to volumetric domains, since the generation of interface elements is also possible between the specified structural area and other types of adjacent elements, such as QUAD and BEAM elements.
 In case that multiple areas are involved in the interface generation for one distinct volume, these interfaces must be generated simultaneously. This refers to areas that share common edges, forming a continuous surface, and the interface generation is performed on the same side of the surface. For this purpose, parameter OPT CONT must be used, in order to continue with the input of the following areas that form the common surface. The command execution is postponed as long as a new INTF OPT CONT record is added, or a different command is issued. However, the group of the generated springs is still allowed to be changed, by inserting a GRP record between the consecutive INTF records.
 Parameter TYPE can be used in order to specify the type of interface elements. Currently, only spring elements are supported.
 Parameter REFT is used to specify the way that the reference QUAD elements, at the interface position, will be selected.
 Parameter NO is an identifier for the reference region or group, as specified by parameter REFT. A +/- sign can be used to select on which side of the QUAD elements the interface will be generated.
 With parameter D, it is possible to specify the thickness of the interface layer, which currently forms a gap between the reference region and the detached elements, by shrinking the ele- ments. This gap is mostly intended for mesh connectivity inspection, after the interface gener- ation, and its presence in the computational model is generally not desired. It should be noted that the introduction of a gap may result in distorted, ill-conditioned elements.

This description breaks down the EXPO input‐table—used to export model data from the database into SOFiMSHA (or related) input files—into its constituent items, their meaning, units, defaults, and interactions with other records.

1. Record Purpose  
   • EXPO controls writing out node, element, and boundary data into an external file suitable for SOFiMSHA or related preprocessors (e.g. DOLFYN).  
   • If no file name is provided, the data are appended to the last‐opened file; otherwise a file called “project_SYS.DAT” is created by default.  
   • The numerical units in the output follow the current UNIE setting from the PAGE record. The textual names follow the active CADINP input language.

2. Table Columns  
   • Item: the keyword or parameter in the EXPO record.  
   • Description: what data this item specifies or controls.  
   • Unit: data type or unit designator (– means unitless; LitNN denotes a literal string of up to NN characters).  
   • Default: value assumed if this item is omitted.

3. Items in Detail  
   a) OPT  (Unit: – / LIT ; Default: 63)  
     • Acts as a bitmask selecting which categories of data to export. Multiple bits may be OR’ed to combine outputs.  
     • Bit codes:  
       – 1    → Nodes and Constraints  
       – 2    → Springs, Dampers and Boundaries  
       – 4    → Beam, Cable and Truss Elements  
       – 8    → Plane elements (QUAD)  
       – 16   → Volume elements (BRIC)  
     • Default value 63 (binary 111111) typically turns on all supported export categories, including any future extensions (e.g. code 32).  
     • In addition to the numeric OPT flags, the same keyword may be used with textual suffixes to generate DOLFYN‐specific mesh files:  
         • OPT DOLG: produce finite‐volume meshes (.DGE) in ASCII (PA), dual–cell (DA) or VTK formats (PAT/DAT).  
         • OPT DOLF: emit DOLFYN preprocessor files (.VRT, .CEL, .BND).  
         • OPT VTK: export surface geometry as a .VTK file for third‐party visualization.

   b) TO  (Unit: Lit96 ; Default: “*”)  
     • Name (and path) of the file to receive the exported data.  
     • Up to 96 characters.  
     • “*” means append to existing file or create the default “project_SYS.DAT” if none exists.

   c) PASS  (Unit: Lit16 ; Default: none)  
     • Password string (≤16 characters) to open the database.  
     • Optional: omit if the database is unprotected.

4. Usage Notes  
   • The combination of OPT settings governs exactly which element types end up in the output. Users can craft custom bit patterns to export, for example, only beams and shells (4+8 = 12).  
   • When generating DOLFYN or VTK outputs, specifying OPT as a keyword with a suffix is mandatory; numeric bit masks alone do not create those specialized formats.  
   • Because the file name (TO) is literal, it must include the proper extension to match the format (e.g. “.DAT”, “.DGE”, “.VTK”).  
   • Always verify that the active UNIE and CADINP settings match the target solver’s expectations to avoid unit mismatches or language‐dependent item names.

EXPO
 With the record EXPO you may export the nodes and elements in the database to an input file for SOFiMSHA. This may be useful in special cases.
 If the file name is not specified the data will be appended to the most recently defined file or a file with the name project_SYS.DAT is generated.
 The units of the values will be set to the current setting of UNIE from record PAGE. The input language of the record and item names in the new file will be the same as the current CADINP input.
 With the input OPT DOLG the finite volume mesh for the program DOLFYN will be generated (.DGE). As identifier for volumes and boundaries the primary group number will be used. For a 2D system the QUADs and their edges will be extruded to volumes and faces with a thickness of 1 m. There are the following options:
 DOLG:PA Create the primal mesh as ASCII-file (equivalent to the FE mesh) DOLG:DA Create the dual mesh as ASCII-file (this is the polyhedral mesh) DOLG:PAT Create also a VTK-File of the generated geometry DOLG:DAT Create also a VTK-File of the generated geometry DOLG:PB Create the primal mesh as binary-file (not yet supported) DOLG:DB Create the dual mesh as binary-file (not yet supported)
 With the input OPT DOLF the files for the DOLFYN preprocessor will be generated (.VRT, .CEL, .BND). These are also required for thr VTK-Export in DOLFYN.
 With the input OPT VTK it is possible to export a .VTK file, so that the system can be visualized with a third-party software. Currently, only surfaces can be exported.

The table presented is a concise summary of the parameters available on the IMPO record in SOFiMSHA, which controls how external geometry or result files are brought into the current model.  Each row corresponds to one keyword, and the columns give:

• Item  
  The name of the keyword as it appears on the IMPO record.  

• Description  
  A brief explanation of the role played by that keyword in the import process.  

• Unit  
  The expected data type or physical unit.  Where a “Lit” notation appears (e.g. Lit32), it denotes a character string of up to that many characters.  A dash (—) indicates a pure integer or real value without an associated physical unit.  

• Default  
  The value assumed if the keyword is omitted.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  

1. OPT  
   • Description: Specifies which part of the external file to read in.  For example, node and element definitions, mesh faces, or post-processing results such as stresses or temperatures.  
   • Unit: Lit32 (up to 32 characters)  
   • Default: “*” (asterisk, meaning “all available data”).  

2. FROM  
   • Description: The name (and path, if needed) of the file to be imported.  Recognizes extensions like .CDB, .STL, .DGF, .FVI, etc.  
   • Unit: Lit96 (up to 96 characters)  
   • Default: “!” (an exclamation mark, indicating that no file has been specified).  

3. PASS  
   • Description: Password string for reading protected files.  Some proprietary formats may require authentication.  
   • Unit: Lit16 (up to 16 characters)  
   • Default: “–” (dash, meaning “no password”).  

4. DEFO  
   • Description: Load-case number whose nodal deformations will be applied to the imported geometry.  This allows one to bring in a deformed configuration rather than the undeformed mesh.  
   • Unit: — (integer)  
   • Default: “–” (dash, meaning “no deformation case selected,” i.e. import the undeformed shape).  

5. FACT  
   • Description: Scalar multiplier applied to the deformations from load case DEFO.  Useful for exaggerating or scaling back displacements during import.  
   • Unit: — (real number)  
   • Default: 1.0  

6. XREF  
   • Description: X-coordinate of a reference point in the global system.  All imported nodes are shifted so that the master node (if one is generated) sits at this point.  
   • Unit: [m]_1001  
   • Default: 0.0  

7. YREF  
   • Description: Y-coordinate of the reference point (analogous to XREF).  
   • Unit: [m]_1001  
   • Default: 0.0  

8. ZREF  
   • Description: Z-coordinate of the reference point (analogous to XREF/YREF).  
   • Unit: [m]_1001  
   • Default: 0.0  

9. PHIZ  
   • Description: Rotation angle, in degrees, about the global Z-axis.  The entire imported body is rotated by PHIZ around the point (XREF, YREF, ZREF).  
   • Unit: [°]_5  
   • Default: 0.0  

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  

How these parameters work together:  

• If you want to pull in an STL file and place it at an offset location, you would set FROM='myPart.stl', OPT='facet', XREF/YREF/ZREF to your desired origin, and PHIZ if you need an in-plane rotation.  
• To import a deformed shape from an existing SOFiSTiK database (.CDB), you would select that database via FROM, pick the load case in DEFO, and optionally scale the displacements with FACT.  
• If your external file is protected, you can supply PASS.  
• Omitting an optional keyword leaves its default in place, usually meaning “do not shift,” “no deformation,” or “import everything.”  

In a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) setting, this table would serve as one of the ground-truth chunks: any user query about how to position imported geometry, apply preloaded deformations, or select subsets of data can be routed to the exact row(s) above, ensuring accurate and context-aware answers.

The import database remains active until another database is selected or a record with record name IMPO only switches back to the primary database. With DEFO a load case number may be selected. With IMPO it is also possible to import very general data, including results, to the database. This generic import interface is reserved for use with import files, that are generated automati- cally by specifically developed and tailored software tools, e.g., for the purpose of visualisation of external data using SOFiSTiK postprocessors.
 Hint
 This is a low-level interface. No checks regarding quality and consistency of the imported data are carried out. Usage of this data within downstream SOFiSTiK processing work- flows is not intended and not asserted.
 • At OPT a literal is defined starting with the name of a structure described in the data base description (CDBASE.CHM) following with a slash and the load case number. Up to six default integer values may be added separated by a : character.
 • At FROM an optional literal may be specified containing the list of the defined items sepa- rated by commas.

Literals are possible if the structure in the database is marked for those possibilities.

The input table defines two configurable items (“OPT” and “VAL”) for the ECHO record in a finite‐element system. Each row in the table has four columns:  
• Item – the parameter name.  
• Description – the meaning of the parameter and, where applicable, its allowed literals.  
• Unit – always “LIT” (a literal string).  
• Default – the default literal if the user does not supply a value.  

1. OPT  
   – Purpose: Selects which subset of system data is printed or stored. OPT can filter by element type, properties, groups, statistics, or a combination thereof.  
   – Allowed Literals:  
     • MAT: material properties only.  
     • SECT: cross‐section definitions.  
     • NODE: node coordinates and parameters.  
     • QUAD: two‐dimensional (2‐D) element properties.  
     • BRIC: three‐dimensional (3‐D) element properties.  
     • BEAM: bending beams and piles, truss and cable elements.  
     • BOUN: spring and boundary element definitions.  
     • SYST: overall system values, lists of groups, cross‐section types, and element summaries.  
     • STAT: analysis statistics (counts, failure checks, load combinations, etc.).  
     • FULL: equivalent to specifying all of the above (MAT, SECT, NODE, QUAD, BRIC, BEAM, BOUN, SYST, STAT).  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: FULL (i.e., if OPT is omitted, the system outputs every available category).  

2. VAL  
   – Purpose: Controls the verbosity or “extent” of the output selected by OPT (or the default). It modulates whether no output, standard information, or progressively more detailed data is shown.  
   – Allowed Literals:  
     • NO: suppresses any output (useful to store statistics internally without printing).  
     • YES: regular, minimal output (default level if VAL is omitted).  
     • FULL: extended output, including additional tables or fields beyond the customary printout.  
     • EXTR: most extended output, adding even deeper details (e.g., per‐element lifecycle data, reinforcements, group ordering, etc.).  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: YES  

Additional Context (ECHO record behavior):  
- The record name ECHO must be repeated verbatim for every dataset to avoid confusion with similarly named records (for example, NODE).  
- If the system runs without errors, a VAL of YES yields the default standard output.  
- An alternative mode is to supply SYST as a numeric bit pattern instead of the literal NO/YES/FULL/EXTR. In that mode, individual bits (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …, 524 288) enable or disable very fine‐grained statistics (primary groups, beam/truss counts, area/volume element stats, ordering by section or material, reinforcement summaries, nodal masses, life‐cycle assessment data, tendon sums, design‐element details, secondary group orderings, database‐only calculations, etc.).  
- When SYST‐bit mode is used, all calculated statistics are also saved into database arrays (e.g., GRP_MASS, SCT_MASS, MAT_MASS, GRP_REIN, SCT_REIN), with index 0 holding the total sums.  

By combining OPT and VAL (or using the numerical SYST option), a user can tailor the ECHO record to print or store exactly the subset and level of detail needed for downstream postprocessing or archiving.

The table in question defines the complete set of output parameters for each four-node (quad) plane element when the analysis option ECHO QUAD YES (the default setting) is enabled.  Each row in the table corresponds to one finite element; the columns capture its identification, geometry, material assignment, thickness properties, foundation stiffness, orientation, and any special thickness variations.  Below is a column-by-column description of the information you will find in the RAG vector store for plane elements:

1. Grp  
   • This integer labels the “group” or subset to which the element belongs.  Grouping is typically used to collect elements with common characteristics (e.g., same loading, boundary conditions, or post-processing filter).

2. Number  
   • The unique element identifier (element number) in the global mesh.  This is the primary key by which all other element data are referenced.

3. Node  (four columns)  
   • Four consecutive columns list the node numbers of the element’s corner points in counter-clockwise (or user-defined) order.  Together, these four node IDs define the element’s geometry in the global mesh.

4. MNo  
   • Material number index.  This integer points to the material definition (elastic, plastic, composite, etc.) assigned to the element.  It ties the element to its elastic constants, density, orthotropic directions, and any non-linear material parameters.

5. t [m]  
   • The nominal (constant) thickness of the element, in meters.  For isotropic, constant-thickness shells or plates, this single value fully defines the out-of-plane dimension.

6. C [kN/m³]  
   • Elastic foundation stiffness (Winkler foundation), expressed in kilonewtons per cubic meter.  A nonzero C indicates that the element is supported by a continuous spring foundation; zero means no elastic foundation.

7. Direction of the local x-axis  
   • A reference value (often an angle or nodal vector ID) that defines the orientation of the element’s local x-axis in the global coordinate system.  This controls the direction in which orthotropic material properties TX and TXY are applied.

8. Orthotropic thicknesses (TX, TY, TXY, TD)  
   • Four entries (each in meters) that define the actual thickness in the local x-direction (TX), local y-direction (TY), shear-coupling direction (TXY), and an optional “thickness deviation” term (TD).  These appear only if the element’s thickness deviates from the nominal value t or if true orthotropic effects are activated.

9. Variable thickness t1–t4  
   • When an element is defined with node-based thickness interpolation, these four values give the thickness at each of the four corner nodes.  The element’s thickness then varies linearly across its surface.  These fields only appear if the input model prescribes different thicknesses at the element’s nodes.

In practice, once ECHO QUAD YES is set, your post-processing routine will generate one line per quad element, containing: group index, element ID, node connectivities, material linkage, thickness data, foundation stiffness, orientation flag, plus any orthotropic or variable thickness details.  This structured output enables efficient storage in a vector database and supports rapid retrieval of geometric, material, and thickness properties during RAG-based queries or downstream automated checks.

The table in question is the standard output list produced when “ECHO BEAM YES” (the default setting) is active in a finite‐element or structural analysis program. It summarizes all of the bending beams and piles that have been defined with the BEAM record, and—once beam sections have also been defined with the BSEC record—it appends section‐specific details such as section type, principal axis orientation, and section position. Below is a detailed walk‐through of each column and how it is used.  

1. Grp (Group Number)  
   • An integer that identifies which group the beam or pile belongs to. Groups can be used to collect beams of the same material, cross‐section, or loading conditions.  
   • Group numbers permit selective post-processing (e.g., plotting, design checks) on a subset of the model.  

2. Number (Beam Number)  
   • A unique identifier for each beam or pile element.  
   • Corresponds to the BEAM record’s element ID.  

3. Node  
   • Lists the node numbers at the start and/or end of the beam.  
   • In a two‐node line element, both the start‐node and end‐node are shown; for single‐node/pile elements you will typically only see one entry.  

4. x [m] (Distance Along Beam)  
   • A floating‐point value giving the distance (in meters) from the beam’s local origin (its “beginning”) to the present output station.  
   • For uniformly discretized beams this may correspond to the node spacing; for variable‐   
     cross‐section beams it may align with section change points defined in BSEC.  

5. NoS (Cross‐Section Number)  
   • An integer index into the list of cross‐sections defined by BSEC.  
   • An “i” flag (e.g. NoS = 3i) indicates that interpolation between neighboring section definitions is allowed at that station, rather than taking a single exact section.  

6. NoP (Bedding/Profile Reference Axis Number)  
   • References the bedding or support profile definition (e.g. Winkler‐spring constants, layered soil profile) associated with that beam segment.  
   • Ensures that correct subgrade reaction or pile‐soil interaction parameters are applied.  

7. Hinges  
   • A code or combination of letters that denote which internal hinges (release conditions) are present at that station.  
   • See the BEAM record for the specific abbreviations (e.g., Mx for moment release about the x‐axis, Vz for shear‐force release in the z direction, etc.).  

8. Direction of Local y‐Axis  
   • A vector or angle specification that defines how the beam’s local y‐axis is oriented in global space.  
   • Essential for correctly interpreting bending stiffness, section orientation, and applied loads.  

9. Beta-y/z (Buckling Length Coefficients)  
   • Two values, βy and βz, giving the effective‐length (buckling) multipliers for bending about the local y‐ and z‐axes, respectively.  
   • These coefficients feed into stability checks (e.g., Euler buckling calculations) for each beam segment.  

How This Table Is Generated  
• When a BEAM definition is processed, the program immediately outputs basic data (Grp, Number, Node, x).  
• After BSEC definitions are read, each beam output line is augmented with NoS, NoP, hinge settings, local axis directions, and β-coefficients.  
• Users can cross-reference BEAM and BSEC records in the input deck to trace back to material properties, section geometry, and assigned boundary or hinge conditions.  

This detailed description will aid in indexing the column semantics and relationships when ingesting the table into a RAG‐based vector store, enabling precise retrieval of beam characteristics, section properties, and stability parameters for downstream queries and design checks.

The “Elapsed Analysis Time” table summarizes, in a step-by-step breakdown, how long each phase of the preprocessing and system-generation pipeline takes—both in terms of CPU time (“CPU”) and wall-clock time (“WCT”).  It is emitted whenever the ECHO STAT FULL command is issued in URSULA (that is, when the statistics button is activated).  The table’s primary purpose is to let users gauge which steps dominate runtime, to help guide performance tuning or resource allocation.

Table Structure  
• Column 1 (implicit): Task description—each major processing stage is listed in order of execution.  
• Column 2 (“CPU = X.XX”): CPU time in seconds, measured as the sum of actual processor cores’ busy time.  
• Column 3 (“WCT = Y”): Wall-clock time in seconds—real elapsed time as seen by the user, including I/O waits and any parallelism overhead.

Detailed Breakdown of Each Row  
1. Initialise the system  
   – CPU = 8.33 s, WCT = 8 s  
   – This is the heaviest single step. It covers loading core libraries, allocating data structures, reading environment parameters, and any one-time setup routines. Its CPU-to-WCT ratio (~1.04) suggests nearly full CPU utilization with minimal idle time.

2. ASCII Input with CADINP and processing  
   – CPU = 0.44 s, WCT = 0 s  
   – Ingests user-supplied ASCII definitions via CADINP, parses them, and converts to internal representations. The very low WCT recorded (rounded to zero) indicates this step completes in under 0.5 s.

3. Saving data from mesh generation  
   – CPU = 0.03 s, WCT = 0 s  
   – Writes out intermediate mesh data to disk or to an in-memory database. I/O here is trivial, hence both times are negligible.

4. Postprocessing of the mesh generation  
   – CPU = 0.06 s, WCT = 0 s  
   – Applies filters, computes element connectivity, and prepares data for downstream stages. Again, completes in under half a second.

5. Printout of generated system  
   – CPU = 0.08 s, WCT = 0 s  
   – Formats and outputs the assembled system matrix, boundary conditions, and load vectors. The quick turnaround reflects small output size or fast I/O channel.

6. Optimum node numbering  
   – CPU = 0.08 s, WCT = 0 s  
   – Applies a reordering algorithm (e.g., reverse Cuthill-McKee) to minimize bandwidth. Fast enough that wall-clock time rounds to zero.

7. Totals  
   – CPU = 9.66 s, WCT = 9 s  
   – Summation of all CPU times yields 9.66 s of processing effort. The wall-clock total is 9 s, showing that overall the workflow is CPU-bound with minimal I/O or idle latency.

Contextual Notes  
• All times are reported in seconds; WCT values under 0.5 s are displayed as zero.  
• Discrepancies between CPU and WCT arise from parallel execution on multi-core hosts or brief I/O stalls.  
• Activating “ECHO STAT FULL” in URSULA is the only way to print this analysis table; it is primarily used for performance diagnostics and benchmarking.
